title: Hindu Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Vedic and Puranic tradition mapped as a relationship graph: the formless Brahman and the Trimurti, the devas and asuras, the avatars of Vishnu, and the heroes of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.

stories.title: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk
stories.summary: Gods and asuras, made allies by necessity, wound the serpent Vasuki around Mount Mandara and churned the milk-ocean for amrita, the nectar of immortality. Vishnu became the tortoise Kurma to bear the sinking mountain. The churning yielded Lakshmi, Airavata, the physician Dhanvantari with the nectar pot — and a world-ending poison that Shiva drank, holding it in his throat, which turned blue.

stories.title: Indra Slays the Dragon Vritra
stories.summary: The serpent Vritra coiled around the mountains and swallowed the world's waters, and the earth withered. Fortified with soma, Indra rode out with the vajra forged from a sage's bones, split the dragon open, and released the seven rivers. It is the central heroic act of the Rig Veda — and later texts add a shadow, making Vritra a brahmin whose killing stains Indra with guilt.

stories.title: Daksha's Sacrifice and the Death of Sati
stories.summary: Daksha held a great sacrifice and pointedly invited every god but his son-in-law Shiva. His daughter Sati came uninvited, heard her husband insulted before the assembly, and gave up her body in the sacrificial fire. Shiva's grief became Virabhadra, who tore the sacrifice apart; carrying Sati's body across the world, Shiva scattered the pieces that became the Shakti Pithas.

stories.title: Parvati Wins Shiva
stories.summary: Sati was reborn as Parvati, daughter of the mountain king. Finding Shiva lost in meditation and unreachable by beauty, she put aside her ornaments and undertook austerities so fierce that the gods trembled. Shiva came disguised as an old brahmin to mock him to her face; when she defended him without wavering, he revealed himself and took her as his wife.

stories.title: Shiva Burns the God of Love
stories.summary: The gods needed Shiva to father a son who could kill Tarakasura, so they sent Kamadeva to shoot the meditating ascetic with a flower arrow. Shiva opened his third eye and burned him to ash on the spot. Rati's grief won a partial reprieve: Kama was restored, but bodiless — Ananga, the limbless one, who is felt and never seen.

stories.title: The Birth and Beheading of Ganesha
stories.summary: Parvati formed a boy from the substance of her own body and set him to guard her door. Shiva, returning and refused entry by a child he had never seen, struck off his head. Facing Parvati's fury, he sent his hosts for the head of the first creature they found facing north — an elephant — and the boy rose again as Ganesha, lord of beginnings, worshipped before every other god.

stories.title: The Birth of Kartikeya and the Fall of Taraka
stories.summary: Tarakasura held a boon that only a son of Shiva could kill him — and Shiva, widowed and ascetic, seemed certain never to have one. Shiva's fiery seed proved too much for Agni and then for Ganga to carry; set down in a reed-bed, it became six infants nursed by the six Krittika stars and fused into the six-faced Kartikeya, who took command of the divine army and killed Taraka.

stories.title: The Descent of the Ganges
stories.summary: King Bhagiratha's ancestors had been burned to ash and could not pass on without the touch of heaven's river. He won Ganga's descent by austerity — but her fall would have shattered the earth, so Shiva caught her in his matted hair and let her out gently. She followed Bhagiratha's chariot to the sea and freed the dead.

stories.title: Durga Slays the Buffalo Demon
stories.summary: Mahishasura's boon made him proof against every male being, and he drove the gods from heaven. Their massed rage streamed out as light and took the form of a woman: Durga, armed by every god at once and riding a lion. After nine nights of battle she pinned the shape-shifting buffalo and beheaded him — the story kept alive each year at Navaratri and Durga Puja.

stories.title: Kali and the Blood-Seed Demon
stories.summary: Every drop of Raktabija's blood that touched the ground became another Raktabija, and the goddess's army was drowning in copies. From Durga's furious brow sprang Kali, black and gaunt, who spread her tongue across the battlefield and drank each drop before it fell. Her victory dance nearly broke the world until Shiva lay in her path and she stopped.

stories.title: Matsya and the Great Flood
stories.summary: A tiny fish begged King Manu for protection, then outgrew every vessel until Manu understood he was holding Vishnu. Warned of the coming deluge, Manu loaded a boat with the seeds of life and the seven sages; Matsya, now vast and horned, towed the boat through the flood and recovered the Vedas from the demon who had stolen them.

stories.title: Varaha Lifts the Earth
stories.summary: The daitya Hiranyaksha dragged the earth to the floor of the cosmic ocean. Vishnu took the form of a colossal boar, dived after her, fought the demon for a thousand years, and killed him — then rose with the earth goddess balanced on his tusks and set her afloat once more.

stories.title: Prahlada and the Man-Lion
stories.summary: Hiranyakashipu's boon made him unkillable by man or beast, indoors or out, by day or night, on earth or in air, by any weapon — and he demanded worship as god. His own son Prahlada worshipped Vishnu instead and survived every torture. At dusk on a threshold, Narasimha burst from a pillar, laid the demon across his lap, and tore him open with his claws, satisfying every clause and breaking none.

stories.title: The Burning of Holika
stories.summary: Unable to kill his devoted son by any other means, Hiranyakashipu sent for his sister Holika, who could not be burned. She sat in the pyre with Prahlada in her lap — and the fire took her and spared the boy. The bonfire on the eve of Holi is lit for this.

stories.title: Three Paces of Land
stories.summary: Mahabali's virtue had won him all three worlds, and no one could fault his rule — which was exactly the problem for the dispossessed gods. Vishnu came to his sacrifice as a dwarf brahmin and asked for three paces of land. Warned by his guru Shukra, Bali gave anyway. Vamana covered heaven with one stride and earth with the second, and Bali bowed his head for the third. Kerala keeps his annual return as Onam.

stories.title: Parashurama's Twenty-One Campaigns
stories.summary: When King Kartavirya's sons murdered the sage Jamadagni over a wish-granting cow, his son Parashurama took up the axe Shiva had given him and destroyed the warrior caste twenty-one times over. Immortal and unspent, he outlived his own age and lived on into the epics as the teacher of Bhishma, Drona and Karna.

stories.title: Garuda Steals the Nectar
stories.summary: The sisters Kadru and Vinata wagered on the color of a divine horse's tail; Kadru's serpent sons darkened it by lying along it, and Vinata lost herself into slavery. Her son Garuda flew to heaven to buy her freedom, scattered the gods, took the amrita — and gave it up on Vishnu's word without drinking a drop, winning instead his place as Vishnu's mount and the serpents' eternal enemy.

stories.title: Why the Sun and Moon Are Swallowed
stories.summary: During the distribution of the nectar, an asura slipped into the gods' line in disguise. Surya and Chandra recognized him and pointed; Vishnu's discus took his head off — but the amrita was already past his throat. The immortal head, Rahu, still chases the two informers across the sky and swallows them, and each eclipse is a moment when he catches one.

stories.title: The Exile of Rama
stories.summary: On the eve of Rama's coronation, Kaikeyi called in two old boons from Dasharatha: the throne for her son Bharata, and fourteen years of forest exile for Rama. Rama went without argument, Sita and Lakshmana with him. Dasharatha died of grief, and Bharata refused the crown — ruling instead as regent with his brother's sandals on the throne.

stories.title: The Breaking of Shiva's Bow
stories.summary: King Janaka had found Sita in a ploughed furrow and would give her only to the man who could string Shiva's bow, which no one had ever lifted. Brought by the sage Vishvamitra, Rama lifted it, strung it, and broke it in half — and the sound carried far enough to bring Parashurama down the road in a temper.

stories.title: Shurpanakha and the Abduction of Sita
stories.summary: Ravana's sister Shurpanakha desired Rama, was refused, turned on Sita, and was disfigured by Lakshmana. Her brother's revenge was a golden deer that lured Rama away and a false cry that drew Lakshmana after him — and Ravana carried Sita off by air. The old vulture Jatayu fought him in the sky and fell, living just long enough to tell Rama which way they had gone.

stories.title: Hanuman's Leap and the Burning of Lanka
stories.summary: Reminded by Jambavan of powers he had been cursed to forget, Hanuman grew vast and crossed the ocean in a single leap. He found Sita alive in Ravana's grove, gave her Rama's ring, allowed himself to be captured — and when they set his tail alight, ran across the rooftops and left Lanka burning behind him.

stories.title: The War at Lanka
stories.summary: The vanara army bridged the sea and the siege began. Vibhishana defected to Rama rather than defend an unjust cause; Kumbhakarna was woken from his half-year sleep and fought loyally to his death; Indrajit twice felled Rama and Lakshmana with sorcery before Lakshmana killed him. At the end Rama took Ravana's ten heads and set Vibhishana on the throne.

stories.title: The Fire, the Exile, and the Earth
stories.summary: Reunited, Rama asked Sita to prove her purity, and she walked into fire and came out untouched. Years later, with Ayodhya still whispering, he exiled her while pregnant; she bore Lava and Kusha in Valmiki's hermitage. Asked to prove herself once more, she called instead on her mother the Earth, who opened and took her back.

stories.title: The Birth of Krishna
stories.summary: A prophecy told Kamsa that his cousin Devaki's eighth son would kill him, so he jailed her and killed her children as they came. On the night of the eighth, the prison doors opened by themselves; Vasudeva carried the newborn across the flooding Yamuna, which parted, and exchanged him for a cowherd's daughter in Gokula.

stories.title: Lifting Mount Govardhan
stories.summary: Krishna told the cowherds to honor their hill and their cattle rather than send the yearly offering to Indra. The slighted king of the gods answered with a storm meant to drown Vrindavan — and Krishna raised the whole of Mount Govardhan on one finger and held it up for seven days while the village sheltered underneath.

stories.title: The Rasa Lila
stories.summary: On an autumn full-moon night Krishna's flute drew the gopis of Vrindavan out of their houses to dance with him on the Yamuna's bank, and he multiplied himself so that each believed he danced with her alone. Devotional tradition reads the night as the soul's love for God — with Radha, who is absent from the older epics, at its center.

stories.title: Krishna Kills Kamsa
stories.summary: Kamsa lured the brothers to Mathura for a wrestling match rigged with a mad elephant and two champion wrestlers. Krishna and Balarama came through all of it, and Krishna dragged his uncle from the royal dais and killed him — freeing Devaki and Vasudeva and restoring the rightful king.

stories.title: Bhishma's Terrible Vow
stories.summary: Shantanu wanted to marry the fisher-chief's daughter Satyavati, whose father demanded that her sons inherit. His son Devavrata gave up the throne — and, to remove even the threat of heirs, swore lifelong celibacy. The gods rained flowers and named him Bhishma, the terrible, and gave him death at a time of his own choosing.

stories.title: The Divine Fathers
stories.summary: A curse meant Pandu could never father children. Kunti held a mantra that summoned any god at will — tested once as an unwed girl on Surya, which gave her Karna, whom she set adrift in a basket. As queen she called Dharma, Vayu and Indra for Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna; Madri called the Ashvins for the twins.

stories.title: Draupadi's Swayamvara
stories.summary: Disguised as brahmins in hiding, the Pandavas came to Drupada's contest, and Arjuna shot the revolving fish through its eye by its reflection. Bringing her home, he called out that they had brought back alms — and Kunti, not looking up, told her sons to share whatever it was equally. Draupadi became the wife of all five.

stories.title: The Game of Dice
stories.summary: Yudhishthira, who could not refuse a challenge, gambled against Shakuni's loaded dice and lost his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and then Draupadi. Dragged into the hall, she asked whether a man who had already lost himself could stake his wife — and no elder answered. Dushasana tried to strip her; her sari became endless. The Pandavas went into thirteen years of exile, and the war became certain.

stories.title: The Song of the Lord
stories.summary: With the armies drawn up at Kurukshetra, Arjuna saw his teachers and cousins on the other side, dropped his bow, and refused to fight. His charioteer Krishna answered him — on duty, action without attachment, the deathlessness of the self — and finally showed his universal form. Arjuna took up the bow. Those seven hundred verses became Hinduism's most-read scripture.

stories.title: Abhimanyu in the Wheel
stories.summary: Abhimanyu had learned to break into the chakravyuha formation while still in the womb — and had never heard how to get out. With Arjuna drawn away, the boy opened the wheel alone, and it closed behind him. Six of the Kaurava's greatest warriors brought him down together, against every rule of war. His son Parikshit would carry the line.

stories.title: The Fall of Karna
stories.summary: Karna gave away the armor he was born with, was cursed by his own teacher, and learned only late whose son he was — refusing Kunti's offer of a throne because Duryodhana alone had honored him when no one else would. On the seventeenth day his chariot wheel sank in the mud, his curses came due, and Arjuna, urged on by Krishna, shot his unarmed half-brother.

stories.title: The Last Journey and the Dog
stories.summary: Their work done, the Pandavas and Draupadi walked north toward the mountains to die, and one by one they fell. Only Yudhishthira reached the gate, with a stray dog that had followed him the whole way. Indra offered him heaven but not the dog; he refused to go. The dog was Dharma, his own father, testing him one last time.

stories.title: The Avatar Still to Come
stories.summary: At the end of Kali Yuga, when scripture is forgotten and rulers plunder rather than protect, Vishnu will be born as Kalki and ride out on a white horse with a blazing sword. He will end the age, destroy the wicked, and turn the wheel back to a golden age — the one story in the cycle that has not happened yet.

stories.title: Speech, the Vedas, and the Goddess of Learning
stories.summary: The Rig Veda hymns a river called Saraswati and a goddess Vak, holy speech, who says of herself that she moves with the gods and that whoever she loves becomes mighty. The two flowed together into the Saraswati of later tradition — Brahma's consort, keeper of the Vedas, and the goddess invoked before study, music, and any first written word.

stories.title: The Guardians of the Directions
stories.summary: The world is fenced by guardians, one to each quarter: Indra in the east, Yama in the south, Varuna in the west, Kubera in the north, with Agni, Vayu, Surya and their fellows holding the corners between. Temples are laid out to face them and rites open by naming them, which is how gods long past their Vedic prime keep a daily place in worship.

stories.title: The Hymns to the Dawn
stories.summary: No goddess gets more beautiful poetry in the Rig Veda than Ushas, who opens the doors of the sky each morning, wakes the sleeping and leaves the dead unwoken, and comes back young while she wears out the lives of those who watch her. She faded almost entirely from later worship — a reminder of how much of the Vedic world the Puranas quietly left behind.

stories.title: The Nine Planets and the Weight of Karma
stories.summary: Nine moving powers govern a life: the sun and moon, five planets, and the eclipse-pair Rahu and Ketu. Brihaspati as Jupiter blesses, Shukra as Venus tutors the asuras, and Shani as Saturn — Surya's own slow, dark-robed son — delivers exactly what a person's deeds have earned, which is why he is more propitiated than loved.

stories.title: The Divine Architect Trims the Sun
stories.summary: Surya's wife Sanjna could not bear her husband's blaze; she left a shadow-double, Chhaya, in her place and fled, and Chhaya bore Shani. When the truth came out, Sanjna's father Vishvakarma — architect of the gods, maker of their cities and weapons — put the sun on his lathe and ground away his excess light, forging Vishnu's discus and Shiva's trident from the shavings.

stories.title: Rukmini's Letter
stories.summary: Rukmini of Vidarbha had chosen Krishna by reputation alone, and her brother had promised her to another man. She sent a brahmin with a letter naming the hour and the temple, and Krishna took her from the procession by chariot with the wedding party chasing behind — an elopement she engineered herself, and the beginning of his chief queenship.

stories.title: The Ninth Avatar, and the Argument About Him
stories.summary: Several Puranas list the Buddha among Vishnu's ten descents, some framing him generously as a teacher of compassion, others as a deliberate deluder of the unworthy. Elsewhere the ninth slot goes to Balarama or to Vithoba instead. Buddhists have never accepted the identification — which makes this the one avatar the tradition still argues about.

stories.title: The Abduction of Tara
stories.summary: Soma the moon took Tara, the wife of his own teacher Brihaspati, and refused every demand to return her. The quarrel spread until it was no longer private: the devas stood with Brihaspati, and Shukra, who had grievances of his own against the gods, brought the asuras in behind Soma. The Tarakamaya war was fought over one woman and went on until Brahma intervened personally and forced the matter closed. Tara went home pregnant. Asked whose the child was, she refused to answer, and kept refusing, until Brahma pressed her and she said Soma. The child was Budha — the planet Mercury, and the mildest of the nine — and through his son Pururavas the entire Lunar dynasty, and therefore the whole cast of the Mahabharata, descends from this affair.

stories.title: Pururavas and Urvashi
stories.summary: The apsara Urvashi agreed to live with Pururavas on terms: she would keep two rams tethered by the bed and he must never let them be taken, and she must never see him naked. It held until the gandharvas, who wanted her back in heaven, stole the rams in the dark. He leapt up to give chase, and a flash of lightning showed him bare. She was gone in that instant. He went looking for her across the whole country in a state the hymn does not flatter, and found her at last on a lake at Kurukshetra, swimming with her companions in the form of swans. Their exchange there is recorded in Rig Veda X.95, one of the oldest surviving dialogues in any language, and in it she tells him plainly that there is no friendship with women and that their hearts are the hearts of jackals.

stories.title: The Curse of Yayati
stories.summary: Yayati married Shukra's daughter Devayani and took her servant Sharmishtha as well, and when Shukra learned of it he cursed him into old age on the spot — not gradual, immediate. Yayati went to his five sons and asked each to take the decrepitude and lend him their youth. The four eldest refused and were disinherited where they stood. The youngest, Puru, agreed, and aged a thousand years in his father's place. Yayati spent those thousand years in every pleasure a king can command and arrived at the end of them at a conclusion he states in a verse quoted ever after: desire is never quieted by indulgence, but grows the way fire grows when butter is poured on it. He gave Puru back his years, gave him the kingdom over his brothers, and walked into the forest.

stories.title: Nahusha, the Indra Who Fell
stories.summary: Indra killed Vritra, incurred the guilt of killing a brahmin, and hid, and heaven was left without a king. Nahusha, a mortal of the Lunar line, was raised to the throne to hold it. Within a reign he had decided the position came with everything attached to it, including Indra's wife Shachi. She stalled him by demanding to be fetched in a palanquin carried by brahmin sages, expecting him to balk; he agreed. Under the pole, the sage Agastya moved too slowly for him and Nahusha kicked him, and Agastya cursed him into the body of a python on the instant. He lay in a forest for an age, until Yudhishthira came past in exile, and answered his questions on dharma well enough to release him.

stories.title: The Trial of Harishchandra
stories.summary: Harishchandra was known for never having spoken an untruth, and Vishvamitra set out to find where the limit was. Having been promised the kingdom, the sage claimed it; Harishchandra handed it over and left. Vishvamitra then observed that a gift of gold was still outstanding on top of the kingdom. To raise it the king sold his wife Shaibya and their son Rohitashva into service, and then sold himself to an outcaste keeper of the burning ground. The test arrives at its point when his wife comes to the cremation ground carrying their son, dead of snakebite, and Harishchandra — who now works for another man — cannot let the body burn without collecting the fee, because the fee is his master's. He holds to it. At that the gods stop the trial and give everything back, and the story has been the standard Indian example of truthfulness ever since.

stories.title: Ahalya and the Stone
stories.summary: Brahma made Ahalya the most beautiful woman in creation and gave her to the sage Gautama, and Indra, who had wanted her, did not let it go. He crowed like a cock long before dawn so that Gautama would rise and leave for the river, then took the sage's own form and went in. Gautama came back too early and understood everything at the door. He cursed Indra, and then he cursed his wife — to lie invisible for an age in the older telling, or as a stone in the version now universally known — until Rama should come along that road. Rama does, years later, walking to Mithila and his own wedding, and the dust of his foot lifts it. Whether Ahalya knew who she was with is the single most argued line in the reception of the Ramayana.

stories.title: The Axe and the Mother
stories.summary: Renuka's discipline was exact enough that she could make a pot from wet clay at the river each morning and carry water home in it unfired. One morning she caught sight of a gandharva king reflected in the water and admired him for a moment, and the clay came apart in her hands. Jamadagni knew what had happened before she reached the house, and ordered each of his sons in turn to behead her. The four eldest refused, and he burnt them to ash. The fifth, Parashurama, took up the axe and did it — and was then offered a boon for his obedience, and used it to ask for his mother's life and his brothers' as well, and got all of them. The texts record the whole exchange without a word of comment on any part of it.

stories.title: Shakuntala and the Ring
stories.summary: Vishvamitra's austerities had alarmed the gods, who sent the apsara Menaka to break them; it worked, and the child they left behind in the forest was sheltered by shakunta birds until the sage Kanva took her in. Dushyanta, hunting, met her at the hermitage and married her there by gandharva rite — consent and nothing else — and went back to his capital leaving his signet ring. When she came to court pregnant he said he had never seen her. In the Mahabharata this is simple denial and she answers it with a speech that wins on its merits, until a voice from the sky confirms the child. Kalidasa could not accept a hero behaving that way and added a curse and a lost ring, swallowed by a carp and found years later by a fisherman. The child was Bharata, who counted lion cubs' teeth for entertainment, and India is named after him.

stories.title: The Field That Kuru Ploughed
stories.summary: Kuru, a descendant of Puru, took a golden plough to the plain north of the Yamuna and began turning it over as an act of austerity, and would not stop. He ploughed for years. Indra came eventually to ask what he thought he was doing and what he wanted for it, and the boon Kuru asked was that whoever died on that ground should go to heaven, whatever they had done in life. It was granted, with argument over the terms. That plain is Kurukshetra, the field of the Kurus, and it is where his descendants met generations later to destroy each other over a throne. The Bhagavad Gita opens by naming the place dharmakshetra, the field of dharma, in its first word — and this is the reason the word is there.

stories.title: The Seven Sages and the Stars
stories.summary: Brahma produced the first sages from his own mind rather than from any body, and they became the Prajapatis, the progenitors, and were fixed afterwards in the seven stars of the Great Bear where they can be checked nightly. The lists disagree about who exactly the seven are — they change from one world-age to the next, and every Purana orders them differently — but the working set includes Marichi, whose son Kashyapa fathers the devas, the asuras, the nagas and most of the animals between them; Angiras, whose son Brihaspati teaches the gods; Atri, from a drop of light in whose eye the moon was born; Bharadvaja, whose son Drona trains both armies at Kurukshetra; Gautama, who cursed his own wife to stone; and Jamadagni, who told his son to behead his mother. The genealogy of nearly everything in this pack passes through six households.

stories.title: Raghu and the Student's Fee
stories.summary: Raghu had conquered the four quarters and then, after a great sacrifice, given away everything he owned down to the clay vessels, which was his habit and had stopped being prudent some time earlier. A student named Kautsa arrived immediately afterwards needing fourteen million gold pieces as his teacher's fee, having been told to ask the most generous king alive. Raghu had nothing at all and would not send him away, so he made preparations to attack Kubera, the god of wealth, and take it out of the treasury of wealth itself. Kubera heard what was coming and rained gold on Ayodhya overnight rather than face it. Raghu gave the student the full amount, the student took only what he needed, and the dynasty is called Raghuvamsha after him — which is why Rama is Raghava.

entities.name: Brahman (Parabrahman)
epithets: Parabrahman — the supreme Brahman, beyond all attributes
Tat — 'That', the pronoun the Upanishads use to point at it
symbols: the formula 'neti neti', not this, not this
entities.worship: Brahman has no temple, image or festival of its own, since it is what every image points toward. It is approached through meditation on Om, through study of the Upanishads and Vedanta, and through the daily recitation of mahavakyas such as tat tvam asi, 'you are that'.
entities.bio: The formless, infinite, unchanging supreme reality of the Upanishads. All deities are understood as manifestations of Brahman.
entities.longBio: Brahman is the answer the Upanishads give when the questioning stops: the single reality underlying every world, god and self. The older Vedic texts approach it obliquely, calling it the imperishable, the unborn, that from which speech turns back along with the mind. Its classic description works by negation, neti neti, not this and not this, because any attribute named would be a limit. Shankara's Advaita Vedanta holds that Brahman alone is real and that the individual soul is identical with it, while Ramanuja's qualified non-dualism keeps a real distinction between souls, world and God, and Madhva's dualism insists the two never merge. Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions each identify Brahman with their own supreme deity, so that Vishnu or Shiva is Brahman with qualities rather than a separate being. Understood this way, the entire crowded pantheon becomes a set of faces worn by one reality that has no face.
entities.variantTraditions: Not a 'god' with genealogy — the ground of all being.

entities.name: Adi Parashakti (Devi)
symbols: the lion or tiger she rides
many arms bearing every god's weapon
entities.mount: Simha — lion
entities.abode: Manidvipa, the island of jewels
festivals: Navaratri — nine nights honouring her forms and her victory over Mahishasura
Durga Puja — her autumn festival, largest in Bengal and eastern India
Vasanta Navaratri — the spring counterpart in the north
entities.worship: She is worshipped across India in Shakta temples and the fifty-one Shakti Pithas, and at village level as the local mother goddess under hundreds of regional names. Household worship centres on Navaratri, on recitation of the Devi Mahatmya, and among initiates on the Sri Yantra and the Lalita Sahasranama.
entities.bio: In Shaktism, the supreme goddess and primordial cosmic energy from whom all goddesses — and in some texts the Trimurti itself — arise.
entities.longBio: Shaktism holds that the ultimate reality is feminine and active, and that the male gods act only because her power moves through them. The Devi Mahatmya, a sixth-century section of the Markandeya Purana, is her charter text: it gathers her scattered local forms into one goddess who declares that she alone exists and takes shape whenever the world needs saving. Her most famous appearances are as Durga, assembled from the massed anger of all the gods to kill the buffalo demon Mahishasura, and as Kali, who steps out of Durga's forehead when the fighting turns desperate. Later texts such as the Devi Bhagavata Purana go further and place her above the Trimurti, making Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva servants who owe their offices to her. Elsewhere, particularly in Vaishnava and Shaiva writing, the same power is presented as the shakti of a male supreme god rather than as the supreme itself, and the disagreement is old and unresolved. Tantric schools add a third reading in which she is consciousness and Shiva is her still ground, inseparable as fire and its heat.
entities.variantTraditions: Supreme deity in Shaktism; in other traditions a power (shakti) of the supreme.

entities.name: Brahma
epithets: Hiranyagarbha — the golden womb or cosmic egg
symbols: the four Vedas in his hands
white beard and red or golden skin
entities.mount: Hamsa — swan or goose
entities.abode: Brahmaloka, also called Satyaloka
festivals: Kartik Purnima at Pushkar — the annual fair around his principal temple
entities.worship: Almost no temples are dedicated to him; the one at Pushkar in Rajasthan is the famous exception, with a handful of others in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. He is nevertheless present in almost every ritual, invoked at the start of ceremonies, honoured in the daily Gayatri prayer, and named in the vastu rites that consecrate a building site.
entities.bio: Creator god of the Trimurti, born from a lotus rising from Vishnu's navel (or self-born). Father of the Prajapatis, including Daksha, and of many sages.
entities.longBio: Brahma inherits the office of the Vedic Prajapati, the lord of creatures who produced the world by sacrifice and heat, and carries it into the Puranas as the working creator of each cosmic cycle. The standard account has him seated on a lotus that grows from the sleeping Vishnu's navel, opening his eyes to find nothing but water, and bringing forth the mind-born sons who become the Prajapatis and the first sages. His four faces are said to have appeared so he could keep watching Shatarupa, the woman he had just created, and several Puranas treat this as the sin that cost him his worship. Another story makes Shiva sever a fifth head for lying about having found the top of the endless pillar of light, and yet another has the sage Bhrigu curse him for arrogance. He grants boons freely and without much judgment, which is why so many demons in the Puranas owe their near-invulnerability to him, and why the plots of those stories exist at all. His lifespan measures cosmic time, one of his days lasting a thousand cycles of the four ages, after which the worlds dissolve and are made again.
entities.variantTraditions: Evolved from Vedic Prajapati. Rarely worshipped independently today.

entities.name: Vishnu
epithets: Narayana — he who rests on the waters
Trivikrama — he of the three strides
symbols: dark blue skin and yellow silk
the Kaustubha gem and Shrivatsa mark
entities.mount: Garuda — the eagle
entities.abode: Vaikuntha, and the ocean of milk where he sleeps on Shesha
festivals: Vaikuntha Ekadashi — the day his heavenly gate is said to open
Janmashtami — the birth of his avatar Krishna
Rama Navami — the birth of his avatar Rama
Holi — connected to Prahlada's rescue by Narasimha
entities.worship: Vaishnavism is one of the largest branches of living Hinduism, with major temples at Tirupati, Srirangam, Puri and Badrinath and daily household worship through the tulsi plant and the salagrama stone. Devotion runs mostly through his avatars, especially Rama and Krishna, and through name-repetition, the twelve-syllable mantra, and the singing of the thousand names.
entities.bio: Preserver of the cosmos who descends as avatars whenever dharma declines. Rests on the serpent Shesha in the cosmic ocean; supreme deity of Vaishnavism.
entities.longBio: In the Rigveda Vishnu is a modest solar figure known chiefly for three strides that measure out the whole of space, and that single act contains the seed of everything he later becomes. By the time of the Puranas the strides have grown into a full theology of descent: whenever dharma weakens and adharma rises, he takes a body and enters the world, a promise the Bhagavad Gita puts in his own mouth. The standard list gives ten avatars from the fish Matsya to the future horseman Kalki, though the Bhagavata Purana counts twenty-two and other texts more, and traditions disagree sharply over whether the Buddha belongs on the list and what that inclusion was meant to accomplish. Between cycles he lies on the thousand-headed serpent Shesha on the ocean of milk, with Lakshmi at his feet, and the next creation begins when a lotus rises from his navel bearing Brahma. His character across the stories is patient and strategic rather than furious: he waits, disguises himself, keeps to the letter of a boon while defeating its purpose, as when he kills Hiranyakashipu at twilight in a doorway as a being neither man nor beast. Shaiva texts return the compliment by subordinating him to Shiva, and the rivalry produced compromise figures such as Harihara, half of each.
entities.variantTraditions: Minor solar deity in the Rigveda; supreme god in Puranic Vaishnavism.

entities.name: Shiva
epithets: Nilakantha — the blue-throated, from the poison he swallowed
Bholenath — the guileless one, easily pleased
entities.mount: Nandi — the bull
entities.abode: Mount Kailash
festivals: Maha Shivaratri — the great night of Shiva, kept with fasting and vigil
Shravan Somvar — Monday fasts through the monsoon month
Thiruvathirai — his Tamil festival of dance and dawn worship
entities.worship: He is worshipped almost everywhere as the linga rather than in human form, bathed daily with water, milk and bilva leaves, and the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines from Somnath to Rameshwaram anchor a pilgrimage circuit that has run for a thousand years. The five-syllable mantra namah shivaya, the Rudram chant from the Yajurveda, and the all-night vigil of Maha Shivaratri are the common forms of his practice.
entities.bio: God of destruction, transformation, yoga and dance (Nataraja). Husband of Sati and later Parvati; supreme deity of Shaivism.
entities.longBio: Shiva grows out of the Vedic Rudra, a dangerous outsider god of storms, arrows and healing herbs who is addressed with careful flattery so that he will turn his weapons elsewhere. That doubleness never leaves him. He is the ascetic who sits motionless on Kailash for ages and the householder married to Parvati, the destroyer of the universe and the god who drinks the world's poison to save it, holding it in his throat until it turns blue. His dance as Nataraja, fixed in bronze by Chola sculptors, sets creation, preservation, destruction, concealment and grace into a single figure ringed by fire. Stories show him quick to anger and quicker to relent: he burns Kamadeva to ash for interrupting his meditation, then restores him bodiless at Rati's plea, and he beheads Parvati's son at her door only to give him an elephant's head and the first place in every ritual. Shaiva Siddhanta in the Tamil south treats him as the supreme lord who liberates bound souls, Kashmir Shaivism reads him as pure consciousness whose vibration is the world, and the Lingayats of Karnataka reject temple hierarchy altogether while wearing his linga on the body. Almost alone among the great gods he takes no avatars in the Vaishnava sense, appearing instead in forms and disguises, as the hunter, the beggar, the wandering madman who tests those who meet him.
entities.variantTraditions: Continuous with the Vedic storm god Rudra.

entities.name: Saraswati
epithets: Sharada — the giver of essence, her name across Kashmir and Karnataka
Vinapani — she who holds the vina
symbols: the swan that separates milk from water
entities.mount: Hamsa — swan; a peacock in some regional images
entities.abode: Brahmaloka, with Brahma
festivals: Vasant Panchami — her spring festival, when children are taught their first letters
Saraswati Puja on Maha Navami — books and instruments are placed before her and left unused for a day
Ayudha Puja — tools and implements of every trade honoured in her name
entities.worship: Students, musicians and scholars keep her image in study rooms and rehearsal spaces, and schools across eastern India close for her puja in spring. On the last days of Navaratri books, pens and instruments are set at her feet and deliberately left idle, then taken up again on Vijayadashami as an auspicious start to study.
entities.bio: Goddess of wisdom, speech and learning; consort of Brahma. One of the few goddesses continuously worshipped since the Rigveda, where she is also a sacred river.
entities.longBio: She begins in the Rigveda as an actual river, praised as the best of mothers and best of rivers, running from the mountains to the sea along a course that later dried up and passed into memory. The hymns already blur the water with what it carries, and she merges with Vach, the goddess of speech who declares in her own hymn that she moves with the gods and holds the worlds together. By the Puranas the river is nearly gone and the speech remains, and she is the consort of Brahma, in some tellings created by him from his own body, in others born of his mind, and in a few she flees his gaze and is pursued, which is one of the accounts given for his four heads. Her whiteness is deliberate: no jewels of consequence, no weapons, no lion, only the instrument and the book, since what she gives cannot be seized. Jains honour her as the goddess of the scriptures and Buddhists carried her to Japan as Benzaiten, where she still holds a stringed instrument. Unlike Lakshmi she is not asked for increase but for clarity, and the old saying that the two goddesses rarely stay in the same house is a joke about wealth and learning that people still repeat.
entities.variantTraditions: Origin stories vary widely between texts.

entities.name: Lakshmi
epithets: Kamala — she who is seated on the lotus
Sthira Lakshmi — the fortune that stays
symbols: gold coins falling from her palm
entities.mount: Ulooka — owl; often shown seated on a lotus instead
entities.abode: Vaikuntha, at Vishnu's side
festivals: Diwali — Lakshmi Puja on the new moon night, when houses are lit to invite her in
Varalakshmi Vratam — a Friday vow kept by married women in the south
Sharad Purnima — the autumn full moon said to be her night
Dhanteras — the buying of metal two days before Diwali
entities.worship: Her worship is domestic and constant: a lamp at the threshold, the Friday vrat, and the Diwali night when doors are opened and floors marked with rice-flour kolam so she will enter a clean house. Businesses open new account books before her at the start of the financial year, and her temples are usually shared with Vishnu, as at Tirupati and Srirangam, or with Ganesha in shopfront shrines.
entities.bio: Goddess of prosperity, beauty and auspiciousness; consort of Vishnu. Emerged from the churning of the cosmic ocean (Samudra Manthana). Incarnates alongside Vishnu's avatars as Sita, Rukmini and others.
entities.longBio: Lakshmi rises from the ocean of milk when gods and demons churn it, standing on a lotus with elephants pouring water over her, and chooses Vishnu from among all the assembled beings. That moment of choosing matters, because in the older Shri Sukta appended to the Rigveda she is already fortune itself, the thing kings must attract and can lose, and her decision to stay or leave a house is treated as her own. Some texts give her an earlier birth as the daughter of the sage Bhrigu, which is why she is called Bhargavi. She descends whenever Vishnu does, as Sita beside Rama, as Rukmini beside Krishna, and in the south as Padmavati beside Venkateshvara at Tirupati. Her opposite and, in one account, her elder sister is Alakshmi or Jyeshtha, misfortune, who arrives first in the churning and must be kept outside the door. Vaishnava theology in the Srivaishnava school makes her more than a consort: she is the mediator who softens Vishnu toward the soul, and no approach to him is made except through her, a doctrine argued over for centuries in the debate about whether she is infinite like him or a liberated soul herself.
entities.variantTraditions: Some texts call her daughter of the sage Bhrigu (hence 'Bhargavi').

entities.name: Parvati
epithets: Uma — the name used from the Kena Upanishad onward
Annapurna — she who is full of food
Aparna — she who took not even a leaf while fasting
domains: shakti, the power that animates Shiva
symbols: vermilion and the marks of a married woman
the ladle and bowl of Annapurna
lion or tiger in her fierce forms
entities.mount: Simha — lion; often shown beside Nandi with Shiva
entities.abode: Mount Kailash
festivals: Teej — monsoon festival where women fast for a husband's long life, recalling her penance
Gauri Puja — kept alongside Ganesh Chaturthi in Maharashtra
Navaratri — through her forms as Durga and the nine Navadurgas
Gangaur — the Rajasthani spring festival of Gauri
entities.worship: She is worshipped with Shiva in nearly every Shiva temple and alone as Annapurna at Kashi, where the goddess feeds the city. Married and unmarried women keep fasts in her name for a good husband or a long marriage, and her lamp is lit in households across the north during Teej and Gangaur.
entities.bio: Daughter of the mountain king Himavan; rebirth of Sati and second consort of Shiva. Mother of Ganesha and Kartikeya. Her fierce forms include Durga and Kali.
entities.longBio: Parvati is Sati reborn, taking a second body in the house of Himavan the mountain king after her first self burned at Daksha's sacrifice, and the story of her second courtship is one of the great set pieces of Sanskrit poetry. Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava tells it: the gods send Kamadeva to shoot Shiva out of his trance, Shiva burns him to ash, and Parvati, refusing the shortcut, goes into the forest and performs austerities so severe that she stops eating even fallen leaves. Shiva finally comes to her disguised as a young brahmin and abuses himself to her face, listing his ash, his snakes, his beggary, and when she defends him without wavering he drops the disguise. Her marriage is not a settling but an argument won, and the texts keep her arguing afterward, questioning Shiva about yoga and dharma in dialogues that become the frame for whole Tantric works. She creates Ganesha alone from the substance of her own body, without Shiva's part in it, and her anger at his beheading is what forces the elephant head and the boy's restoration. Shakta traditions treat Durga and Kali as her forms and Parvati as their gentle aspect, while some texts reverse the direction and make the great goddess primary with Parvati as her domestic appearance.
entities.variantTraditions: As Shakti, she is the energy that animates Shiva.

entities.name: Indra
entities.role: King of the Devas; storms & rain
symbols: a thousand marks on his body
entities.mount: Airavata — the white elephant; also the horse Uchchaihshravas
entities.abode: Amaravati in Svarga, with the Nandana garden
festivals: Indra Jatra — eight days in Kathmandu marking the end of the monsoon
Onam — kept in Kerala for Mahabali, whose defeat restored Indra's throne
entities.worship: He receives almost no independent worship today, though he is invoked in Vedic fire rituals, in the dikpala niches on temple walls, and in the sankalpa formulas that place a rite in space. Nepal's Indra Jatra is the largest surviving public festival in his name, and Tamil literature preserves the memory of the once-great Indra Vizha of Puhar.
entities.bio: Chief of the gods in the Vedas, wielder of the thunderbolt (vajra), slayer of the dragon Vritra. In the Puranas, a son of Kashyapa and Aditi and ruler of Svarga (heaven).
entities.longBio: No god dominates the Rigveda as Indra does, with roughly a quarter of its hymns addressed to him, drinking soma by the vatful and smashing the dragon Vritra so the pent rivers run. He is the warrior-king of a mobile people, breaker of enemy strongholds, and the hymns admire his appetite and boasting as much as his victories. The Puranas cut him down. He becomes an office rather than a person, held in turn by whoever accumulates the merit for it, nervous about his throne and forever sending nymphs to break the penances of sages who might qualify. Story after story humbles him: Krishna lifts Govardhan against his rain, Vishnu as Vamana wins back his heaven for him rather than by him, and Gautama's curse for the seduction of Ahalya leaves him marked all over his body, the marks later softened into a thousand eyes. Killing Vritra costs him too, since the Puranas make the dragon a brahmin and the brahminicide follows him until it is divided among earth, water, trees and women. He remains guardian of the east, and his diminishment is itself the clearest record of how Vedic religion gave way to Puranic devotion.
entities.variantTraditions: Diminished in the Puranas — often humbled by Vishnu, Shiva or great devotees.

entities.name: Agni
entities.role: God of fire; messenger to the gods
epithets: Jatavedas — knower of all beings born
Vaishvanara — the fire belonging to all people
domains: sacrifice and the passage of offerings
symbols: two faces and seven tongues of flame
flaming hair and red or gold body
entities.mount: Mesha — ram
entities.abode: Agniloka; and every domestic and sacrificial hearth
festivals: Holika Dahan — the bonfire on the night before Holi
Lohri and Bhogi — winter fires kept in Punjab and the south
Agnihotra — the twice-daily fire offering rather than a festival
entities.worship: Agni is present at more Hindu rituals than any other god without needing a temple: the seven steps of a wedding are taken around him, the sacred thread ceremony is performed before him, and the last offering is the cremation fire. Brahmin households that maintain the agnihotra still feed a fire at dawn and dusk, and the fire kindled at a wedding is treated as the witness that makes the marriage binding.
entities.bio: Fire god who carries sacrificial offerings to the gods; second most-invoked deity in the Rigveda. Witness of vows and marriages.
entities.longBio: Agni opens the Rigveda in its very first word and is addressed in more hymns than any god but Indra, because without him no offering reaches anyone. He stands in two places at once, the priest among the gods and the god among priests, eating what is given on earth and carrying its essence upward. The hymns delight in his birth: rubbed out of two sticks, born from water in the form of lightning, hidden in plants and in the sun, so that he is described as having three births and many mothers. His parentage varies by text, given as Dyaus and Prithvi, as a son of Brahma, or as one of Kashyapa and Aditi's children. Narrative texts show him with an unusual weakness, a hunger that becomes dangerous, as when he burns the Khandava forest with Krishna and Arjuna guarding the edges so nothing escapes, a cure for the indigestion of too much ghee. He fathers Kartikeya in one version of that contested birth, carrying Shiva's seed when no one else can hold it, and he is guardian of the southeast, which is why kitchen hearths are placed in that corner of a traditional house.
entities.variantTraditions: Parentage varies: son of Dyaus-Prithvi, of Brahma, or of Kashyapa-Aditi by text.

entities.name: Varuna
entities.role: God of waters, oceans, cosmic law
epithets: Rtasya Gopa — guardian of cosmic order
symbols: makara, the sea creature he rides
a pot of water or jewels
entities.mount: Makara — a sea creature, part crocodile part fish
entities.abode: Sukha, his ocean palace in the western waters
festivals: Chettikulangara and coastal Varuna offerings — rites by fishing communities before the sea season
Narali Purnima — coconuts offered to the sea on the Konkan coast
entities.worship: He is invoked chiefly by people whose lives depend on water: fishermen offering coconuts to the sea before the season opens, priests performing rain rituals in drought, and anyone taking a formal oath. Temples to him are rare, though he holds the western niche on temple walls and appears in the tarpana offered with water to the ancestors.
entities.bio: Guardian of rita (cosmic order) in the Vedas, later god of oceans and the western direction. An Aditya, son of Kashyapa and Aditi.
entities.longBio: In the earliest Vedic layer Varuna is the most morally serious god the tradition has: he sits in a high house with a thousand eyes, sees every lie told and every debt unpaid, and binds offenders with his noose, which is also the name given to dropsy. The hymns addressed to him are unlike any others, closer to confession than to praise, asking what sin was committed and pleading for release. He rules rita, the order by which the sun keeps its path and promises hold, usually paired with Mitra, who governs contracts between people while Varuna governs the vow itself. That standing did not last. As Indra rose he was pushed toward the water he had always been associated with, and by the Puranas he is a dignified sea king, one of the eight dikpalas, holder of the west, who lends weapons to heroes and loses arguments to them. The Ramayana has Rama threaten to dry up the ocean before Varuna appears and grants passage to Lanka, which is a fair measure of how far he had fallen. His name shares a root and a temperament with Zoroastrian Ahura Mazda, and the Iranian parallel is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for a shared Indo-Iranian religion.

entities.name: Vayu
epithets: Marut — the storm wind, also the name of his troop
Anila — the one that does not rest
symbols: a banner or flag streaming in wind
entities.mount: Mriga — an antelope or deer; a chariot drawn by many horses in some texts
entities.abode: Vayuloka; and everywhere air moves
festivals: Hanuman Jayanti — kept for his son, and by Madhva Vaishnavas as his own day
Madhva Navami — the Dvaita commemoration of Madhvacharya, held to be his third incarnation
entities.worship: Direct worship of Vayu is uncommon, but it survives strongly in the Dvaita tradition of Karnataka, where Madhvacharya taught that Vayu is the chief of the gods and the son of Vishnu's grace, and where he is honoured through his three incarnations as Hanuman, Bhima and Madhva himself. Elsewhere he is reached through pranayama, the breath discipline that treats him as the life within the body, and in the northwest niche of temple walls.
entities.bio: Wind god and lord of the vital breath (prana). Divine father of the monkey god Hanuman and of the Pandava Bhima.
entities.longBio: The Vedas make Vayu the first to receive the soma, quick enough to arrive before any other god, and they hold him inseparable from Indra in the joint form Indra-Vayu. He is also prana, the breath, and the Upanishads use him to argue a point: in the Chandogya and Brihadaranyaka the senses quarrel over which is most important, each departs in turn and the body limps on, but when breath begins to leave they all give way and admit its rule. As a character in narrative he is best known through his sons. Hanuman is his by Anjana, and the Ramayana explains the monkey's leap across the ocean by his father's nature, while Bhima is his by Kunti in the Mahabharata, which accounts for the strength that does the Pandavas' heavy work. He also fathered the hundred Maruts in some accounts, and a well-known episode has him break the peaks off Mount Meru at Narada's prompting, one of which lands in the sea and becomes Lanka. Madhvacharya's Dvaita school gives him the highest place after Vishnu, teaching that Vayu is the eternal mediator between God and souls, so a god almost unworshipped elsewhere sits at the centre of a major Vedantic theology.

entities.name: Surya
epithets: Savitr — the impeller, the sun as quickener
Martanda — the dead egg, from his difficult birth
symbols: a chariot with seven horses and one wheel
two lotuses held at shoulder height
boots, unusual in Hindu iconography, from Iranian influence
the charioteer Aruna, who has no legs
entities.mount: A chariot drawn by seven horses, driven by Aruna
entities.abode: Suryaloka, the solar sphere
festivals: Makar Sankranti — his turn northward, kept across India in January
Chhath — four days of offerings to the setting and rising sun in Bihar and eastern UP
Pongal — the Tamil harvest festival of the sun
Ratha Saptami — the day his chariot turns north
entities.worship: The Gayatri mantra, addressed to the sun's light, is the most widely recited verse in Hinduism, and the surya namaskara sequence of postures is his daily salutation. Chhath in the eastern Gangetic plain is the largest surviving festival of direct sun worship anywhere, with hundreds of thousands standing in rivers at dawn, and the ruined temple at Konark and the living one at Modhera mark an older Saura tradition that once rivalled the Vaishnavas.
entities.bio: The sun personified, riding a chariot drawn by seven horses driven by Aruna. An Aditya; father of Yama, Shani, the Ashvins, Karna, and the vanara Sugriva.
entities.longBio: Surya is one of the few Vedic gods whose worship never broke, running unbroken from the Rigvedic hymns to the sun's eye to the Chhath vows kept in Bihar this year. He drives a single-wheeled chariot behind seven horses, the wheel being the year and the horses variously the metres of the Veda or the colours of light, and his charioteer Aruna, the red of dawn, was born half-formed when his mother Vinata opened the egg too early. His wife Sanjna could not bear his heat and left a shadow double, Chhaya, in her place while she hid in the forest as a mare, and when Vishvakarma discovered the trick he ground away an eighth of the sun's brilliance, using the trimmings to forge Vishnu's discus and Shiva's trident. From him come Yama and the Yamuna by Sanjna, Shani by Chhaya, the twin Ashvins, and Karna, born to Kunti before her marriage and given away, which drives the tragedy of the Mahabharata. The Saura sect that worshipped him as supreme absorbed Iranian priestly influence, visible in the boots and belted coat of his images, and though the sect itself faded its temples and its mantra remain in daily use.

entities.name: Chandra (Soma)
epithets: Soma — the moon and the sacrificial drink together
domains: the lunar calendar and its festivals
symbols: a chariot drawn by ten white horses or antelopes
a white body and white garments
the crescent, worn also by Shiva
entities.mount: A chariot drawn by ten white horses; antelopes in some descriptions
entities.abode: Chandraloka, the lunar sphere
festivals: Sharad Purnima — the autumn full moon, when rice pudding is left out in the moonlight
Karva Chauth — the fast broken only after sighting the moon
Kojagari and Karthika Purnima — full-moon observances tied to his light
entities.worship: He is addressed mainly as one of the Navagraha, in the planetary shrines of south Indian temples where a circuit is walked and a lamp lit for whichever graha troubles a horoscope. Popular practice reaches him through the moon itself: the Karva Chauth fast ends only when the moon is seen through a sieve, and Monday, his day, is kept by many with observances shared with Shiva.
entities.bio: The moon personified, identified with the sacred drink Soma. Married the 27 lunar-mansion daughters of Daksha; ancestor of the lunar dynasty of kings.
entities.longBio: Vedic Soma is the pressed drink of the sacrifice, the plant, and the exhilaration it produces, praised in a whole book of the Rigveda; the identification with the moon comes later and completely, so that by the Puranas the moon is the cup from which the gods drink and its waning is that cup being emptied. He is usually called a son of the sage Atri and Anasuya, and in another account he rises from the churning of the ocean. Daksha gave him twenty-seven daughters, the lunar mansions, and when he spent all his time with Rohini alone the others complained; Daksha's curse of wasting was softened to a monthly cycle, which is how the tradition explains the phases. His worst act was abducting Tara, the wife of Brihaspati, provoking a war among the gods and producing Budha, the planet Mercury, whose descendants form the lunar dynasty that includes the Kauravas and Pandavas. Rahu's grudge from the churning explains lunar eclipses, and Ganesha's curse for laughing at his fall is why the moon of Ganesh Chaturthi night is not to be looked at. Since the Hindu ritual calendar is lunar, almost every festival date is a position of his.
entities.variantTraditions: Usually called a son of the sage Atri.

entities.name: Yama
domains: death and the passage of souls
symbols: dark green or black skin and red garments
the ledger kept by his scribe Chitragupta
the two four-eyed dogs that guard his path
entities.mount: Mahisha — buffalo
entities.abode: Yamaloka, with his city Samyamani
festivals: Yama Dvitiya, also called Bhai Dooj — sisters honour brothers, recalling Yami's welcome of Yama
Naraka Chaturdashi — a lamp lit at Diwali to keep the way to hell shut
entities.worship: He is not petitioned for favours but placated and remembered, chiefly through the shraddha rites for the dead and the water offering of tarpana. A lamp is set outside the house on the night before Diwali as a Yama deepam, and his sister's festival of Bhai Dooj keeps his name in an entirely domestic setting.
entities.bio: Lord of death and righteous judgment of the departed; guardian of the southern direction. Son of Surya; divine father of Yudhishthira.
entities.longBio: In the Rigveda Yama is not a god of death but the first man to die, who found the road to the other world and so became host to everyone who follows, sitting under a tree with the fathers and drinking with the gods. His twin sister Yami urges him to father the human race with her and he refuses on grounds of dharma, in one of the oldest dialogue hymns; the refusal sets his character. Later texts turn him into a judge with a bureaucracy, his scribe Chitragupta keeping an exact record of every act, and a system of hells calibrated to the offence, and the Garuda Purana describes the journey and the accounting in detail. He loses more arguments than a god of death should. Savitri follows him down the road and talks her husband's life back out of his hands, the boy Nachiketa refuses every bribe until Yama teaches him the secret of what survives death in the Katha Upanishad, and Markandeya clings to a Shiva linga so that Shiva kicks Yama away. His son Yudhishthira inherits his exactness, and the dog that follows the Pandavas up the mountain at the end of the Mahabharata turns out to be Yama testing whether his son will abandon a companion at the gate of heaven.
entities.variantTraditions: In the Vedas, the first mortal who died and became ruler of the ancestors.

entities.name: Kubera
entities.role: God of wealth; king of Yakshas
epithets: Nidhipati — keeper of the nine treasures
symbols: a money bag or pot of gold
a heavy paunch and dwarfish body
entities.mount: Nara — a man, or man-shaped spirit; a ram in some texts
entities.abode: Alaka on Mount Gandhamadana, near Kailash
festivals: Dhanteras — his name invoked alongside Lakshmi when metal is bought
Diwali Lakshmi Puja — worshipped with her as the keeper rather than the giver of wealth
entities.worship: He is worshipped with Lakshmi at Diwali and Dhanteras, in shop shrines and in the locked room or safe of a house, where a Kubera yantra is often placed facing north. Independent temples are few, though he stands in the northern niche of temple walls and holds an important place in Buddhist and Jain traditions, where as Vaishravana or Jambhala he guards the north and grants prosperity.
entities.bio: Lord of riches and guardian of the northern direction; original ruler of Lanka until his half-brother Ravana seized it.
entities.longBio: Kubera began as something less respectable than a god, a chief of yakshas, the tree and treasure spirits of the earlier folk religion, and his lopsided body keeps that origin visible even after the Puranas made him a dikpala. He won his position and the flying chariot Pushpaka through long austerity, and the Ramayana gives him Lanka as his city until his half-brother Ravana, born of the same father Vishrava by a rakshasa mother, drove him out and took both the city and the chariot. He retreated north to Alaka, the garden capital that Kalidasa's Meghaduta describes as the destination of the cloud, a place of perpetual spring where nobody ages. He is Shiva's friend and neighbour, and one story explains his deformity as the result of looking at Parvati with envy, which cost him an eye. Unlike Lakshmi he does not create wealth or bestow fortune; he stores it, counts it and guards it, which is why the two are worshipped together but asked for different things. Buddhism took him up as Vaishravana, one of the four heavenly kings, and he travelled in that form through Central Asia to Japan as Bishamonten.
entities.variantTraditions: Son of the sage Vishrava — making him Ravana's elder half-brother.

entities.name: Ushas
epithets: Duhitar Divah — daughter of the sky
Suryasya Yosha — bride or maiden of the sun
domains: the passing of days and of lifespans
symbols: a chariot drawn by ruddy cows or horses
a bright garment drawn back like a dancer's
entities.mount: A chariot drawn by red cows or horses
entities.abode: The eastern sky
entities.worship: She has no temple and no festival, but the hour she governs, the brahma muhurta before sunrise, is still the prescribed time for prayer and study, and the Gayatri is recited into the same light. Her hymns are read and sung today mainly as poetry, in Vedic recitation and in Sanskrit teaching.
entities.bio: Radiant dawn goddess of the Rigveda, among the most exalted goddesses of the Vedic age, driving away darkness each morning.
entities.longBio: About twenty hymns of the Rigveda are addressed to Ushas and they are among the finest poetry in the collection, praising a young woman who uncovers her breast like a dancer, opens the doors of the sky and drives the darkness back with red cattle. The poets who praise her know exactly what she costs: she has worn away the lives of those who watched her before, and each dawn she wakes is one day less for the man watching now, so the hymns hold delight and dread in the same breath. She is called daughter of Dyaus the sky, sister of Night whose road she shares without quarrel, and in some verses the wife or the lover of Surya who follows her without catching up. One curious hymn has Indra shatter her chariot with the vajra, a violence never fully explained, which some read as a myth of a dawn that came too slowly or too proudly. Her name is cognate with the Greek Eos, the Latin Aurora and the Lithuanian Ausrine, making her one of the clearest inherited figures from the common Indo-European past. Later Hinduism let her fade, keeping only fragments, and it is a genuine loss, since no later goddess is described with quite that mixture of pleasure and knowledge of time.
entities.variantTraditions: Largely faded from later worship.

entities.name: Prithvi (Bhumi)
epithets: Medini — she formed from the fat of the demons Madhu and Kaitabha
symbols: a lotus and a pot of grain
the cow, her most common form in narrative
a boar carrying her on its tusk
entities.abode: The earth itself; Vaikuntha in her form as Vishnu's consort Bhudevi
festivals: Bhumi Puja — the rite performed before any building or ploughing begins
Pongal and Bihu — harvest festivals that thank the earth
Kurma and the ploughing rites at the start of the agricultural season
entities.worship: She is touched more than she is invoked: many people touch the ground and then the forehead on rising, in apology for treading on her, and no house foundation is dug and no field ploughed without a bhumi puja. In the south she stands beside Vishnu as Bhudevi opposite Sridevi in temple images, most prominently at Srirangam and Tirupati.
entities.bio: The earth personified; paired with the sky father Dyaus in the Vedas. As Bhudevi she is rescued from the ocean by Vishnu's boar avatar Varaha.
entities.longBio: In the Vedas Prithvi is almost always half of a pair, Dyavaprithivi, sky and earth spoken of as one word and one parental couple, and the Atharvaveda's long Prithvi Sukta is the fullest hymn to her, addressing her as the one who bears the burden of rock and dust and asking that what is dug from her heal quickly. Puranic narrative gives her a plot: the demon Hiranyaksha rolls her up and sinks her under the cosmic waters, and Vishnu takes the form of the boar Varaha, dives, kills him and lifts her out on his tusk, after which she becomes his consort Bhudevi. She often appears as a cow, going to the gods to complain when the weight of armies and wicked kings becomes unbearable, and that complaint is the standard trigger for a divine incarnation, including Krishna's. Through Varaha she is the mother of Narakasura, the demon Krishna kills, and she asks that his death be remembered as a festival of light rather than mourning, which is one account of Naraka Chaturdashi. The Ramayana gives her a final scene: Sita, having proved herself once, calls on her mother the earth to take her back, and the ground opens and closes. Her characteristic quality in every text is kshama, the patience that bears what is put on it, and the same word means forgiveness.

entities.name: The Ashvins
epithets: Nasatyas — the truthful ones, or those who never fail
Divo Napata — sons of the sky
symbols: honey and the madhu they carry
entities.mount: A three-wheeled golden chariot drawn by horses or birds
entities.abode: The sky at the boundary of night and dawn
festivals: Ashvini Nakshatra observances — the first lunar mansion, named for them, marked in some almanac rites
Dhanvantari Jayanti — they are honoured alongside the physician of the gods on Dhanteras
entities.worship: They receive little independent worship, but Ayurvedic practitioners invoke them at the head of the tradition's lineage, since the Charaka and Sushruta traditions trace healing knowledge from Brahma through them to Indra and on to human physicians. Their names are still recited in the daily prayers of some vaidya families and in the invocation verses of Ayurvedic texts.
entities.bio: Twin horsemen physicians of the gods, sons of Surya. Divine fathers of the Pandava twins Nakula and Sahadeva.
entities.longBio: The Ashvins are the emergency service of the Rigveda, arriving in a three-wheeled chariot at the last possible moment, and the hymns list their rescues like a catalogue of debts: they pull Bhujyu from the sea, give the sage Chyavana back his youth, fit an iron leg to the warrior queen Vishpala, restore sight to Rijrashva, and give Vadhrimati a son. They are always two, always young, and always associated with the joining of night and day, which is why some readings make them morning and evening star. The gods long refused them a share of the soma on the grounds that they wandered too much among human beings, and the story of how they won it is telling: Chyavana, grateful for his restored youth, forced Indra to admit them, and when Indra raised the thunderbolt the sage froze his arm. They also taught the sage Dadhyanch to reveal the secret of the sacrifice by replacing his head with a horse's so that Indra's threat to behead him would fall on the wrong head. In the Mahabharata they father Nakula and Sahadeva by Madri, giving the younger Pandavas their beauty and Sahadeva his knowledge, and their Indo-European cousins, the Greek Dioscuri and the Baltic divine twins, do the same rescuing work with the same horses.

entities.name: Brihaspati
entities.role: Guru of the Devas; planet Jupiter
epithets: Guru — the teacher, and the planet Jupiter
Jiva — the giver of life, an astrological name
domains: the planet Jupiter and its benefic influence
symbols: a rosary and a water pot
a golden chariot drawn by eight horses
entities.mount: A chariot drawn by eight pale horses; an elephant in some Navagraha panels
entities.abode: Svarga, in Indra's court
festivals: Guru Purnima — the full moon honouring teachers, his day by association
Thursday observances — Brihaspativar vrat kept with yellow food and clothing
entities.worship: He is worshipped chiefly as the graha Jupiter in the Navagraha shrines that stand in most south Indian temples, approached when a horoscope calls for strengthening. The Thursday fast in his name, kept with yellow clothes, chana dal and turmeric, is common in north Indian households, particularly for the education and marriage prospects of children.
entities.bio: Preceptor and priest of the gods, lord of prayer and eloquence, identified with the planet Jupiter.
entities.longBio: Brihaspati enters the Rigveda as Brahmanaspati, lord of the sacred formula, whose speech has force in itself: he cracks open the Vala cave with a shout and releases the cattle hidden inside, a myth that runs parallel to Indra's dragon-slaying but is won by utterance rather than a weapon. As the gods acquired a court he became its chaplain, the one who performs their rites and blocks the rites of their enemies, which sets him permanently against Shukra, the Asuras' teacher, in a rivalry the Puranas develop at length. His household provides the tradition with its most awkward scandal: Chandra abducted his wife Tara, refused to return her, and the resulting war among the gods ended only when Brahma intervened, after which Tara bore a son, Budha, whom both fathers claimed. Another episode has him refuse to teach his nephew Kacha, sent by the Asuras to steal the secret of reviving the dead, and the resulting story of Kacha, Devayani and Shukra is one of the great Mahabharata set pieces. Astrology made him the most auspicious of the planets, the one whose aspect on a chart can rescue an otherwise bad configuration, and a Sanskrit school of materialism unrelated to him borrowed his name as Barhaspatya, which is why he is sometimes mistakenly connected with atheist doctrine.
entities.variantTraditions: Son of the sage Angiras.

entities.name: Shukra
entities.role: Guru of the Asuras; planet Venus
epithets: Kavi or Ushanas — the seer, his oldest Vedic name
Ekakshi — the one-eyed, after Vamana blinded him
domains: the planet Venus and its influence
revival of the dead through sanjivani vidya
symbols: the staff and rosary of a teacher
a chariot drawn by white horses
entities.mount: A chariot drawn by eight or ten white horses
entities.abode: Shukraloka; and the courts of the asura kings
festivals: Friday observances — Shukravar vrat kept for marital happiness and prosperity
entities.worship: Like the other grahas he is worshipped in the Navagraha shrine, offered white flowers, rice and curd, and approached in horoscopes for matters of marriage, art and comfort. The Friday fast in his name, widespread in north India, is kept by women for household prosperity and is often merged with the worship of Santoshi Mata or Lakshmi.
entities.bio: Son of the sage Bhrigu and preceptor of the Asuras, who knew the secret of reviving the dead (Sanjivani vidya); identified with the planet Venus.
entities.longBio: Shukra is the son of Bhrigu and appears in the Rigveda as Kavi Ushanas, a seer of unusual insight, before the Puranas cast him as the counsellor of the asuras and permanent counterpart to Brihaspati. His decisive advantage is sanjivani vidya, the knowledge that brings the dead back, won by austerity from Shiva, which meant that asura armies could be reassembled after every defeat while dead devas stayed dead. The gods answered by sending Brihaspati's son Kacha to study under him and steal the knowledge, and Shukra's daughter Devayani fell in love with the boy, who learned the vidya from inside his teacher's stomach after being killed, ground up and mixed into his drink, then refused Devayani as a wife because he had been reborn from her father. He lost an eye in the Vamana story, when he took the form of a bee or an insect to block the spout of Bali's water pot and stop the fatal gift of three paces, and Vishnu pierced the obstruction with a blade of kusha grass. Texts treat him with respect rather than as a villain: he warns his students against ruinous pride, he is credited with a work on statecraft, the Shukra Niti, and his loyalty to pupils the gods considered enemies is presented as the mark of a real teacher. In astrology he governs love, luxury, vehicles and the arts, and he is the most benefic planet after Jupiter.

entities.name: Vritra
epithets: Vritra — the encloser, he who covers or obstructs
Aparva — the jointless one, without hands or feet
symbols: mountains that hold the waters back
the foam that finally kills him
entities.abode: The mountain enclosure where he penned the rivers
entities.worship: He receives no worship and never did; he exists in living culture only as the thing Indra defeated, recalled in the title Vritrahan and in Vedic recitation. Where the drought myth survives in village practice it survives as rain ritual, not as any attention to him.
entities.bio: The dragon who imprisoned the world's waters until Indra slew him with the thunderbolt — the central heroic myth of the Rigveda. Counted among the Danavas.
entities.longBio: Vritra is the central antagonist of the Rigveda, a limbless serpent lying across the mountains with the world's waters penned behind him, and Indra's killing of him with the vajra is the act the hymns return to more than any other. The word vritra means the coverer or obstructor, and the fight reads at once as the monsoon breaking, as light returning after darkness, and as order asserting itself over inertia. He is called a Danava, son of Danu, and the name links him to a wide family of Indo-European water-blocking dragons from Iranian Azhi Dahaka to the serpents killed by Thor and by Zeus. The Puranas complicate the story considerably. There Vritra is made by Tvashtr to avenge a son Indra had killed, and he is a brahmin, so that killing him incurs brahmahatya, the gravest sin, which pursues Indra out of heaven and is finally divided among earth, water, trees and women, each taking a share with a compensation. In the Bhagavata Purana he is a devotee of Vishnu who speaks calmly about death before the fight, and Indra hesitates. A boon that no weapon of wood, metal or stone, wet or dry, could kill him forces the strange solution of foam from the sea, in which Vishnu hides.
entities.variantTraditions: In some Puranic tellings a Brahmin, whose killing stains Indra.

entities.name: Shani
symbols: black clothes, black sesame and iron
a limp, from an injured leg
entities.mount: Kaka — crow; a vulture or buffalo in some descriptions
entities.abode: Shanidhama; the planetary sphere of Saturn
festivals: Shani Jayanti — his birth day on the new moon of Jyeshtha
Saturday observances — oil, black sesame and iron offered at his shrine
entities.worship: Saturdays bring the largest crowds of any planetary worship in India, at Shani Shingnapur in Maharashtra, Tirunallar in Tamil Nadu and countless roadside shrines where mustard oil is poured over a black stone. He is approached during the seven-and-a-half-year sade sati, and giving oil, black cloth, iron or food to the poor on a Saturday is the standard remedy.
entities.bio: Slow-moving dispenser of the fruits of one's deeds, feared and propitiated; son of Surya and Chhaya (Shadow).
entities.longBio: Shani is the son of Surya and Chhaya, the shadow woman Sanjna left in her place, and his mother's nature explains his own: he was born dark and cold to the hottest of fathers, who is said to have doubted the child was his, and the resentment between them is fixed in the tradition. His gaze is the problem. Whatever he looks at directly is damaged, and several stories have him keep his eyes lowered for that reason, including one in which a glance at the infant Ganesha takes off his head, an alternative to the more common account of Shiva's anger. He is not malicious. The tradition is consistent that Shani gives exactly what has been earned, neither more nor less, and that his slowness is the delay between an act and its result, which is why his period is dreaded by people who have something to answer for. The famous story of Vikramaditya, or in other tellings King Nala, shows him stripping a good man of everything for the duration of his transit and returning it afterward, the point being endurance rather than escape. He is Yama's brother, and the two divide the work between judgment after death and consequences during life. At Shani Shingnapur the villagers traditionally build houses without doors, on the reasoning that a god who ensures nobody keeps what is not theirs makes locks unnecessary.

entities.name: Rahu
epithets: Rahu — the seizer, the one who grabs
Svarbhanu — his older Vedic name, the light of heaven
domains: the north lunar node in astrology
symbols: a severed head without a body
a serpent's tail below the neck
a chariot drawn by eight black horses
entities.mount: A chariot drawn by eight black horses
entities.abode: The lunar nodes, moving always backward through the zodiac
festivals: Rahu Kalam — the inauspicious hour of each day that is avoided rather than celebrated
Eclipse observances — bathing, fasting and charity while the sun or moon is covered
entities.worship: He is propitiated rather than praised, at Navagraha shrines and at specialised temples such as Thirunageswaram in Tamil Nadu, where milk poured over his image is said to turn blue.
