The daily ninety-minute Rahu Kalam is avoided for beginning anything important across much of south India, and eclipse days are kept with bathing and giving.
entities.bio: A Danava who drank the nectar of immortality in disguise; beheaded by Vishnu, his immortal head now periodically swallows the sun and moon, causing eclipses.
entities.longBio: The Rigveda already knows an eclipse demon named Svarbhanu who pierces the sun with darkness until Atri finds the sun again and restores it, and the Puranas rewrite him as Rahu, a Danava born to Viprachitti and Simhika. During the churning of the ocean he slipped into the line of gods in disguise and drank the nectar; the sun and moon recognised him and pointed him out, and Vishnu as Mohini cut his head off with the discus before the nectar passed his throat. Because the nectar had already reached the head, the head could not die, and it has been chasing the two informers ever since, swallowing them at intervals and letting them fall out of the open neck. The body, joined to a serpent's tail, became Ketu, the descending node, so the pair are one being divided. Astronomically the nodes are the points where the moon's path crosses the sun's, which is exactly where eclipses can happen, so the myth encodes a correct observation. Astrology gives them no physical body and calls them shadow planets, and Rahu's influence is read as amplification without limit: hunger, ambition, brilliance and delusion, whatever he touches taken past its natural size.
entities.variantTraditions: His body became Ketu, the south lunar node.

entities.name: Kamadeva
epithets: Ananga — the bodiless, after he was burned
Pushpadhanva — he whose bow is of flowers
domains: the force that drives creation onward
symbols: sugarcane bow strung with humming bees
the cuckoo and the south wind, his companions
entities.mount: Shuka — parrot
entities.abode: Wherever spring is; he has no fixed heaven after losing his body
festivals: Holi — in some regions the bonfire is read as Kamadeva's burning, and in the south Kama Dahanam is kept explicitly for it
Vasant Panchami — the opening of spring, his season
Madanotsava — the classical spring festival of love, largely lapsed but preserved in poetry
entities.worship: He has few temples and little formal worship, but he is thoroughly alive in Sanskrit and regional poetry, in classical dance where his five arrows are named and mimed, and in the vocabulary of romance across Indian languages. In parts of the south, Kama Dahanam at Holi enacts his burning, with Rati's lament performed as song.
entities.bio: Archer of love with a sugarcane bow and flower arrows. Burned to ash by Shiva's third eye for disturbing his meditation, then restored bodiless ('Ananga').
entities.longBio: Kamadeva shoots with a bow of sugarcane strung with bees and five arrows tipped with flowers, each named for a stage of longing, and his approach is announced by the cuckoo and the south wind. The Atharvaveda already speaks of kama as a cosmic force older than the gods, the first movement in the mind of the one, and the Puranic archer is a personification of that. His central story is his death: the gods, needing a son of Shiva to defeat the demon Taraka, send him to break Shiva's meditation and turn him toward Parvati, and he does it knowing what it will cost, taking the shot and being burned to ash by the third eye. Rati's grief brings the gods to intercede, and Shiva restores him without a body, which is why he is Ananga, present everywhere and visible nowhere, a compromise the poets found more interesting than either outcome. Kalidasa builds the Kumarasambhava around the episode and treats it as the moment desire becomes invisible and therefore inescapable. The Puranas add a rebirth: he returns as Pradyumna, son of Krishna and Rukmini, stolen as an infant by the demon Shambara and raised by Mayavati, who is Rati waiting for him. In the Vaishnava reading, love that was burned by asceticism is restored inside a family.
entities.variantTraditions: Reborn as Krishna's son Pradyumna in the epics.

entities.name: Rati
epithets: Rati — pleasure, delight, the act of love
Mayavati — the illusion-holder, her name in the Pradyumna story
Preeti — affection, her name or her sister depending on the text
symbols: flowers and vines in her hair
the parrot she shares with Kamadeva
a bow and arrows in some southern images
entities.abode: With Kamadeva, wherever spring is
festivals: Kama Dahanam at Holi — her lament for the burned Kamadeva is performed in southern and Deccan tradition
Vasant Panchami — kept with Kamadeva as the festival of spring and love
entities.worship: She is not worshipped alone but appears with Kamadeva in temple sculpture, particularly on gateways and in erotic panels, and in wedding contexts where the couple is compared to Rati and Kama. Her strongest living presence is performative: her lament is sung and danced at Holi in Karnataka and Andhra, and classical dance repertoire includes her mourning as a set piece.
entities.bio: Consort of Kamadeva, daughter of Daksha; personification of desire and pleasure, who won her husband's restoration after Shiva burned him.
entities.longBio: Rati is a daughter of Daksha in most accounts, and the Kalika Purana gives her a stranger origin, produced from the sweat of Daksha or from Brahma at the moment desire first entered the world, so that she and Kama are born of the same impulse. Her name is the plain Sanskrit word for sexual pleasure, and unlike many consorts she is not a softened version of her husband but the experience to his intention: he is the wish, she is the having. Her defining scene is a widow's. When Shiva burns Kamadeva to ash she throws herself over the ashes and refuses to move, and the gods, unable to make her stop, bring her before Shiva, who relents so far as to restore her husband invisibly, promising that she alone will see him. Kalidasa's account of her lament is among the most affecting passages in Sanskrit poetry, and it is the part of the myth that regional performance keeps alive. The Bhagavata Purana continues her story: she is reborn as Mayavati in the house of the demon Shambara, who has stolen the infant Pradyumna, and she raises the child who is her own husband, waiting until he is grown to tell him who they both are, a resolution that has troubled commentators and fascinated storytellers ever since.

entities.name: Vishvakarma
epithets: Tvashtr — the fashioner, his older Vedic identity
Prajapati — lord of creatures, in his creator aspect
Sutradhara — holder of the measuring line
domains: metalwork and the forging of weapons
design of cities and divine vehicles
symbols: four arms and a white beard
the swan he rides in some images
entities.mount: Hamsa — swan; an elephant in some regional depictions
entities.abode: Vishvakarmaloka; his workshop among the gods
festivals: Vishvakarma Puja — held in September, when workers garland and rest their tools and machines
Vishvakarma Jayanti — kept in some regions in the winter month of Magha
entities.worship: Vishvakarma Puja is one of the few festivals organised around work itself: on his day factories, garages, workshops and taxi stands stop, machines are washed, garlanded and left idle, and the tools that earn a living are worshipped. Artisan communities across India, particularly the Vishwakarma castes of blacksmiths, carpenters, goldsmiths and stone-carvers, claim descent from him and hold him as their lineage deity.
entities.bio: Architect of the gods who built the cities of the devas, forged their weapons, and fashioned divine chariots.
entities.longBio: In the Rigveda Vishvakarma is a name for the maker of everything, asked in a famous hymn what he stood on and what he used for material when he fashioned the earth and sky, a question the hymn does not answer. He merges with Tvashtr, the Vedic artisan who shaped the vajra for Indra and whose son Indra killed, provoking the creation of Vritra. Puranic literature turns him from a cosmogonic figure into a working architect with a body of famous commissions: golden Lanka, built for Shiva and later occupied by Ravana, Krishna's city of Dvaraka raised overnight from the sea, Indra's Amaravati, the Pandavas' hall of illusions at Indraprastha, Pushpaka the flying chariot, and the weapons of most of the gods. His most consequential job was surgical rather than architectural, trimming an eighth from Surya's brilliance on a lathe when his daughter Sanjna could not bear her husband's heat, and forging Vishnu's discus, Shiva's trident and Kubera's weapon from the shavings. The Vastu Shastra and the Shilpa Shastras, India's manuals of building and image-making, are attributed to him, which makes him the patron of a technical literature as well as of the people who use it. He is sometimes paired or confused with Maya, the asuras' architect, and the two are set against each other as rival builders.
entities.variantTraditions: Father of Sanjna, wife of Surya.

entities.name: Ganga
epithets: Jahnavi — daughter of the sage Jahnu, who swallowed and released her
Tripathaga — she who travels three worlds
domains: the river Ganga and its waters
symbols: Shiva's matted hair, where she falls
entities.mount: Makara — a crocodile-like river creature
entities.abode: Shiva's hair, and the river from Gangotri to the sea
festivals: Ganga Dussehra — the day of her descent to earth
Ganga Saptami — her second birth from Jahnu's ear
Kumbh Mela — the great bathing gathering at her confluences
Kartik Purnima — lamps floated on the river at Varanasi
entities.worship: Bathing in her is the central act: at Haridwar, Varanasi, Prayagraj and Gangotri, and at the Kumbh Mela, which draws the largest gatherings of people anywhere on earth. Her water is carried home sealed in copper pots for rituals and placed in the mouth of the dying, and ashes of the dead are given to her in the belief that she carries them past rebirth.
entities.bio: The Ganges personified. Descended from heaven through Shiva's matted hair; carried the infant Kartikeya; as Shantanu's wife, mother of Bhishma.
entities.longBio: Ganga is a river before she is a goddess and never stops being both, which is why her worship happens standing in her rather than in front of an image. The descent myth explains the arrangement: the sixty thousand sons of King Sagara were burned to ash by the sage Kapila's glance, and only the heavenly river could give them the water rites they needed, so Bhagiratha performed austerities for generations until Brahma agreed to release her. Her fall would have shattered the earth, so Shiva took the impact on his head and let her out slowly through his matted hair, and she is shown falling there in temple images across India. On the way down the sage Jahnu swallowed her when she flooded his rite and released her from his ear, which is why she is Jahnavi. In the Mahabharata she takes human form as the wife of King Shantanu on the condition that he never question her, and she drowns seven newborn sons, who are cursed Vasus she is releasing, before he breaks the condition and she leaves with the eighth, Bhishma. She is also foster-mother to Kartikeya, carrying Shiva's fire when the Krittikas take over. The contradiction between her ritual purity and her measurable pollution today is the subject of serious argument within Hindu practice, and the cleanup campaigns are argued in religious as well as environmental terms.

entities.name: Daksha
epithets: Ajamukha — the goat-faced, after his head was replaced
domains: procreation and the peopling of the worlds
symbols: a goat's head on a man's body
the enclosure of a fire altar
entities.abode: Kankhal near Haridwar, the site of his sacrifice
festivals: Maha Shivaratri and Navaratri observances at Kankhal — where his sacrifice is located and Sati's story retold
entities.worship: He is not worshipped as a benefactor but remembered as a cautionary figure, and the Daksheshwar Mahadev temple at Kankhal in Haridwar marks the site of his ruined sacrifice, drawing pilgrims for Shivaratri. His name survives most actively in genealogy, since almost every divine family in the Puranas traces back to one of his daughters.
entities.bio: A mind-born son of Brahma and lord of created beings. His many daughters — Sati, Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kadru, Vinata and more — mothered gods, demons, serpents and birds. His insult to Shiva led to Sati's self-immolation.
entities.longBio: Daksha is a mind-born son of Brahma whose job is to populate the worlds, and he does it through daughters: Aditi mothers the gods, Diti the Daityas, Danu the Danavas, Kadru the serpents, Vinata the birds, and twenty-seven more become the lunar mansions married to Chandra. His name means competent, and his failing is exactly that competence turned into pride in his own rank. He objected to his daughter Sati's marriage to Shiva, a matted ascetic who kept company with ghosts in cremation grounds, and when he held a great sacrifice he invited every god except his son-in-law. Sati went uninvited, was insulted, and gave up her body in the fire, either by yoga or by walking into the flames depending on the text. Shiva tore a hair from his head and produced Virabhadra, who destroyed the sacrifice, scattered the gods and beheaded Daksha; when the gods pleaded, Shiva restored him with a goat's head, the animal of the sacrifice he had been so proud of. Some Puranas end the story with Daksha becoming Shiva's devotee and composing a hymn to him, while others keep the humiliation as the point. Shiva's wandering with Sati's body, and the fifty-one places where pieces of it fell, produced the Shakti Pithas, so the whole map of goddess pilgrimage in India begins with a family quarrel over a guest list.

entities.name: Kashyapa
epithets: Kashyapa — the tortoise, from an old etymology
Aristanemi — an alternative name used in the Mahabharata
domains: progeniture of gods, demons and animals
lineage and the ordering of species
symbols: the water pot and deerskin of an ascetic
the tortoise associated with his name
entities.abode: His hermitage; and among the Saptarishi stars
festivals: Guru Purnima — honoured with the Saptarishi as one of the founding sages
entities.worship: He is not worshipped with images but invoked constantly in a way few gods are: the Kashyapa gotra is among the most widely claimed brahmin lineages, so his name is spoken in the sankalpa that opens rituals and in the introductions of weddings across India. Kashmir takes its name from him in local tradition, which holds that he drained the valley's lake to make it habitable.
entities.bio: Grandson of Brahma through Marichi and husband of thirteen daughters of Daksha. Through Aditi he fathered the Devas, through Diti the Daityas, through Danu the Danavas, through Kadru the Nagas, and through Vinata Garuda and Aruna — making him father of nearly all beings.
entities.longBio: Kashyapa is the great-grandson of Brahma through Marichi, and Puranic genealogy makes him the bottleneck through which almost every category of being passes. Married to thirteen of Daksha's daughters, he fathered the Adityas by Aditi, the Daityas by Diti, the Danavas by Danu, the serpents by Kadru, Garuda and Aruna by Vinata, and through others the cattle, trees, birds and demons, so that gods and their enemies are half-brothers, which is why the conflict between them in the Puranas is a family conflict rather than a war of good against evil. That structure has consequences the texts exploit: Diti performs a vow to produce a son who will kill Indra, Indra sabotages it, and the fragments become the Maruts, and Kadru and Vinata's wager over the colour of a horse's tail leads to the enmity between serpents and birds and to Garuda's theft of the nectar. He is counted among the Saptarishi, the seven sages fixed in the stars of the Great Bear, though the lists differ from text to text, and he presides over the current Manvantara. The Mahabharata and the Vishnu Purana do not agree on the details of his marriages or his children, and the discrepancies are old enough that commentators treat them as separate traditions rather than errors. In Kashmir he is remembered locally as the sage who cut the hills and let the water out of the valley.
entities.variantTraditions: Genealogies differ between the Vishnu Purana and Mahabharata.

entities.name: Aditi
epithets: Aditi — the unbound, the free one
Akhilajanani — mother of all that exists
Devaki-in-a-former-birth — named in Puranic accounts as her later rebirth
symbols: the cow as image of nourishment
the earth as her extended body
entities.abode: the celestial sphere, with Kashyapa's hermitage in Puranic accounts
entities.worship: Aditi has few temples of her own but is invoked constantly in Vedic liturgy, in the Aditya hymns recited at dawn, and in the Gayatri and Surya rites where her sons are addressed. Priests still name her in sankalpa formulas that place a rite within a lineage.
entities.bio: Boundless sky-mother of the Adityas — Indra, Surya, Varuna and the other celestial gods — and, in the Puranas, of Vishnu's dwarf avatar Vamana.
entities.longBio: Aditi belongs to the oldest layer of the Rigveda, where her name means the unbound or the limitless, the opposite of diti, restriction. She is less a character with a biography than a principle: the open expanse from which the Adityas emerge, among them Varuna, Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga and, in later reckoning, Surya and Indra. Hymns describe her paradoxically as both mother and daughter of Daksha, a deliberate riddle about origins that Vedic poets enjoyed rather than resolved. The Puranas domesticate her considerably, making her a daughter of Daksha and wife of the sage Kashyapa, and setting her against her sister Diti, whose sons became the Asuras. In that later frame her defining act is ascetic: stripped of heaven by Bali, she performs the Payovrata fast until Vishnu is born from her as the dwarf Vamana and wins the worlds back. Some Vaishnava texts extend the line further and identify her as reborn as Devaki, mother of Krishna, so that the same womb bears the god twice.

entities.name: Diti
symbols: the broken womb split into seven
ascetic fire and the unfinished penance
the twin sons Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu
entities.abode: the hermitage of Kashyapa
entities.worship: Diti receives no independent cult, but her story is retold in Puranic recitation and in temple discourse wherever the Varaha and Narasimha episodes are performed. She functions in living tradition as the counterweight who explains why the world contains adversaries at all.
entities.bio: Sister and rival of Aditi; mother of the Daitya demons including Hiranyakashipu and Hiranyaksha, and grandmother-ancestor of Mahabali and Tarakasura.
entities.longBio: Diti is the sister and structural opposite of Aditi: her name means the bound or divided, and her children, the Daityas, are the gods' half-brothers and permanent rivals. The Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas give her a famous double tragedy. Grieving after Vishnu kills her sons Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu, she begs Kashyapa for a child strong enough to kill Indra, and he grants it on the condition that she keep a year-long vow with perfect purity. She falters once, sleeping at twilight with unwashed feet, and Indra enters her womb and cuts the embryo into pieces with his thunderbolt. Each piece cries out, Indra says ma ruda, do not weep, and the fragments become the forty-nine Maruts, storm gods who serve Indra instead of destroying him. It is a story about how an act of vengeance can be turned into an alliance, and Diti accepts the reversal. Some Puranas soften her further into a penitent figure, while the older Vedic material barely knows her except as a shadow-word paired with Aditi.

entities.name: Danu
epithets: Danu — the flowing one, from a root meaning stream
entities.abode: the hermitage of Kashyapa
entities.worship: Danu has no temple cult. She survives in Puranic genealogy and in the Vedic imagery of held-back waters, and her name is invoked mainly by scholars and storytellers explaining the many-branched family of Kashyapa.
entities.bio: Daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa; mother of the Danava class of Asuras, among them the drought serpent Vritra.
entities.longBio: In the Rigveda, Danu appears chiefly as the mother of Vritra, who is called Danava after her, and one striking hymn shows her lying beside her slain son like a cow beside its calf after Indra has cut them both down. The word danu itself carries the sense of flowing liquid, which fits a mythology in which Vritra hoards the waters and Indra's thunderbolt releases them. Later genealogy tidies this into a family tree: Danu becomes one of Daksha's many daughters, married with her sisters to the sage Kashyapa, and the ancestress of a whole class of Asuras distinct from Diti's Daityas. Her sons include Vritra, the shape-shifting Maya, and in many lists Rahu, whose severed head swallows the sun and moon at eclipses. The Danavas are not simply evil in these texts; several are skilled architects and ascetics, and the line between Danava and Deva is drawn by allegiance more than by nature. Puranic authors differ on where exactly to place several of her sons, and the lists rarely agree in detail.

entities.name: Kadru
epithets: Kadru — the tawny or reddish-brown one
Sarpamata — she from whom snakes descend
symbols: the black hairs cast onto Uchchaihshravas's tail
the tawny colour of her name
entities.abode: Patala, the serpent realm below the earth
festivals: Naga Panchami — the summer day when snakes and their divine mothers are honoured with milk and offerings
entities.worship: Kadru is not worshipped directly, but the Nagas she bore are, at anthills, serpent stones and Naga shrines across India, especially on Naga Panchami. Her story is recited in the Astika Parva of the Mahabharata as a protective charm against snakebite.
entities.bio: Wife of Kashyapa and mother of a thousand serpents, including Shesha and Vasuki. Her rivalry with her sister Vinata led to Garuda's enmity with snakes.
entities.longBio: Kadru opens the Mahabharata's serpent cycle. Given a boon by Kashyapa, she asks for a thousand serpent sons while her co-wife Vinata asks for only two of surpassing strength, and the contrast between quantity and quality drives everything that follows. The two women wager their freedom on the colour of the tail of Uchchaihshravas, the horse risen from the churned ocean; Kadru orders her sons to cling to its tail as black hairs, and when some refuse she curses them to burn in a future snake sacrifice. Vinata loses and becomes her slave, an injustice that Kadru enforces without apology and that Garuda later ends by fetching the nectar of immortality. The curse hangs over the epic and eventually comes due at King Janamejaya's sarpa satra, halted only by the sage Astika. Kadru is one of the sharper portraits of maternal ambition in Sanskrit literature, willing to sacrifice her own children to win a bet, and the texts do not excuse her. Some Puranic versions soften the wager into a misunderstanding, but the Mahabharata is blunt about the deceit.

entities.name: Vinata
epithets: Vinata — the bowed or humbled one
Suparnamata — mother of the fair-winged one
domains: birds and the winds of the upper air
entities.abode: the hermitage of Kashyapa
entities.worship: Vinata has no cult of her own; she is remembered through her sons, invoked in Garuda hymns and in the Garuda Panchami vow observed in parts of western India, where women fast for the wellbeing of their brothers and children.
entities.bio: Wife of Kashyapa and mother of the divine birds Aruna and Garuda; enslaved by her sister Kadru until Garuda ransomed her with the nectar of immortality.
entities.longBio: Vinata chose two mighty sons over Kadru's thousand ordinary ones, and then could not wait for them. Impatient after long years, she cracked the first egg early and found a child formed only to the waist, who cursed her to serve her rival for five hundred years before flying up to become Aruna, the red glow that precedes the sun. She left the second egg alone, and from it came Garuda. Her enslavement to Kadru is the epic's picture of dignity in humiliation: she serves without complaint, and her son takes the injustice on himself. When Garuda asks how to free her, the serpents demand the amrita, and he raids Indra's heaven to get it. Vinata's freedom is bought and the serpents are cheated of the nectar by a legal trick, which is why snakes shed their skins and why Garuda hunts them. She is a study in the difference between what a mother asks for and what she can bear to wait for.

entities.name: Garuda
epithets: Tarkshya — swift one, an old Vedic bird name
Periya Thiruvadi — the great servant, his Tamil Vaishnava title
symbols: eagle beak and talons with a human torso
a serpent gripped in claw or beak
hands folded in anjali before Vishnu
entities.abode: Vaikuntha, at Vishnu's side
festivals: Garuda Panchami — a vow day in the month of Shravana honouring him and the serpents
Garuda Seva — temple processions, notably at Tirumala and Srirangam, where the deity rides a great Garuda vahana
entities.worship: Nearly every Vishnu temple sets a Garuda shrine or pillar directly facing the sanctum, and devotees pass their prayers through him. He is invoked against snakebite and poison through the Garuda mantra and Garuda Panchakshari, and his image on temple flags and processional mounts is one of the most common sights in Vaishnava practice.
entities.bio: Colossal eagle son of Kashyapa and Vinata, eternal enemy of serpents, who stole the nectar of immortality from the gods to free his mother — and became Vishnu's mount.
entities.longBio: Garuda hatched from Vinata's second egg fully grown and blazing so brightly that the gods mistook him for Agni. Learning that his mother was a slave to Kadru, he flew to the gods' heaven, scattered the celestial army, passed a wall of fire and a wheel of spinning blades, and carried off the pot of amrita, defeating Indra's thunderbolt with a single dropped feather. He never drank a drop of it. Vishnu, impressed by that restraint, granted him immortality without the nectar and took him as his mount, while Indra recovered the amrita by a bargain that left the serpents licking sharp kusha grass and splitting their tongues. Vaishnava tradition made him the model of the servant whose strength is entirely at another's disposal, and the Garuda Purana is framed as Vishnu's instruction to him, largely on death and the fate of the soul. He is worshipped in his own right in parts of South and Southeast Asia, and appears as the national emblem of Indonesia and Thailand's royal insignia, carried there by centuries of Hindu and Buddhist exchange.

entities.name: Aruna
entities.role: Charioteer of the Sun; the dawn-red sky
epithets: Aruna — the reddish glow of dawn
Anuru — the thighless one, from his broken birth
symbols: a body formed only to the waist
red and saffron light on the horizon
entities.abode: the chariot of Surya
entities.worship: Aruna is honoured indirectly in every sunrise rite: the arghya offered to the rising sun and the Aruna Prashna, a Vedic hymn recited at dawn in South Indian temples and at Surya shrines such as Konark, where the eastern approach is dedicated to him.
entities.bio: Elder brother of Garuda, born prematurely without lower limbs; drives Surya's chariot. Father of the vulture brothers Jatayu and Sampati.
entities.longBio: Aruna is the light that arrives before the sun does, personified as a charioteer whose body stops at the waist because his mother opened his egg too soon. Rather than resenting the flaw, he took the front seat of Surya's chariot, where his half-formed body shields the world from the full heat behind him, an explanation the Puranas offer with some satisfaction. He cursed Vinata for her impatience, then softened it by promising that her second son would free her. One well-known episode has him take female form as Aruni to enter the women's assembly in Indra's heaven, and from that night comes Vali, while a similar union with Surya produces Sugriva, which is why the two vanara brothers of the Ramayana are sons of the sun and its dawn. In another line he fathers the vultures Jatayu and Sampati, so the bird who dies defending Sita descends from the dawn itself. The older Vedic material personifies dawn as the goddess Ushas instead, and Aruna belongs to the later reworking of that imagery into a chariot scene.

entities.name: Shesha (Ananta)
epithets: Shesha — what is left over when all else is dissolved
Sankarshana — his cosmic form in Pancharatra theology
symbols: a thousand raised hoods forming a canopy
coils spread as a couch on the causal ocean
plough and pestle in his Balarama form
a jewel blazing on each hood
entities.abode: the Kshira Sagara, the ocean of milk, and Patala below the worlds
festivals: Naga Panchami — serpent worship in the month of Shravana
Ananta Chaturdashi — a vow to Ananta Padmanabha, when a fourteen-knotted cord is tied on the wrist
entities.worship: He is worshipped wherever Vishnu reclines, above all at Anantha Padmanabhaswamy in Thiruvananthapuram, a city named for him, and at Srirangam. The Ananta Vrata performed on Bhadrapada Chaturdashi, with its knotted thread, is his principal household observance.
entities.bio: Thousand-headed king of the Nagas, son of Kashyapa and Kadru, upon whose coils Vishnu rests between cosmic ages. Incarnates as Lakshmana and (traditionally) Balarama.
entities.longBio: Shesha is what remains when the universe is folded up, which is what his name means, and his other name Ananta says the same thing from the other side: he does not end. He is a son of Kashyapa and Kadru who left his brothers in disgust at their cruelty to Vinata and performed austerities until Brahma gave him the task of holding the earth steady on his hoods. Between world ages Vishnu sleeps on his coils on the causal ocean, with Ananta's hoods raised as a canopy, and when he yawns or shifts, earthquakes follow; at the end of a kalpa the fire of dissolution comes from his mouths. Vaishnava tradition holds that he incarnates alongside Vishnu to serve him, as Lakshmana beside Rama and as Balarama beside Krishna, though some schools give Balarama a fuller divine status rather than treating him as Shesha alone. Ramanuja, the great Srivaishnava teacher, is likewise regarded by his followers as an incarnation of Shesha. In every version his character is the same: he carries, and he does not complain about the weight.

entities.name: Vasuki
epithets: Vasuki — of the class of the Vasus, the excellent one
Sarpahara — the serpent worn as a garland by Shiva
domains: the churning of the ocean and the winning of amrita
symbols: a serpent coiled around Shiva's throat
the churning rope wound round Mount Mandara
halahala poison spilling from his mouths
entities.abode: Bhogavati, the serpent city in Patala, and the neck of Shiva
festivals: Naga Panchami — snakes are offered milk and turmeric, and Vasuki is named among the eight great Nagas
entities.worship: Vasuki is named in the standard list of eight Nagas invoked in temple ritual and in snakebite mantras, and he is present in almost every image of Shiva, coiled at the throat. Serpent shrines in Kerala, Karnataka and the Himalayas, including the Vasuki temples of Uttarakhand and Kashmir, take him as their principal deity.
entities.bio: Naga king worn by Shiva as a necklace, who served as the churning-rope wound around Mount Mandara during the churning of the ocean of milk.
entities.longBio: Vasuki is the second of Kadru's sons after Shesha, and where Shesha withdrew from the world, Vasuki stayed to rule it. His best-known service is also his worst suffering: when gods and Asuras churned the ocean of milk, he agreed to be the rope, with the Asuras gripping his heads and the gods his tail, and the friction of the churning made him vomit the halahala poison that Shiva then drank to save the worlds. Shiva took him afterward as an ornament, and the serpent at Shiva's throat in nearly all iconography is Vasuki. He appears again in the Mahabharata as the ruler who shelters his people during Janamejaya's snake sacrifice and whose sister Jaratkaru bears Astika, the boy who stops the sacrifice and saves the serpent race. Some regional traditions conflate him with Shesha or with Takshaka, but the major Puranas keep the three distinct. He is the rare figure whose importance rests entirely on what he was willing to be used for.

entities.name: Sati
epithets: Sati — the true one, she who is
Uma — a name shared with her rebirth as Parvati
Shivaduti — she whose messenger is Shiva, in Tantric usage
domains: the sacred geography of the Shakti Pithas
rebirth and continuity of the goddess
symbols: the sacrificial fire of Daksha's yajna
her body carried on Shiva's shoulder
the fifty-one pithas marked where her limbs fell
entities.abode: Mount Kailash with Shiva, and Daksha's court before her death
festivals: Navaratri — the pithas born from her body are the focus of the nine nights of goddess worship
Ambubachi Mela — at Kamakhya in Assam, where her yoni is said to have fallen
entities.worship: Sati is worshipped through the network of Shakti Pithas, from Kamakhya in Assam to Kalighat in Kolkata and Hinglaj in Pakistan, each site claiming a part of her body. Pilgrimage to these shrines, rather than any single temple to Sati herself, is how her presence is kept.
entities.bio: Daughter of Daksha who married Shiva against her father's wishes and immolated herself when Daksha insulted him; reborn as Parvati.
entities.longBio: Sati was born to Daksha, a son of Brahma, and fixed her heart on Shiva, an ascetic her father regarded as unwashed and unsuitable. She won him through austerity, married him, and lived at Kailash until Daksha held a great sacrifice and pointedly invited every god except his son-in-law. She went uninvited, was insulted before the assembly, and gave up her body, in some accounts by yogic fire generated from within, in others by walking into the sacrificial flames; the practice later called sati takes its name from her, though the Puranic story is about a wife's refusal of dishonour rather than a widow's death. Shiva's grief unmade the sacrifice: he created Virabhadra, who beheaded Daksha, and then wandered the worlds carrying her corpse until Vishnu's discus cut it into pieces that fell across the subcontinent and became the Shakti Pithas. Shakta traditions read the dismemberment as the goddess distributing herself into the land itself, so that the map of India becomes her body. She returns as Parvati, daughter of the mountain, and wins Shiva a second time by penance, which is why the two goddesses are treated as one continuous person in most Puranic telling.

entities.name: Ganesha
entities.role: Remover of obstacles; god of beginnings
symbols: the broad belly and large ears
a snake tied about the waist
entities.mount: Mushika — a mouse or rat
entities.abode: Mount Kailash, and the threshold of every house and temple
festivals: Ganesh Chaturthi — ten days marking his birth, ending with clay images immersed in water
Sankashti Chaturthi — a monthly fast on the fourth day of the waning moon
Angarki Chaturthi — Sankashti falling on a Tuesday, held especially potent
entities.worship: No Hindu rite of any sect begins without invoking him first, from weddings and housewarmings to the opening of an account book. His image guards doorways, vehicles and shopfronts, and the Ganesh Chaturthi processions of Maharashtra, revived as a public festival by Tilak in the 1890s, draw millions.
entities.bio: Elephant-headed son of Parvati and Shiva, lord of wisdom and new undertakings, invoked at the start of every venture; scribe of the Mahabharata.
entities.longBio: Ganesha's most famous birth story has Parvati forming a boy from the turmeric paste of her bath and setting him to guard her door, where he refuses entry to Shiva, who strikes off his head; Parvati's fury is answered by fitting the head of the first creature found facing north, an elephant. Other Puranas give quite different accounts, including one where Shiva creates him directly and another where Parvati's laughter or Shani's gaze causes the beheading, and the Ganapatya sect went further, making him the supreme reality rather than Shiva's son. He broke his own tusk, by most tellings, to keep writing when his pen failed as Vyasa dictated the Mahabharata, on the condition that Vyasa never pause and Ganesha never transcribe without understanding. His nature is double: he is Vighnakarta as well as Vighnaharta, the one who sets obstacles as much as the one who clears them, which is why he is placated before any undertaking. The mouse he rides is variously explained as a subdued demon or as the small gnawing desire that a wise mind keeps under it. He travelled with trade and Buddhism into Central Asia, Tibet, Java and Japan, where he appears as Kangiten.
entities.variantTraditions: Birth stories vary — most famously fashioned by Parvati and beheaded, then revived, by Shiva.

entities.name: Kartikeya (Murugan)
entities.role: God of war; commander of the Devas
epithets: Skanda — the attacker, the one who leaps
Murugan — the youthful and beautiful one, his Tamil name
Devasenapati — commander of the divine army
domains: Tamil devotion and the hill country
symbols: the vel, a barbed spear given by his mother
the vibhuti and rudraksha of an ascetic
the staff and begging bowl of Palani
entities.mount: Paravani — a peacock
entities.abode: Mount Kailash by northern account; the six sacred hill sites of Tamil Nadu, chiefly Palani and Tiruchendur, by southern account
festivals: Thaipusam — his receiving of the vel from Parvati, marked by kavadi processions and vows
Skanda Sashti — six days recalling his defeat of Surapadman
Panguni Uthiram — his marriage to Deivanai
entities.worship: In Tamil Nadu, Sri Lanka, Malaysia and the wider Tamil diaspora he is the central deity, worshipped at the Arupadai Veedu, his six battle-camp temples, with kavadi carrying, head shaving and milk offerings. Northern India largely dropped his cult after the Gupta period, though he remains important in Bengal as Kartik and in parts of Andhra as Subrahmanya.
entities.bio: Six-faced son of Shiva, born to destroy the demon Tarakasura; carried by Ganga and nursed by the six Krittika stars. Widely worshipped as Murugan in South India.
entities.longBio: Kartikeya was conceived when Shiva's seed, too fierce for any womb, was carried by Agni and then by Ganga and finally deposited in a reed thicket, where the six Krittika stars nursed the child; he grew six faces to drink from all of them at once, and their name became his. He was made for a single purpose, to kill Tarakasura, whom Brahma's boon had made invulnerable to everyone except a son of Shiva, and he did it while still a boy, leading the gods' army with the vel that Parvati placed in his hand. In the Tamil tradition, which absorbed the older indigenous god Murugan into him, the great enemy is Surapadman, split by the vel into the peacock he rides and the rooster on his banner, so that the defeated becomes the vehicle. Tamil sources give him two wives, Deivanai the daughter of Indra and Valli the hunter girl he courted in the hills, and this pairing of the arranged and the chosen marriage is the heart of his southern story. His two personalities differ sharply: the northern Skanda is a martial youth of the Gupta courts, while the Tamil Murugan is a god of hills, love poetry and ecstatic vows, and at Palani he stands as a shaven ascetic with only a loincloth and staff after losing a contest with Ganesha over a fruit.

entities.name: Nandi
epithets: Nandi — the delightful, the happy one
domains: dharma, in the bull's ancient symbolism
music and dance, as Shiva's instructor
symbols: a white couchant bull facing the shrine
a bull's hump and lowered head
hands folded in worship in his anthropomorphic form
entities.abode: the entrance of every Shiva temple, and Mount Kailash
festivals: Mahashivaratri — the night vigil to Shiva, when Nandi is bathed and garlanded first
Mattu Pongal — the Tamil day honouring cattle, associated with him
entities.worship: Every Shiva temple has a Nandi couchant before the sanctum, and worshippers whisper their requests into his ear or look at the linga between his horns before approaching. Large monolithic Nandis at Lepakshi, Chamundi Hill and Thanjavur are pilgrimage sights in their own right.
entities.bio: Bull mount, gatekeeper and foremost devotee of Shiva; his statue faces the sanctum in every Shiva temple.
entities.longBio: Nandi began in the Vedas as the bull associated with Rudra and with dharma itself, whose four legs are said to be truth, purity, compassion and charity, and only later became a distinct attendant. The Puranas give him a human origin as the son of the sage Shilada, born through Shiva's grace and destined to die young until Shiva made him deathless and his own gatekeeper, chief of the ganas. He is also credited with a share of Shiva's arts: the treatise attributed to Nandikeshvara on gesture and dramatic expression makes him the teacher of dance and music, and he keeps time while Shiva performs the tandava. His posture is always the same, couchant, alert, eyes on the sanctum, which devotees read as the model of attention that never wanders. In some Shaiva temples he is shown fully human with a bull's head, and in Shaiva Siddhanta he stands for the individual soul turned permanently toward god. He is not a mount that merely carries; the tradition is quite firm that he is the foremost devotee, and worship offered to Shiva passes his gaze first.

entities.name: Durga
epithets: Mahishasuramardini — crusher of the buffalo demon
Sherawali — she of the lion, a north Indian name
domains: the gathered power of all the gods
symbols: eight or ten arms bearing the weapons of every god
trishula driven into the buffalo demon
a lion or tiger beneath her
the conch, discus, bow and thunderbolt
unbound hair and a serene face in the midst of battle
entities.mount: Simha or Dawon — a lion, sometimes a tiger
entities.abode: the Vindhya mountains, and Kailash as Shiva's consort
festivals: Durga Puja — five days in Bengal, Assam and Odisha celebrating her victory and her annual visit home
Navaratri — nine nights of the goddess, culminating in Vijayadashami
Chaitra Navaratri — the spring counterpart, observed across north and west India
entities.worship: Durga Puja in Bengal is among the largest religious festivals in the world, with commissioned clay images installed in temporary pandals and immersed on the tenth day. She is worshipped year-round at Vaishno Devi, Kamakhya and thousands of village shrines, and the Devi Mahatmya is chanted during Navaratri in homes and temples across India.
entities.bio: Ten-armed rider of the lion, created from the combined energies of the gods to slay the buffalo demon Mahishasura, whom no male being could kill.
entities.longBio: The Devi Mahatmya, composed around the sixth century and embedded in the Markandeya Purana, is the text that made Durga central. In it the buffalo demon Mahishasura has won a boon that no man or god can kill him, and the defeated gods pour their concentrated anger out as light that fuses into a woman; each god gives her his own weapon, so that her many arms are the assembled armoury of heaven. She rides a lion into the field, mocks the demon's marriage proposal, and pins him with her trident as he shifts between buffalo and man. The same text gives her further battles against Shumbha and Nishumbha and against Raktabija, and it argues theologically that she is not a helper of the gods but the primordial power from which they draw their own. Most traditions treat her as a form of Parvati and therefore of Adi Shakti, while Shakta schools reverse the hierarchy and make Shiva and Vishnu expressions of her. Bengal reads her annual festival domestically, as a married daughter coming home to her parents with her children Ganesha, Kartikeya, Lakshmi and Saraswati, which gives the fiercest image in Hindu art a strong undertone of homecoming.
entities.variantTraditions: Understood as a fierce form of Parvati / Adi Shakti.

entities.name: Kali
epithets: Kalika — the dark one, the feminine of time
Chamunda — slayer of Chanda and Munda
Dakshinakali — the southern-facing form worshipped in Bengal
Smashanakali — Kali of the cremation ground
symbols: a garland of fifty severed heads
a curved khadga sword and a severed head
black or deep blue skin, and four arms in abhaya and varada
entities.abode: the cremation ground
festivals: Kali Puja — the new moon night of Kartik, coinciding with Diwali in Bengal
Navaratri — she is honoured among the nine nights, particularly in the Kalaratri form
entities.worship: Her major temples are Kalighat and Dakshineswar in Kolkata, Kamakhya in Assam and Kalikambal in Chennai, and she is worshipped at night with hibiscus flowers, lamps and in some places animal sacrifice. Bengali devotional song, the Shyama Sangeet of Ramprasad Sen and others, addresses her as a mother in terms of startling intimacy.
entities.bio: The dark, wild goddess who sprang from Durga's brow in battle; garlanded with skulls, she destroys evil and ego alike, and dances upon the prone Shiva.
entities.longBio: Kali steps out of Durga's forehead in the Devi Mahatmya when the goddess's anger blackens her face, and she is loosed on the demon Raktabija, whose every spilled drop of blood becomes a new demon; she solves the problem by drinking the blood before it lands and swallowing the copies. Her best-known image comes from a related episode in which, drunk on victory, she dances until the world begins to break, and Shiva lies down in her path; she steps on him, and her tongue shoots out in shock, which is the pose that Bengali icons show. The reading of that image is disputed: Tantric interpreters take the protruding tongue as a sign of appetite and the trampling as shakti's precedence over inert consciousness, while popular devotion reads it as a mother's embarrassment. She is not simply a goddess of destruction; the black colour is explained as the absence in which all colours dissolve, and what she destroys is attachment, so she is called the giver of liberation. Bengali poet-devotees from the eighteenth century onward transformed her from a battlefield and cremation-ground figure into Ma Kali, an intimate mother scolded and pleaded with in song, and Ramakrishna's visions at Dakshineswar carried that devotion into the modern era. Tantric schools place her at the head of the ten Mahavidyas.

entities.name: Hanuman
epithets: Bajrangbali — he of limbs hard as the vajra
symbols: the mountain of healing herbs carried in one hand
a chest torn open to show Rama and Sita within
orange sindoor smeared over the body
a long tail raised behind him
entities.abode: no fixed abode; tradition holds he remains alive on earth wherever the Ramayana is recited
festivals: Hanuman Jayanti — his birth, observed on the full moon of Chaitra in the north and in Margashirsha in Tamil Nadu
Tuesdays and Saturdays — weekly days of fasting and temple visits in his honour
entities.worship: Hanuman shrines stand at village edges, roadsides, gyms and railway platforms across India, and the Hanuman Chalisa of Tulsidas is probably the most widely recited devotional text in the country. Wrestlers and bodybuilders take him as patron, offerings of sindoor and oil are standard, and he is invoked against fear, illness and malefic planetary influence.
entities.bio: Vanara son of the wind god Vayu (born to Anjana and Kesari), of limitless strength and humility. Leapt the ocean to find Sita and burned Lanka; the ideal of selfless devotion to Rama.
entities.longBio: Hanuman was born to the apsara Anjana, cursed into monkey form, and the vanara chief Kesari, with Vayu as his divine father, and as a child he leapt at the sun mistaking it for fruit until Indra's bolt broke his jaw, which is where the name Hanuman, from hanu or jaw, is usually traced. The sages then cursed him to forget his own powers until reminded, a device that explains why the mightiest being in the Ramayana must be told what he can do before he can do it. He crosses the ocean to Lanka in a single leap, finds Sita in the ashoka grove, delivers Rama's ring, allows himself to be captured, and burns the city with his blazing tail; later he carries the entire Dronagiri mountain when he cannot identify the herb that will revive Lakshmana. What the tradition prizes in him is not the strength but the disposition: asked what he wants, he asks only to remain in Rama's service, and he is counted a chiranjivi, deathless, present at every recitation of the story. Shaiva sources describe him as an amsha or full incarnation of Shiva, which lets him stand as a bridge between Shaiva and Vaishnava devotion. He is also called a master of Sanskrit grammar and the ninth teacher of that science, a side of him that the temple art rarely shows.
entities.variantTraditions: Often described as an amsha (partial incarnation) of Shiva.

entities.name: Dhanvantari
epithets: Amritakalasha-hasta — bearer of the pot of nectar
symbols: conch and discus, marking him as Vishnu
entities.abode: Vaikuntha; Kashi in his royal incarnation
festivals: Dhanteras or Dhanvantari Trayodashi — two days before Diwali, marking his emergence from the ocean and observed as National Ayurveda Day in India
entities.worship: Ayurvedic practitioners begin study and practice with the Dhanvantari mantra, and his image stands in Ayurvedic colleges, pharmacies and hospitals. His main temples are in Kerala, notably Nelluvaya and Thottuva, and Dhanteras brings household worship for health along with the customary purchase of metal.
entities.bio: Physician of the gods who rose from the churning ocean bearing the pot of amrita (nectar of immortality); regarded as a form of Vishnu.
entities.longBio: Dhanvantari appears at the climax of the churning of the ocean of milk, rising last from the water in dark robes with the pot of amrita in his hands, after which the gods and Asuras fight over it and Vishnu takes the form of Mohini to settle the matter. The Puranas treat him as a partial or full form of Vishnu who descends specifically to bring the science of healing to human beings, and the Bhagavata calls him the one who established Ayurveda as a branch of the Vedas. A second Dhanvantari appears in medical literature as a king of Kashi and teacher of the surgeon Sushruta, and the Sushruta Samhita is framed as his instruction, which lets the tradition connect divine origin with an actual textual lineage. Scholars generally distinguish these figures while the devotional tradition treats them as one continuous presence. He is unusual among deities in being worshipped chiefly by a profession, and the Indian government's placing of National Ayurveda Day on his festival gave that professional cult a modern institutional form. Iconographically he carries four items in Kerala usage, and the leech among them is a plain reminder that the medicine he represents is practical rather than miraculous.

entities.name: Airavata
epithets: Abhramu-pati — husband of the she-elephant Abhramu
Erawan — his Thai and Southeast Asian name
domains: royal power and the war elephant
the eastern quarter of the world
symbols: four tusks and seven trunks in the fullest descriptions
clouds drawn up from the underworld through his trunk
entities.abode: Amaravati, Indra's capital in Svarga
entities.worship: Airavata is not worshipped independently in India, but he is carved on temple gateways and on the Ashtadikgaja panels that mark the eight directions, and temple elephants are treated as his descendants. In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia the three-headed Erawan is a major public emblem, with the Erawan shrine in Bangkok among the busiest in the region.
entities.bio: Four-tusked white king of elephants who emerged from the churning of the ocean and bears Indra into battle.
entities.longBio: Airavata rose from the ocean of milk during the churning, white as a mountain of snow, and Indra claimed him as his mount. The Puranas connect him to weather directly: he is said to reach down into the waters of the underworld with his trunks, draw them up, and spray them into the clouds so that Indra can release them as rain, which makes the elephant a working part of the monsoon rather than just a means of transport. He heads the Ashtadikgaja, the eight elephants who stand at the compass points holding up the world, and his position is the east. One well-known episode has the sage Durvasa give Indra a garland which Indra sets carelessly on Airavata's head; the elephant throws it down, Durvasa curses the gods to lose their strength, and the whole churning of the ocean follows from that moment of pride, so Airavata is both a cause and a product of the same event. In Southeast Asia he became Erawan, usually shown with three heads and sometimes thirty-three, and lent his name to kingdoms, capitals and the royal white elephants of Siam.

entities.name: Matsya
epithets: Shaphari — the small horned fish of the first appearance
domains: the waters at the start of a world age
symbols: a golden horn on the fish's head
the rope tied from Manu's boat to the horn
conch and discus in the upper hands of the half-fish form
entities.abode: the cosmic waters; Vaikuntha as Vishnu
festivals: Matsya Jayanti — the third day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra, marking the first avatar
entities.worship: Matsya has few dedicated temples, the best known at Nagalapuram in Andhra Pradesh, but he appears in every dashavatara panel, painting and dance cycle. He is invoked at the head of the ten avatars in the widely sung Dashavatara Stotra of Jayadeva.
entities.bio: Saved Manu, the first man, and the Vedas from the great deluge by towing his ship through the flood.
entities.longBio: The story is older than the avatar scheme it now heads. The Shatapatha Brahmana already has Manu find a tiny fish in his washing water that begs protection, grows too large for every vessel in turn, and finally warns him of a coming flood; there the fish is simply a fish. Later texts identify it with Prajapati or Brahma, and the Puranas make it the first descent of Vishnu. In the Bhagavata and Matsya Puranas the fish tows Manu's boat, with the seven sages and the seeds of all living things aboard, through the deluge, tied to its horn by the serpent Vasuki, and kills the demon Hayagriva who had stolen the Vedas from the sleeping Brahma. During the crossing Vishnu instructs Manu, and the Matsya Purana presents itself as that conversation. Some versions make the flood the dissolution at the end of a kalpa and others a local catastrophe at the start of a manvantara, and the Mahabharata's telling in the Vana Parva differs again in detail. The comparison with Mesopotamian and biblical flood accounts is old and much argued, and Indian tradition itself treats the story primarily as an argument about what is worth saving: not people first, but the Vedas and the seed of every species.

entities.name: Kurma
epithets: Akupara — the unbounded, an old name for the world tortoise
domains: the churning and the winning of amrita
symbols: a tortoise shell bearing a mountain
the serpent Vasuki wound as rope
conch, discus, mace and lotus in the upper form
entities.abode: the floor of the ocean of milk
festivals: Kurma Jayanti — the full moon of Vaishakha, when the second avatar is remembered
entities.worship: The principal Kurma temple is Sri Kurmam in Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh, one of very few in India with a tortoise-form deity. Elsewhere he is honoured within the dashavatara sequence, and Kurma Jayanti is regarded as an auspicious day to lay foundations.
entities.bio: Bore Mount Mandara on his back so gods and demons could churn the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality.
entities.longBio: When gods and Asuras set Mount Mandara in the ocean of milk to churn out the amrita, the mountain began to sink into the seabed, and Vishnu took the form of a tortoise and slid beneath it so the churning could go on. Some Puranas describe him as also present in three ways at once, as the tortoise below, as a form pulling with the gods, and as a presence steadying the mountain from above, which is a theological way of saying that the whole enterprise was his. The churning yielded the moon, the goddess Lakshmi, the wish-granting cow, Airavata, the physician Dhanvantari with the nectar, and first of all the halahala poison that Shiva drank. The Kurma Purana is narrated by Vishnu in this form to the sages, and it is unusual among Vaishnava Puranas for the amount of Shaiva material it carries. Behind the avatar lies an older image, the world tortoise Akupara on whose back the earth rests, and Vedic ritual already used tortoise imagery in the construction of the fire altar. The figure carries a plain moral in devotional retelling: the work of the world gets done by whoever is willing to take the weight underneath it.

entities.name: Varaha
epithets: Yajna Varaha — the boar whose body is the sacrifice
symbols: a boar's tusk with the earth goddess seated on it
one foot raised on the coiled serpent Shesha
conch and discus in the upper hands
Bhudevi as a small figure at his shoulder
entities.abode: the cosmic ocean during the rescue; Vaikuntha otherwise
festivals: Varaha Jayanti — the third day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada
entities.worship: Varaha is worshipped at Sri Varahaswami temple in Tirumala, where pilgrims are traditionally expected to visit him before Venkateswara, and at Bhu Varaha temples across Andhra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Massive Gupta and Chalukya sculptures at Udayagiri, Eran and Badami made his image a statement of royal power as well as devotion.
entities.bio: Dived into the cosmic ocean and lifted the earth goddess Bhudevi on his tusks, slaying the demon Hiranyaksha.
entities.longBio: The Daitya Hiranyaksha, son of Diti, dragged the earth down into the cosmic waters, and Vishnu took the form of a boar to go after her, an animal chosen because a boar roots in mud and holds its breath under water. He fought Hiranyaksha for a thousand years by some accounts, killed him with the mace, and brought Bhudevi up on his tusk, setting her back on the waters. The scene is one of the great subjects of Indian sculpture, and the classic image shows a colossal man with a boar's head, one leg planted, the goddess perched delicately on his tusk like someone being lifted from a river. Older Vedic material has Prajapati or a boar named Emusha raise the earth, and the Puranas absorbed that into the avatar scheme; the Shatapatha Brahmana version is markedly different in tone. Some texts allegorise him as the sacrifice itself, with his tusks as the stakes, his sound as the chants and his limbs as the ritual implements, a reading called Yajna Varaha. He is paired permanently with Bhudevi, and in Srivaishnava theology his rescue of her is the standard illustration of how god comes down bodily into the mess of the world.

entities.name: Narasimha
epithets: Yoga Narasimha — the seated, meditative form
Lakshmi Narasimha — with the goddess on his knee, pacified
Stambhodbhava — he who burst from the pillar
domains: the breaking of unjust boons and legalisms
wrath in the service of justice
removal of fear and evil influence
symbols: a lion's head on a human body
the demon across his thighs at the threshold
a garland of intestines and a mane of fire
entities.abode: Ahobilam in the Nallamala hills, and Vaikuntha
festivals: Narasimha Jayanti — the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaishakha, observed at dusk
Holika Dahan — the bonfire on the eve of Holi recalls Prahlada's survival of the fire
entities.worship: The nine Narasimha shrines of Ahobilam in Andhra Pradesh form his principal pilgrimage, and major temples stand at Simhachalam, Yadagirigutta and Melkote. He is invoked for protection against enemies, illness and hostile forces, most often through the Narasimha Kavacha, and his fierce forms are frequently kept behind a screen or approached with cooling rituals.
entities.bio: Burst from a pillar at twilight — neither man nor beast, indoors nor out — to disembowel Hiranyakashipu and save the devoted Prahlada.
entities.longBio: Hiranyakashipu extracted from Brahma a boon that he could not be killed by man or beast, by day or night, inside or outside, on earth or in the air, by any weapon, and then set about forcing the worlds to worship him. His own son Prahlada refused and kept praising Vishnu through poison, fire, elephants and cliffs, and when the boy insisted that god was present even in a pillar of the hall, his father struck it and Narasimha came out of it. The killing is a piece of exact legal engineering: neither man nor lion, at twilight, on the threshold, on his own lap, with claws rather than a weapon. Afterward his rage was so great that no one could approach him, and traditions differ on how it was quenched, some saying Prahlada's praise cooled him, others that Shiva took the Sharabha form to subdue him, a Shaiva claim that Vaishnavas reject, and others that Lakshmi seated herself on his knee. He is the most emotionally direct of Vishnu's forms, invoked when a devotee is in danger rather than in need, and the Srivaishnava Ahobila Matha takes its authority directly from him. His iconography ranges from the terrifying disembowelling scene to the entirely calm Yoga Narasimha seated in meditation.

entities.name: Vamana
epithets: Trivikrama — he of the three strides
domains: cosmic measurement and the three worlds
the moral force of a promise
symbols: a small brahmin boy with parasol and staff
the kamandalu water pot used to seal the gift
one leg raised to the sky in the Trivikrama form
entities.abode: Vaikuntha; Sutala, which he gave to Bali, as the realm he guards
festivals: Onam — Kerala's harvest festival, welcoming Bali back for his annual visit
Vamana Jayanti — the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada
Balipratipada — the day after Diwali, marking Bali's return in western India
entities.worship: Vamana is worshipped at Thrikkakara in Kerala, the ritual centre of Onam, and at Ulagalantha Perumal in Kanchipuram, where the Trivikrama form stands with leg raised. Across Kerala the festival attention falls on Bali rather than on Vamana, which is unusual for a story in which the avatar wins.
entities.bio: Born to Aditi and Kashyapa; asked the generous asura king Mahabali for three paces of land, then covered heaven and earth in two strides and set his foot on Bali's head with the third.
entities.longBio: Mahabali, grandson of Prahlada, ruled the three worlds so well and so generously that the displaced gods could find no fault with him, which is the point of the story: the problem is not that he is wicked but that he holds what is not his to hold. Aditi performed the Payovrata fast and Vishnu was born from her as a dwarf brahmin boy, who came to Bali's sacrifice and asked for three paces of ground. Shukra, the Asura preceptor, recognised the guest and tried to stop the gift by blocking the spout of the water pot, and Bali gave anyway, knowing what it would cost. The dwarf then grew until two strides covered earth and heaven, and for the third Bali offered his own head, on which Vishnu set his foot and pressed him down to the underworld realm of Sutala, granting him lordship there and, by most accounts, standing as his gatekeeper. Kerala remembers the episode as the loss of a golden age and celebrates Onam as the one day each year when Bali returns to see his people, so the festival's emotional weight sits with the defeated king. The three strides are much older than the dwarf: the Rigveda already praises Vishnu for measuring out the worlds in three paces, and the Puranic story is a narrative built around that ancient image.

entities.name: Parashurama
entities.role: Avatar 6 — the Warrior with the Axe
epithets: Bhargava — of the line of Bhrigu
Rama Jamadagnya — Rama son of Jamadagni
domains: the land of the Konkan and Kerala coast
symbols: the parashu, an axe given by Shiva
bow and quiver alongside the sacred thread
entities.abode: Mount Mahendra, where he is said to remain in penance
festivals: Akshaya Tritiya — the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaishakha, kept as his birth day
Parashurama Jayanti — observed particularly in the Konkan and Kerala
entities.worship: He is worshipped along the western coast, especially in Kerala, Konkan and Goa, where tradition credits him with raising the land from the sea, and at temples such as Parashurama Kshetra at Chiplun. Kalaripayattu practitioners and several martial and brahmin communities claim him as founder and patron.
entities.bio: Brahmin warrior of the Bhrigu line who annihilated the tyrant warrior caste twenty-one times; immortal, he later trained Bhishma, Drona and Karna.
entities.longBio: Parashurama is the sixth avatar and the only one who remains in the world after his own age is over. He was the youngest son of the sage Jamadagni and Renuka, and his character is set early by two acts: at his father's command he beheaded his own mother, then used the granted boon to have her restored, and having pleased Shiva by austerity he received the axe that names him. When the Haihaya king Kartavirya Arjuna stole his father's wish-fulfilling cow and his sons killed Jamadagni, Parashurama swore to clear the earth of the warrior caste and did so, by the epic's count, twenty-one times, filling five lakes at Samanta Panchaka with blood before his ancestors told him to stop. He then gave away all the land he had conquered and withdrew to Mahendra. Because he is a chiranjivi he keeps reappearing in other stories: he confronts the young Rama after the breaking of Shiva's bow and yields his power to him, teaches Bhishma and then fights him to a standstill over Amba, trains Drona, and curses Karna for lying about his birth so that his knowledge fails him at the end. Tradition also credits him with creating the coastal strip from Gujarat to Kerala by hurling his axe into the sea. He is the least comfortable of the avatars, a brahmin who kills, and the texts present his violence as both sanctioned and something he must eventually renounce.

entities.name: Rama
epithets: Maryada Purushottama — the perfect man who keeps every boundary
Kodandarama — Rama of the great bow
domains: family duty and the given word
symbols: the Kodanda bow and inexhaustible quiver
blue or green skin and princely crown
the sacred thread and simple bark garments of exile
his sandals, enthroned by Bharata in his absence
entities.abode: Ayodhya
festivals: Rama Navami — the ninth day of Chaitra, his birth
Vijayadashami — his victory over Ravana, marked by burning effigies in Ramlila performances
Diwali — his return to Ayodhya after fourteen years, welcomed with rows of lamps
entities.worship: Rama is worshipped across India, most intensely in the Hindi belt, where Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas is read in households and Ramlila is performed each autumn, and in the south at Bhadrachalam and Rameswaram. His name alone functions as a mantra and a greeting, and Ram Naam recitation is a devotional practice in itself.
entities.bio: Prince of Ayodhya, hero of the Ramayana. Exiled fourteen years, he rescued his abducted wife Sita by defeating the demon king Ravana with an army of vanaras; the embodiment of dharma.
entities.longBio: Valmiki's Ramayana presents Rama first as an ideal man and only gradually as a god, and the earliest layers of the text are noticeably restrained about his divinity. Born to Dasharatha of Ayodhya, he won Sita by bending and breaking Shiva's bow at Mithila, and then accepted fourteen years of forest exile without argument when Kaikeyi called in an old promise, because his father's word had to stand. In the forest, Ravana abducted Sita in revenge for the mutilation of his sister Shurpanakha, and Rama built an alliance with the vanaras, crossed to Lanka on a bridge, and killed Ravana in a long war. The ending troubles the tradition and is meant to: he asks Sita to prove herself by fire, and later, as king, banishes her on the strength of a laundryman's gossip, so that the man who never breaks a rule is undone by the rules he keeps. Tulsidas in the sixteenth century recast the whole story in Awadhi as an outpouring of devotion, and Kamban in Tamil, Krittibas in Bengali and the Jain, Buddhist and Southeast Asian versions all differ substantially in emphasis and sometimes in plot. Modern retellings by writers and dramatists have taken Sita's side of the ending openly, and that argument is now part of the story's life.

entities.name: Krishna
epithets: Govinda — finder or protector of cows
Murari — enemy of the demon Mura
Jagannatha — lord of the world, his form at Puri
domains: love and devotion in all its forms
the teaching of dharma and yoga
symbols: dark blue or black skin and yellow silk
butter, and the pot he stole it from
entities.mount: Garuda, in his Vishnu aspect
entities.abode: Vrindavan and Dvaraka; Goloka in Vaishnava theology
festivals: Janmashtami — his midnight birth, with fasting, cradle rites and dahi handi pot-breaking
Holi — the spring colour festival tied to his play with the gopis
Govardhan Puja — the day after Diwali, recalling the lifted mountain
Rath Yatra — the Puri chariot festival of Jagannatha
entities.worship: Krishna is worshipped everywhere from Vrindavan and Dvaraka to Puri, Udupi and Guruvayur, and the Bhagavata Purana and Bhagavad Gita are read daily by millions. Gaudiya Vaishnavism, Pushtimarg, the Warkari tradition of Vithoba and ISKCON abroad have carried his name-chanting into a global practice.
entities.bio: Cowherd, flute-player, slayer of Kamsa, and counselor of the Pandavas who revealed the Bhagavad Gita to Arjuna. Worshipped in his own right as the complete incarnation of Vishnu.
entities.longBio: Krishna was born in a Mathura prison to Devaki and Vasudeva under a prophecy that he would kill his uncle Kamsa, and was carried across the flooded Yamuna that same night to be raised by Yashoda and Nanda among cowherds. The childhood is the part of the story that devotion has most cherished: stealing butter, subduing the serpent Kaliya, lifting Mount Govardhan on one finger to shelter the village from Indra's rain, and the rasa lila, the circle dance with the gopis that later theologians read as the soul's love for god rather than as romance. He returns to kill Kamsa, founds the coastal city of Dvaraka, marries Rukmini after she writes asking to be taken, and in the Mahabharata becomes the Pandavas' kinsman, envoy and charioteer, refusing to fight but delivering the Bhagavad Gita to Arjuna on the field and advising several morally hard manoeuvres during the war. He dies quietly, shot in the heel by a hunter who mistakes him for a deer, and Dvaraka sinks into the sea. Vaishnava schools differ on his status: most lists count him as the eighth avatar of Vishnu, while Gaudiya and Nimbarka traditions hold the reverse, that Krishna is the source and Vishnu his expansion. The Bhagavata's version, composed perhaps in the ninth or tenth century, is what gave the child and the flute-player their enduring shape.

entities.name: Buddha (as avatar)
epithets: Mayadevisuta — son of Mayadevi, in the Puranic accounts
domains: teaching by persuasion rather than force
symbols: the shaven head and monastic robe
eyes half closed, hands in dhyana mudra
entities.abode: Bodh Gaya and the Gangetic plain in his historical setting; Vaikuntha in Vaishnava theology
festivals: Buddha Purnima — the full moon of Vaishakha, kept as his birth, awakening and passing
entities.worship: As an avatar he receives worship in a handful of Vaishnava settings, notably at Jagannath Puri where some traditions identify him with Buddha, and he appears in dashavatara panels, paintings and dance. His far larger following is as the founder of Buddhism, which does not accept the avatar claim.
entities.bio: In many Puranic lists, Vishnu incarnated as the Buddha. Traditions differ on the ninth avatar — some substitute Balarama or Vithoba.
entities.longBio: The inclusion of the Buddha among Vishnu's ten avatars is a late development, appearing in Puranic lists from roughly the sixth century onward, and its motives were plainly polemical in the earliest versions: several Puranas say that Vishnu took this form to teach a false doctrine and lead the Asuras away from the Vedas so they could be defeated, a hostile framing that treats the Buddha as a deliberate deceiver. Later poets and theologians reversed the tone entirely, and Jayadeva's twelfth-century Gita Govinda praises him for condemning animal sacrifice out of compassion, which is how most modern Hindus understand the avatar. The historical Siddhartha Gautama of the Shakya clan, who left his household life, awakened under a tree at Bodh Gaya and taught the four noble truths, has no connection to this Puranic material, and Buddhists have consistently rejected the identification as an absorption of their founder into a system he did not accept. Not every tradition uses him for the ninth place: Vaishnava lists in Maharashtra often put Vithoba there, Bengal and several Puranas give it to Balarama and shift Krishna to the ninth slot with Buddha omitted, and Jayadeva himself counts Balarama separately. The slot is the most contested in the whole avatar scheme, and any list should be read as a claim rather than a consensus.
entities.variantTraditions: Not to be confused with Budha, the planet Mercury, who appears separately in this pack among the Navagraha. The names are close and the figures are unrelated. Note also the two frames in play here: the Puranic Buddha-avatar is a theological claim made by Vaishnava texts, while Yashodhara and Rahula belong to the historical prince and come from Buddhist sources, not the Puranas - which never mention that he had a household at all.

entities.name: Kalki
epithets: Kalki — from kalka, meaning filth or the destroyer of it
Devadatta-arudha — rider of the horse Devadatta
domains: the end of the Kali Yuga
the turning of the world ages
symbols: the shining figure at the world's end
entities.mount: Devadatta — a white horse
entities.abode: Shambhala, the village of his future birth
festivals: Kalki Jayanti — the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Shravana, observed in some Vaishnava calendars
entities.worship: Kalki has few temples, the best known at Jaipur, built by Sawai Jai Singh II with a stall kept ready for the horse. He functions less as an object of daily worship than as the tradition's statement that the present age has an end and that the cycle continues.
entities.bio: The avatar yet to come: a rider on a white horse with a blazing sword who will end the dark age of Kali Yuga and restart the cycle of ages.
entities.longBio: Kalki is the only avatar still in the future, and he belongs to a cyclical rather than final eschatology: he does not end history but closes the Kali Yuga so that a new Satya Yuga can begin. The Bhagavata, Vishnu and Kalki Puranas describe him born to a brahmin named Vishnuyasha in a village called Shambhala, trained by Parashurama, armed by Shiva, riding a white horse named Devadatta and carrying a sword that shines like a comet, riding down the barbarian kings and thieves who rule at the end of the age. The signs given for that time are recognisably social rather than cosmic: rulers who plunder, wealth taken as the only measure of worth, marriage reduced to arrangement, and priests who sell learning. Estimates of when he arrives vary enormously, since the Kali Yuga is usually reckoned at 432,000 years beginning around 3102 BCE, which puts the event impossibly far off, though sectarian and millenarian movements have repeatedly claimed a nearer date. Comparisons with Buddhist Maitreya and with the Shambhala of the Kalachakra tradition are frequently drawn, and the direction of borrowing is disputed. Several modern figures have claimed the title, and mainstream tradition has rejected all of them.

entities.name: Balarama
epithets: Halayudha — he whose weapon is the plough
Sankarshana — the one drawn across, from his transfer between wombs
symbols: fair skin contrasted with Krishna's dark
a pot of wine and blue garments
the serpent hood above his head
entities.abode: Vrindavan and Dvaraka
festivals: Balarama Jayanti or Hal Shashthi — the sixth day of Bhadrapada's dark fortnight, when farmers honour the plough
Rath Yatra — he rides beside Jagannatha and Subhadra at Puri in his own chariot
entities.worship: He is worshipped as Balabhadra at Puri, where he stands as one of the three deities of the Jagannatha triad, and as a patron of farmers and wrestlers across north India. Hal Shashthi is kept by mothers in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar with offerings of unploughed produce.
entities.bio: Son of Vasudeva and Rohini, of immense strength; incarnation of the serpent Shesha (and the ninth avatar in some lists). Taught mace-fighting to both Bhima and Duryodhana.
entities.longBio: Balarama was conceived in Devaki as her seventh child and transferred by Vishnu's power to the womb of Rohini, Vasudeva's other wife, which saved him from Kamsa and earned him the name Sankarshana, the one drawn across. He grew up in Gokul as Krishna's older brother, and their temperaments were deliberately drawn as opposites: Balarama is fair, blunt, fond of wine, quick to anger and enormously strong, where Krishna is dark, subtle and playful. His weapons are farm implements, the plough and the pestle, and among his feats are dragging the Yamuna out of its course with the plough when it would not come to him and killing the ape Dvivida and the wrestler Mushtika. In the Mahabharata he taught mace fighting to both Bhima and Duryodhana, loved Duryodhana as a student, and refused to take either side in the war, going on pilgrimage instead and returning only to object furiously when Bhima broke the rules by striking below the waist. Most traditions identify him as an incarnation of Shesha, the serpent on whom Vishnu rests, and Pancharatra theology gives him a place as one of the four vyuhas; several Puranic lists count him as the ninth avatar in place of the Buddha, and Jain tradition includes him among its Baladevas. He dies at Prabhasa before Krishna, leaving his body in yoga while a great serpent issues from his mouth and returns to the sea.

entities.name: Hiranyakashipu
epithets: Hiranyakashipu — clothed in gold, or he whose bed is gold
domains: asura sovereignty over the three worlds
pride and the demand for worship
symbols: a jewelled crown and golden ornaments
a sword raised against his own son
the boon-granting fire of his long penance
entities.abode: his conquered capital in the three worlds, usually placed at Multan or Hiranyapura in Puranic geography
festivals: Holika Dahan — the bonfire on Holi eve burning his sister Holika, who failed to kill Prahlada in the flames
entities.worship: He is not worshipped but is thoroughly present in living practice as the figure burned in effigy at Holi and destroyed on stage in Narasimha temple dramas and in Prahlada Nataka in Odisha. His name is used colloquially for a tyrannical father or an arrogant ruler.
entities.bio: Son of Diti who won near-invulnerability from Brahma and demanded worship as god; slain by Narasimha for persecuting his own Vishnu-devoted son Prahlada.
