Vaishnava tradition treats her as Lakshmi incarnate and therefore as Krishna's consort in the strict theological sense, which sets up the long-running devotional question of her relation to Radha; northern Braj tradition gives the heart to Radha, while western and southern tradition centers the queen. In Maharashtra she is Rakhumai, standing arms akimbo beside Vitthal, and there she is not a supporting figure at all but half of the presiding pair.

entities.name: Subhadra
entities.role: Sister of Krishna; wife of Arjuna
epithets: Yogamaya — identified at Puri with the goddess of divine illusion
symbols: the chariot reins she held herself
yellow or golden complexion in the Puri image
armless abstract form flanked by her brothers
entities.abode: Dwarka, later Indraprastha; enshrined at Puri
festivals: Rath Yatra — her chariot Darpadalana rolls between her brothers' at Puri
Snana Yatra — the bathing festival of the three Puri deities
entities.worship: She is worshipped at the Jagannath temple in Puri as the central figure of the triad, standing between Jagannath and Balabhadra, and is identified there with Yogamaya or Bhuvaneshwari rather than treated merely as a sister. Her chariot in the Rath Yatra draws the same crowds as her brothers', and the triad is reproduced in Odia household shrines and in Jagannath temples worldwide.
entities.bio: Daughter of Vasudeva and Rohini; her elopement with Arjuna (with Krishna's connivance) united the Yadava and Pandava houses; mother of Abhimanyu.
entities.longBio: Subhadra was the daughter of Vasudeva by Rohini, and so half-sister to both Krishna and Balarama. When Arjuna, in exile and disguised as a wandering ascetic, came to Dwarka, Krishna encouraged the match, and the Mahabharata has Subhadra take the chariot reins herself and drive Arjuna out of the city while the Yadava army gave chase, until Balarama's anger was talked down and the marriage was recognized. She bore Abhimanyu, whose death at sixteen in the chakravyuha is the epic's cruelest single loss, and through Abhimanyu's son Parikshit the Kuru line survived the war at all. The epic keeps her mostly offstage after the wedding, so her later prominence comes from a different direction entirely: at Puri she is the middle figure of a triad whose wooden images are periodically renewed, and Odia tradition identifies her with the goddess Yogamaya, the power that concealed Krishna's birth. Some accounts explain the triad's unfinished form by the story of the sculptor Vishvakarma interrupted at work, while others read the images as older tribal deities absorbed into Vaishnavism. Between the epic sister and the Puri goddess there is a wide gap, and the traditions do not try very hard to close it.
entities.variantTraditions: Worshipped between her brothers at the Jagannath temple, Puri.

entities.name: Shantanu
epithets: Shantanu — he whose touch brings healing and calm
Gangeya's father — parent of the son of Ganga
Mahabhisha reborn — the king of heaven's court returned to earth
symbols: the ferry and the fisher village
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.worship: Not worshipped; he survives as a character in Mahabharata recitation, in Hastinapura's pilgrimage lore, and in every stage and screen retelling of the epic, where his two marriages open the story. Genealogists of the Kuru line invoke him as the ancestor from whom the whole tragedy descends.
entities.bio: King of Hastinapura who married the goddess Ganga and, later, the fisher-maiden Satyavati — a price his son Bhishma paid with a vow of lifelong celibacy.
entities.longBio: Shantanu was a king of Hastinapura in the line of Bharata, and the Mahabharata explains his birth as the rebirth of the celestial Mahabhisha, cursed for looking too long at Ganga in Brahma's court. He met Ganga on the riverbank, married her on the condition that he never question anything she did, and watched her drown seven newborn sons before he broke the promise at the eighth; she left him, explaining that the children were the Vasus working off a curse, and returned the surviving son years later as Devavrata. Then, in old age, he wanted Satyavati, and her father's price was that her sons should inherit, which Shantanu could not pay because the throne was Devavrata's. His son solved it by renouncing the crown and swearing lifelong celibacy, which earned him the name Bhishma and earned Shantanu the boon of granting his son death at will. Shantanu died leaving two young sons by Satyavati, both of whom died without heirs, and the succession crisis that follows produces Dhritarashtra, Pandu and everything after. The epic does not treat him as a villain, only as a man whose ordinary appetites had extraordinary consequences, and it is careful to note that he never asked Bhishma for the vow.

entities.name: Bhishma
epithets: Bhishma — he of the terrible vow
Devavrata — vowed to the gods, his birth name
Svachchhanda-mrityu — master of his own hour of death
domains: dharma and the keeping of oaths
martial command and instruction in kingship
symbols: white hair and beard of the grandsire
the arrow-fountain Arjuna drew for his pillow
entities.abode: Hastinapura
festivals: Bhishma Ashtami — the eighth of the bright fortnight of Magha, held to be the day he left his body
entities.worship: On Bhishma Ashtami, households across north India and among Brahmin communities offer water and sesame to him, an unusual rite since he died childless and has no descendants to make the offering. His teaching from the arrow-bed, the Shanti and Anushasana Parvas, is quoted as scripture on kingship and duty, and the Vishnu Sahasranama he recited there is chanted daily in Vaishnava homes.
entities.bio: Son of Shantanu and Ganga, an incarnate Vasu; renounced throne and marriage for his father's happiness. Invincible commander with the boon of chosen death, he fell on a bed of arrows and taught from it.
entities.longBio: Born Devavrata to Shantanu and Ganga, the last of the eight Vasus condemned to human birth and the only one his mother did not release into the river, he was raised by his mother and by Parashurama and Brihaspati and came back to Hastinapura as heir. He gave up that inheritance and swore never to marry so that his father could wed Satyavati, and the gods rained flowers and named him Bhishma, the awful one, for a vow that costly. The vow then governed everything: he abducted the princesses of Kashi for his half-brother, refused to marry Amba when she said she loved another, and Amba's rebirth as Shikhandi became the instrument of his death fifty years later. He fought Parashurama, his own teacher, to a standstill over that quarrel. As commander of the Kaurava army he could not be killed and would not fight a woman-born warrior, so he laid down his bow when Shikhandi came before him and fell riddled with Arjuna's arrows, then used his boon of chosen death to wait on that bed until the sun turned north. From it he delivered the longest discourse in the epic, on kings, castes, gift, grief and liberation, and readers ever since have argued whether his silence in the dice-game hall, when Draupadi appealed to him, was the fidelity of a servant of the throne or the failure that damns him.

entities.name: Satyavati
epithets: Matsyagandha — she who smelled of fish
Yojanagandha — she whose fragrance carries a yojana
Kali — the dark one, her earliest name
Kuru-matri — mother of the Kuru line
symbols: the ferry boat on the Yamuna
fish, from her birth and upbringing
the mist that hid her island
a queen's veil over a fisher girl's face
entities.abode: Hastinapura, and before it the Yamuna ferry
entities.worship: Not worshipped; she is remembered as the ancestress whose bargain reshaped the Kuru succession, and as the mother of Vyasa she stands at the origin of the Mahabharata itself. Her story is a staple of epic performance and of modern retellings that read her as the epic's most effective political operator.
entities.bio: Fisher chief's daughter, mother of Vyasa by the sage Parashara before marrying Shantanu; her ambition shaped — and nearly ended — the dynasty.
entities.longBio: Satyavati was born from a fish, in the epic's account the daughter of a king and an apsara under a curse, and raised by a fisher chief who set her to ferrying travellers across the Yamuna. The sage Parashara desired her mid-crossing; she bargained for a mist to hide them, for the restoration of her virginity, and for the fish smell to be replaced by a fragrance that carried for miles, and their son Vyasa was born on an island and left at once, promising to come when called. When Shantanu wanted her, her father demanded that her sons inherit the throne, and Bhishma's double renunciation met the price. Both her sons by Shantanu died young and childless, so she called Vyasa as promised, and by niyoga on the widows of her son he fathered Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura, which means the entire Kuru generation that fights at Kurukshetra descends from her fisher line rather than from Shantanu. She had also, before that, tried to make Bhishma break his vow and take the throne, and he refused. Late in life she went to the forest with her daughters-in-law on Vyasa's advice and died there before the war she had made possible. The epic is unusually direct about her: it gives her the intelligence, names the cost, and lets both stand.

entities.name: Dhritarashtra
epithets: Dhritarashtra — he who holds the kingdom
Prajnachakshu — one whose eyes are his understanding
Kuru-vriddha — the old man of the Kurus
domains: the responsibility of those who see and do nothing
symbols: the iron statue of Bhima he crushed
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.worship: Not worshipped. He is invoked in Indian moral discourse as the standard example of a leader ruined by partiality toward his own children, and the phrase putra-moha, blind love of a son, is attached to his name in sermons, editorials and school lessons.
entities.bio: Born blind, fathered by Vyasa; his helpless love for his hundred sons, above all Duryodhana, let the rivalry with the Pandavas burn into war.
entities.longBio: Dhritarashtra was fathered by Vyasa on Ambika, the widow of Vichitravirya, and was born blind because his mother closed her eyes at the sight of the ascetic. Blindness cost him the throne, which went to his younger brother Pandu, and he received it only when Pandu withdrew to the forest, a second-hand kingship he never stopped resenting. He is not stupid and he is not without dharma; the epic gives him long passages of genuine moral insight, immediately followed by the decision to do whatever Duryodhana wants. He permits the house of lac, permits the dice game, and sits through Draupadi's humiliation before granting her boons in a panic when jackals howl at the door. The Bhagavad Gita opens with his question to Sanjaya about what his sons and the Pandavas are doing on the field, and the possessive in that first verse is usually read as the whole diagnosis of his character. After the war he lived on under Yudhishthira's care, crushed the iron effigy Krishna substituted for Bhima when he tried to embrace him, and finally left with Gandhari and Kunti for the forest, where the three died in a wildfire. Vidura's counsel and Vyasa's warnings run through his story as the record of everything he was told and could not act on.

entities.name: Gandhari
epithets: Shatputra-mata — mother of a hundred sons
domains: the moral authority of the wronged
symbols: the cloth bound over her eyes
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.worship: Not worshipped, though her blindfold is a standing image in Indian discourse for solidarity that becomes complicity. Her lament over the battlefield in the Stri Parva is among the most performed passages of the epic in dance, theatre and film.
entities.bio: Princess of Gandhara who bound her own eyes for life on marrying the blind king; mother of the hundred Kauravas; her grief-curse doomed Krishna's own clan.
entities.longBio: Gandhari was the daughter of Subala of Gandhara and had a boon from Shiva of a hundred sons; on learning that her husband would be blind, she bound her own eyes with cloth and did not remove the blindfold for the rest of her life. Interpretations of that act vary sharply, from perfect wifely devotion to a silent protest at a marriage arranged without warning, and the epic itself allows both. Her pregnancy lasted two years and produced a mass of flesh that Vyasa divided into a hundred and one pieces incubated in jars of ghee, yielding the hundred Kauravas and their sister Duhshala. She warned Duryodhana repeatedly and told him plainly that victory follows dharma, but she never withdrew her support from her sons, and when he asked for her blessing before battle she gave him only that line again. Once, she opened the blindfold to look at him and made his body invulnerable everywhere the gaze fell, and Krishna's trick of shaming him into covering his thighs left the one weakness Bhima used. After the war she walked the field naming her dead and cursed Krishna, who could have stopped it, with the destruction of his own clan within thirty-six years, and he accepted the curse. She died in the forest fire with Dhritarashtra and Kunti.

entities.name: Pandu
epithets: Bharata-shreshtha — best of the Bharatas, as a conqueror
symbols: the hunting bow and the fatal arrow
the mating deer that were a sage and his wife
entities.abode: Hastinapura, then the Himalayan hermitage of Shatashringa
entities.worship: Not worshipped. He is remembered chiefly through his sons, who are named for him, and through local Himalayan traditions, including sites in Uttarakhand and the Pandu Lena caves near Nashik, that attach his name to places of exile.
entities.bio: Fathered by Vyasa; a curse barred him from fatherhood, so his queens invoked gods to beget the five Pandavas.
entities.longBio: Pandu was fathered by Vyasa on Ambalika, who turned pale at the sight of the ascetic, and the epic gives that pallor as the reason for his name and his weak constitution. He took the throne because Dhritarashtra was blind, and he was an effective conqueror who extended Kuru power widely before retiring to hunt in the Himalaya. There he shot a mating deer that was the sage Kindama and his wife in animal form, and the dying sage cursed him to die the moment he approached a woman in desire. Pandu renounced the kingdom, took Kunti and Madri into forest asceticism, and it was Kunti's mantra from Durvasa that solved the problem of heirs: she summoned Dharma, Vayu and Indra for Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna, and gave the mantra once to Madri, who used it on the twin Ashvins and got two sons in a single invocation. The curse killed him in the end, in a spring moment with Madri, and Madri went to the pyre with him blaming herself. His sons were then taken to Hastinapura as orphans, which is the position from which their whole claim has to be argued. The epic treats him with sympathy and a certain irony: a king who won everything by force and lost everything to a single careless arrow.

entities.name: Kunti
epithets: Pritha — her birth name, daughter of Shura
Kunti — the adopted daughter of Kuntibhoja
Parthanam mata — mother of the sons of Pritha
Kausalya-tulya — likened to Kausalya as a mother of heroes
domains: hospitality to sages and the boons it wins
symbols: the basket set adrift on the river
the sun disc, for her firstborn's father
widow's white and the forest hermitage
entities.abode: Hastinapura, and the forests of exile
entities.worship: Not worshipped as a deity, though Kunti Devi shrines exist in parts of north India and Nepal and she is invoked in folk performance as a model of maternal endurance. Her prayer in the Bhagavata Purana, the Kunti Stuti, in which she asks Krishna for calamities so that she will never forget him, is recited as devotional text.
entities.bio: Aunt of Krishna, granted a mantra to summon any god. Bore Karna to Surya as an unwed girl — and, as Pandu's queen, Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna to Dharma, Vayu and Indra.
entities.longBio: Born Pritha to the Yadava Shura and given away to his childless cousin Kuntibhoja, she served the irascible sage Durvasa so well that he gave her a mantra to summon any god and receive a son. She tried it on Surya out of curiosity, could not refuse him once he came, and bore Karna with armour and earrings already fused to his skin; unmarried and frightened, she set the child adrift on the Ashva river, an act the epic never lets her forget. Married to Pandu and living under his curse, she used the same mantra deliberately for Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna, and shared it with Madri, who bore the twins. After Pandu's death she raised all five as a widow in a hostile court, survived the house of lac, and lived in disguise in Ekachakra, where she sent Bhima to face the demon Baka rather than let a host family lose a son. Her offhand instruction after Draupadi's swayamvara, to share among themselves whatever Arjuna had won, produced the epic's most famous marital arrangement and is presented as a mother's words that cannot be taken back. Before the war she went to Karna and told him the truth, and he promised only that he would kill no Pandava but Arjuna, so that she would keep five sons either way. She refused to live in her sons' victory and went to the forest with Dhritarashtra and Gandhari to die.

entities.name: Madri
epithets: Ashvineya-mata — mother of the sons of the Ashvins
Bahliki — of the Bahlika lands, as some passages name her people
symbols: the spring forest where Pandu died
the bride-price paid for a Madra princess
entities.abode: Hastinapura, then the Himalayan hermitage with Pandu
entities.worship: Not worshipped; she is remembered in the epic's telling as the mother who gave her sons to Kunti and followed her husband onto the pyre. Her name recurs in the patronymic Madreya used for Nakula and Sahadeva throughout the Mahabharata.
entities.bio: Second wife of Pandu who bore Nakula and Sahadeva to the twin Ashvins.
entities.longBio: Madri was the sister of Shalya, king of Madra, and Bhishma obtained her for Pandu with the bride-price that Madra custom required, a detail the epic mentions without embarrassment. She shared Pandu's forest exile with Kunti under the terms of Kindama's curse, and when Kunti was permitted to give her the summoning mantra once, Madri used it cleverly on the twin Ashvins and received two sons at a single invocation, which annoyed Kunti enough that she refused to lend it again. In the spring, alone with Pandu, she could not prevent him from approaching her, and the curse killed him; she held herself responsible and insisted on the pyre, giving Nakula and Sahadeva to Kunti with the argument that Kunti would treat all five equally while she could not be trusted to. The epic keeps her brief, but that final speech has been read as both genuine remorse and a clear-eyed calculation that her sons stood a better chance as Kunti's. Her brother Shalya later fought on the Kaurava side, tricked into it by Duryodhana's hospitality, and served as Karna's charioteer against her own sons, a knot the epic sets up quietly and leaves the reader to feel.

entities.name: Yudhishthira
epithets: Ajatashatru — he who has no enemy born
Kanka — his alias in Virata's court
symbols: the dog that followed him to heaven's gate
a chariot that rode a hand's breadth above the ground
entities.abode: Indraprastha, later Hastinapura
entities.worship: Not worshipped in temples, but constantly cited in ethical instruction, and his Yaksha Prashna, the riddle dialogue at the lake, is memorized and quoted as a compendium of Hindu moral reasoning. He appears in the Pandava temples of Uttarakhand and Himachal, and Garhwali Pandav Lila performances stage his story every winter.
entities.bio: Son of Kunti by Yama-Dharma; truthful to a fault, his one gambling weakness cost the Pandavas their kingdom and queen. The only one to reach heaven in the body.
entities.longBio: Yudhishthira was born to Kunti by Dharma himself, and the epic makes his defining trait not strength or skill but a scrupulous attachment to truth that his chariot wheels are said to reward by never touching the ground. He performed the Rajasuya sacrifice at Indraprastha and was recognized as emperor, and then accepted an invitation to dice with Shakuni because a kshatriya may not refuse a challenge, staking kingdom, brothers, himself and finally Draupadi, whose question about whether he had already lost himself before he wagered her the assembly could not answer. Thirteen years of exile followed, during which he answered the Yaksha's questions at the poisoned lake and, given one brother back, chose Nakula so that both of Pandu's wives would have a living son. At Kurukshetra he told the war's one great lie, that Ashvatthama was dead, and his chariot came down to earth. He won and hated it, ruled from Hastinapura with Bhishma's teaching as his manual, and at the end walked north with his brothers and a dog that turned out to be Dharma testing him one last time; he refused heaven rather than abandon it. Even in heaven he refused to stay while his brothers were shown in hell, and that refusal is the epic's last verdict on him. He is the character the Mahabharata is hardest on, and the one it finally vindicates.

entities.name: Bhima
epithets: Ballava — his cook's alias in Virata's kitchen
domains: vengeance carried out to the letter
symbols: the cook's ladle of Virata's kitchen
the uprooted tree used as a club
entities.abode: Indraprastha, and the forests of exile
entities.worship: Not worshipped as a deity, though hill shrines in Uttarakhand, Himachal and Nepal, including Bhimakali at Sarahan and numerous Bhim temples and rock formations, carry his name. Garhwali Pandav Lila performers who take his role are said to be possessed by him, and the mace is danced with accordingly.
entities.bio: Son of Kunti by Vayu — wind-born like Hanuman, his spiritual brother. Wolf-bellied eater, mace-fighter, and the slayer of Duryogana's hundred brothers including Dushasana.
entities.longBio: Bhima was Kunti's son by Vayu and the wind gave him the strength of ten thousand elephants; dropped as an infant, he is said to have shattered the rock he fell on. He is the brother who acts while others deliberate, and his career is a chain of physical solutions: eating Duryodhana's poison and surviving, carrying his mother and brothers out of the burning house of lac, killing the man-eaters Baka and Hidimba, and tearing Jarasandha in half on Krishna's silent instruction. Through Hidimbi he fathered Ghatotkacha, whose death absorbs the missile Karna had saved for Arjuna. He also swore two oaths in the dice hall, to drink Dushasana's blood and to break Duryodhana's thigh, and he kept both, the second by a strike below the belt that Balarama called a foul and Krishna defended as the payment of a debt. His kinship with Hanuman, both sons of Vayu, produces the fine scene in the forest where an old monkey will not move his tail and teaches Bhima the limits of strength. He is the epic's comic figure as often as its brutal one, hungry, loud and unsubtle, and he is also the only Pandava who never once argues for peace. He dies on the northward walk, told by Yudhishthira that his fault was pride in his own power and his appetite.

entities.name: Arjuna
entities.role: Peerless archer; hearer of the Gita
epithets: Savyasachin — ambidextrous, able to draw with either hand
Brihannala — his eunuch dance-teacher alias at Virata's court
domains: the struggle between duty and conscience
symbols: the monkey banner with Hanuman on it
the white horses of his chariot
entities.abode: Indraprastha
festivals: Gita Jayanti — the eleventh of the bright fortnight of Margashirsha, marking the day the Gita was spoken to him
entities.worship: He is not worshipped in his own right, but as the questioner of the Bhagavad Gita he is present in daily recitation wherever the Gita is read, and devotees are taught to place themselves in his position. Tamil kuttu and Garhwali Pandav Lila stage his exploits, and the Iravan or Koothandavar cult of Tamil Nadu venerates his son by the naga princess Ulupi.
entities.bio: Son of Kunti by Indra; Drona's greatest pupil and Krishna's dearest friend. His crisis of conscience at Kurukshetra occasioned the Bhagavad Gita.
entities.longBio: Arjuna was Kunti's son by Indra, and Drona's favourite pupil from the day he was the only boy who could see nothing but the bird's eye. He won Draupadi by stringing the bow and shooting the revolving fish at her swayamvara, then had to share her with his brothers on his mother's word. Exiled for a year over a technicality about entering Yudhishthira's chamber, he married Ulupi, Chitrangada and Subhadra along the way, and later went to Indra's heaven to gather celestial weapons, earning from the apsara Urvashi a curse of impotence that he spent as his year in disguise as the dance teacher Brihannala. At the opening of the battle he set down his bow, unwilling to kill teachers and cousins, and the seven hundred verses Krishna spoke to him then became the Bhagavad Gita, the most widely read Hindu text of all. He fought the war through, killed Bhishma with Shikhandi before him, Jayadratha before sunset, and finally Karna, learning only afterward that he had killed his eldest brother. Later tradition treats him as Nara, the eternal companion of Narayana, so the friendship with Krishna is not new in this life but resumed. The epic gives him the best of everything except peace of mind, and that is exactly the problem the Gita addresses.

entities.name: Nakula
epithets: Nakula — the mongoose, quick and deadly
Damagranthi — his alias as Virata's horse-keeper
symbols: a banner with a red-backed deer
entities.abode: Indraprastha
entities.worship: Not worshipped separately; he is included wherever the five Pandavas are honored together, as in the Himalayan Pandava temples and the Garhwali Pandav Lila cycle. His treatise on horses, the Ashvashastra attributed to him, kept his name alive in the veterinary and equestrian literature of premodern India.
entities.bio: Son of Madri by the Ashvins; swordsman and master of horses.
entities.longBio: Nakula was born to Madri by the elder of the twin Ashvins, physicians and horsemen of the gods, and the epic says he was the handsomest man of his time, a distinction it awards him plainly and repeatedly. He conquered the western kingdoms including his mother's Madra during Yudhishthira's campaign for the Rajasuya, and he fought at Kurukshetra as a chariot warrior, killing several of Karna's sons. His particular expertise was horses and their care, and during the year in disguise he served Virata as Damagranthi, master of the royal stables, a role that fits him exactly. When the Yaksha at the lake offered Yudhishthira one brother restored to life, Yudhishthira chose Nakula on the reasoning that Kunti had one son alive in himself and Madri should also have one, and the Yaksha revived all five for the fairness of the answer. He and Sahadeva are the Pandavas the epic characterizes least, always paired, always deferential to their elders, and later tradition compensated by attributing to him the Ashvashastra, a manual of horse medicine. He is the first to fall on the final northward walk after Draupadi, and Yudhishthira names his fault as vanity about his looks.

entities.name: Sahadeva
epithets: Tantripala — his alias as Virata's cowherd
symbols: a banner bearing a silver swan
entities.abode: Indraprastha
entities.worship: Not worshipped separately; he is honored with his brothers in Himalayan Pandava shrines and in Pandav Lila performance. Folk tradition in several regions invokes him as the patron of astrologers, and cattle-keeping communities remember him as an authority on cows.
entities.bio: Son of Madri by the Ashvins; astrologer and keeper of secrets who knew the war's outcome but was bound to silence.
entities.longBio: Sahadeva was the younger twin, born to Madri by the second of the Ashvins, and the epic calls him the wisest of the five, a judgment more often stated than demonstrated because his gift works against him. He knew the future, by astrology in some tellings and by a boon in others, but was bound by a condition that he would die if he spoke what he knew unasked, so his foreknowledge is dramatically useless and that is the point of it. Folk versions push this further with the story that he tasted Duryodhana's blood or ate a portion of the dead Yadava sage's flesh and gained omniscience along with the constraint. He conquered the southern kingdoms for the Rajasuya and killed Shakuni at Kurukshetra, the one death the whole family owed him. In disguise at Virata's court he took the name Tantripala and managed the royal cattle, which suits a son of the Ashvins and matches the epic's interest in the practical competence of the twins. He was the last of the four brothers to fall on the final journey, and Yudhishthira told him his fault was thinking no one was as wise as himself. Later tradition credits him with works on astrology, and in south Indian village performance he sometimes takes a much larger role than the Sanskrit text gives him.

entities.name: Karna
entities.role: Tragic hero; son of the Sun
epithets: Radheya — son of Radha, his foster mother
Vasusena — born with wealth, for the armour he wore
domains: loyalty and the claims of gratitude
symbols: kavacha and kundala, the golden armour and earrings
the Shakti dart given by Indra
the chariot wheel sunk in the earth
entities.abode: Champa, capital of Anga
entities.worship: He is worshipped as a folk deity in parts of Uttarakhand, where Karna temples at Sarmoli and elsewhere hold annual fairs, and among some communities in Bihar and Maharashtra who claim descent or affinity. Elsewhere he lives in performance and modern retelling as the epic's great study in unearned disadvantage, and his name is proverbial for a giver who refuses no one.
entities.bio: Kunti's abandoned firstborn by Surya, raised by a charioteer; unmatched in generosity and archery. Loyal to Duryodhana who alone honored him, he died at his own brother Arjuna's hands.
entities.longBio: Karna was Kunti's firstborn by Surya, conceived before her marriage and set adrift in a basket, and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha, from whom he takes the name he preferred. Denied instruction as a suta, he learned weapons from Parashurama by claiming to be a brahmin and was cursed to forget the decisive mantra at the hour of need, and a second curse from a brahmin whose cow he killed doomed his chariot wheel to stick. At Drona's tournament he matched Arjuna and was refused a contest for want of rank, and Duryodhana made him king of Anga on the spot, a debt Karna paid with lifelong loyalty even when he knew whose side dharma was on. Indra begged his armour and earrings from him as alms and he cut them from his body, taking in exchange a single-use dart he spent on Ghatotkacha instead of Arjuna. Krishna and then Kunti each told him the truth of his birth and offered him the throne and his brothers, and he refused both, promising Kunti only that she would still have five sons. He died with his wheel in the mud and his bow lowered, killed by Arjuna at Krishna's urging, and the epic makes clear that the rules were broken to do it. Vyasa is careful never to let him be simply a victim: he mocked Draupadi in the hall and endorsed the dice-game outrage, and that stain sits alongside everything else.

entities.name: Draupadi
epithets: Yajnaseni — born of the sacrificial fire
Sairandhri — her alias as Virata's queen's maid
domains: fire and the vow of vengeance
symbols: unbound hair, left loose until avenged
the Akshaya Patra, the never-empty vessel
dark complexion and blue lotus fragrance
entities.abode: Indraprastha
festivals: Draupadi Amman firewalking festivals — Tamil and Sri Lankan temple cycles culminating in walking across coals in her honor
entities.worship: She is a full goddess in Tamil Nadu, southern Karnataka, Sri Lanka and the Tamil diaspora, where Draupadi Amman temples stage the Mahabharata over weeks and end with devotees walking on fire in memory of her purity and her vow. In Garhwal she is worshipped in Pandav Lila as a village goddess who possesses her dancers, while in most of north India she remains a character rather than a deity.
entities.bio: Born from King Drupada's sacrificial fire; wife of all five Pandavas. Her humiliation in the dice-game hall — and Krishna's rescue of her honor — made the war inevitable.
entities.longBio: Draupadi rose fully grown from King Drupada's sacrificial fire alongside her brother Dhrishtadyumna, a fire lit to produce the death of Drona, so she enters the epic already as an instrument of destiny. Won by Arjuna at the swayamvara and married to all five brothers on Kunti's unretractable word, she was given a rotation among their houses and a boon of restored virginity, and the epic treats the arrangement as an anomaly it must justify at length. Her humiliation in the dice hall is the pivot of the whole poem: dragged in during her menstrual period, she asked the assembly the legal question of whether a man who has lost himself can stake his wife, received no answer from Bhishma or anyone else, and was saved from stripping by the cloth that would not end, in most versions by Krishna's intervention. She vowed to leave her hair unbound until it could be tied with hands washed in Dushasana's blood, and Bhima kept that vow for her. In exile she argued with Yudhishthira about the value of patience more sharply than any other character dares, and at Virata's court she engineered Kichaka's death. She is the first to fall on the last journey, and Yudhishthira says her fault was partiality to Arjuna. South Indian tradition rejects that ending and makes her Mahakali or Adi Parashakti descended to earth, which is why she has temples there and not elsewhere.

entities.name: Duryodhana
epithets: Suyodhana — the good fighter, his given name
Rajaraja — the king of kings, as his partisans call him
symbols: the crystal floor of the Maya sabha where he fell
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.worship: He is worshipped at the Duryodhana temple at Poruvazhy in Kerala and at Malanada, where the Malakkuda festival honors him as Malanada Appooppan, and at a shrine in Osla in Uttarakhand's Har-ki-Dun valley whose villagers hold him a just ruler. Everywhere else he is the epic's antagonist, played with relish in Kathakali and Yakshagana, where his roles are among the most demanding on the stage.
entities.bio: Firstborn of the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari; able, proud and consumed by envy of the Pandavas, he chose war over yielding five villages.
entities.longBio: Duryodhana was the eldest of Gandhari's hundred sons, born to omens of jackals and screech-owls that Vidura read as a warning to expose him, advice Dhritarashtra refused. His grievance is real in its own terms: he was the son of the reigning king and the Pandavas were the sons of a king who abdicated, and the epic lets him state the case. But his methods run from poisoning Bhima as a boy through the house of lac to the dice game he ran through his uncle Shakuni, and the humiliation of Draupadi, which he capped by baring his thigh at her. Offered peace for five villages he answered that he would not yield land enough to stand a needle on. He was a generous patron and a genuinely loyal friend, and his elevation of Karna against every rule of birth is the one act the epic praises without qualification. He fought the eighteen days and died last of all, ambushed in a lake, brought out by taunts, and killed by a mace blow to the thigh that broke the rules of mace combat, which he pointed out with his last breath while flowers fell on him from the sky. Some Kerala and Himalayan communities take that last detail seriously and treat him as a wronged king, and the epic itself, having condemned him for a hundred thousand verses, gives him heaven in its final book.

entities.name: Drona
epithets: Bharadvaja-putra — son of the sage Bharadvaja
Ashvatthama's father — parent of the immortal warrior
domains: the guru's claim on the pupil
symbols: the bow and the celestial weapons
the deer-skin seat and the teacher's dais
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.worship: Not worshipped, but named in India's highest coaching award, the Dronacharya Award, and cited as the archetype of the teacher, for good and ill. The Ekalavya episode makes him a standing reference in Indian debates about caste and access to education, and Gurgaon takes its older name Gurugram from the tradition that the village was his.
entities.bio: Brahmin master of weapons who trained Pandavas and Kauravas alike, favoring Arjuna; fought for the Kauravas out of duty and fell to a half-truth about his son's death.
entities.longBio: Drona was born from his father Bharadvaja's seed collected in a vessel, and learned weapons alongside Drupada, prince of Panchala, who promised him half his kingdom in boyhood and laughed at him when he came to claim it as a poor brahmin with a hungry son. That insult shaped him: he took service at Hastinapura, trained the Kuru princes, and demanded as his teaching fee that they defeat Drupada and hand him half of Panchala, which Arjuna did. His favouritism toward Arjuna is explicit, and it produced the epic's most disturbing scene when the forest boy Ekalavya, self-taught before a clay image of Drona, was made to cut off his right thumb as the same kind of fee. He fought for the Kauravas because he ate their salt, told Yudhishthira frankly how he could be killed, and designed the chakravyuha that trapped Abhimanyu. Krishna's counsel to break him was to announce the death of Ashvatthama, and Yudhishthira, who would not lie, said the words with an inaudible qualification about an elephant; Drona laid down his weapons and Dhrishtadyumna, Drupada's fire-born son, beheaded him. His death by a deliberate half-truth, at the hands of the child born to kill him, is the epic's clearest statement that no one in this war leaves clean.

entities.name: Abhimanyu
epithets: Karshni — descendant of Krishna's line through his mother
Varchas reborn — held to be the son of the moon god come to earth
symbols: the chariot wheel he lifted as a weapon
entities.abode: Indraprastha and Dwarka
entities.worship: Not worshipped as a deity, though his death is one of the most performed episodes in Indian theatre, from Kathakali and Yakshagana to Javanese and Balinese wayang, where the Abimanyu story is a fixed favourite. His name in Indian usage stands for anyone who knows how to get into a situation but not how to get out.
entities.bio: Son of Arjuna and Subhadra who learned to enter — but not exit — the chakravyuha formation in the womb; died at sixteen fighting six warriors at once. His son Parikshit continued the line.
entities.longBio: Abhimanyu was the son of Arjuna and Subhadra, and tradition holds him to be the moon god's son Varchas, lent to earth for a short span on the condition that he return quickly, which is offered as the reason for his early death. The famous story of his learning is that Krishna explained the chakravyuha to the pregnant Subhadra and she fell asleep before the account of the exit, so the child heard only half; the Mahabharata itself is less explicit than the folk versions here, saying only that he had learned the entry from his father. He was raised largely in Dwarka, married Uttara of Virata, and came to Kurukshetra at sixteen. On the thirteenth day Drona formed the chakravyuha to capture Yudhishthira, and Abhimanyu was the only warrior present who could breach it; he went in, Jayadratha sealed the gap behind him under a boon from Shiva, and the boy fought alone through the formation before Drona, Karna, Kripa, Ashvatthama and others broke his bow, chariot and armour together and he was clubbed down after fighting on with a chariot wheel. Arjuna's vow to kill Jayadratha before the next sunset, and Krishna's eclipse trick to fulfil it, follow directly from his death. His posthumous son Parikshit, revived by Krishna in the womb after Ashvatthama's weapon, is the sole survivor of the Kuru line and the king to whom the Bhagavata Purana is later recited.

entities.name: Mangala
entities.role: The planet Mars; the red graha of war, born from a drop of Shiva's sweat
symbols: a mace, trident, spear and lotus
entities.mount: A ram; in some panels a chariot drawn by eight red horses
entities.abode: Svarga, and the Navagraha shrine of every temple
festivals: Mangalvar vrat — the Tuesday fast, kept with red flowers and jaggery
Angaraka Chaturthi — a Ganesha fourth-day falling on a Tuesday
entities.worship: He is approached in the Navagraha shrine that stands in the courtyard of most south Indian temples, circumambulated in his own direction, and petitioned over land disputes, debts and delayed marriages.
entities.bio: A drop of Shiva's sweat fell on the earth, and the earth raised it as a son.
entities.longBio: Shiva, deep in meditation, let a single drop of perspiration fall to the ground, and Bhumi the earth took it up and raised it — which is why the red planet is Bhauma, the son of the earth, as well as Angaraka, the burning coal. He is four-armed, red as coral, and rides a ram. Astrologically he is a malefic and a difficult tenant: a chart in which he sits badly carries Mangal dosha, still a live consideration in marriage negotiations today. He also cancels debts, and the Tuesday fast kept in his name is as often about money as about courage.
entities.variantTraditions: Some Puranas make him a son of Bhumi by Vishnu in his Varaha form rather than by Shiva's sweat; the Skanda Purana gives the sweat version.

entities.name: Budha (Mercury)
entities.role: The planet Mercury; the child of an abduction who grew up the gentlest of the grahas
entities.mount: A lion, or a chariot drawn by eight wind-born horses
entities.abode: Svarga, and the Navagraha shrine
festivals: Budhvar vrat — the Wednesday fast, kept with green cloth and moong
entities.worship: Petitioned for success in study, examinations, trade and negotiation, and for children with a gift for speech. Green cloth, emeralds and moong dal are the standard offerings.
entities.bio: His father stole his mother from his father's own teacher, and the war that followed was fought over her.
entities.longBio: Chandra the moon abducted Tara, the wife of Brihaspati — his own preceptor — and would not give her back. The gods and the asuras took sides and fought the Tarakamaya war over one woman, until Brahma forced the matter and Tara was returned pregnant. She would not name the father, and only under pressure admitted it was Soma. The child was Budha, and he turned out to be the mildest and most intelligent of the nine planets, benefic wherever he sits alone. He married Ila and fathered Pururavas, which makes this scandal the origin of the entire Lunar dynasty.
entities.variantTraditions: Budha the planet Mercury and the Buddha are entirely unrelated figures who happen to have similar names. Budha is a graha, son of Chandra and Tara, husband of Ila and father of Pururavas. The Buddha is a historical teacher, listed separately in this pack as Vishnu's contested ninth avatar. Nothing connects them but three letters.

entities.name: Ketu
entities.role: The headless half of the asura Rahu — the body that kept moving after the head was cut off
entities.mount: A vulture, or a headless body seated on a serpent
entities.abode: The southern lunar node, moving always backwards
festivals: Ketu Peyarchi — observances at his transit between signs
entities.worship: Approached in the Navagraha shrine for release from entanglement, for occult study, and by those whose charts place him badly. Offerings are grey — sesame, iron, smoke-coloured cloth.
entities.bio: Vishnu cut the asura in half at the moment he swallowed the nectar. Both halves were already immortal.
entities.longBio: When the amrita was churned from the ocean, the asura Svarbhanu slipped into the line of gods and drank. The sun and moon saw him and told Vishnu, who took off his head with the Sudarshana — but the nectar had already passed his throat, so neither half could die. The head is Rahu, who swallows the sun in revenge. The body is Ketu. Where Rahu is appetite, Ketu is the opposite: he governs renunciation, detachment and the sudden loss that turns someone towards liberation. Astrologically he is the moksha-karaka, the planet of letting go.
entities.variantTraditions: Ketu is also the generic Sanskrit word for a comet or banner, and older texts sometimes use it for comets in general rather than the node.

entities.name: Tara
entities.role: Brihaspati's wife, carried off by the moon, and the cause of a war between gods and asuras
entities.abode: The house of Brihaspati, and for a time the house of Soma
entities.bio: She was taken, fought over by both halves of the universe, returned — and then asked whose child she was carrying.
entities.longBio: Soma the moon took Tara from Brihaspati, his own teacher, and refused every request to return her. Brihaspati had the devas; Shukra, who had his own grudge against the gods, brought the asuras in on Soma's side, and the Tarakamaya war was fought over one woman until Brahma intervened and ended it. Tara went back pregnant. Asked repeatedly whose the child was, she said nothing, and only when pressed by Brahma admitted it was Soma's. The child was Budha. She is one of the few figures in the Puranas whose silence is the whole of her characterisation.
entities.variantTraditions: Distinct from Tara the vanara queen, Vali's wife in the Ramayana, and from the Buddhist and Tantric goddess Tara. Three different figures share the name.

entities.name: Ila
entities.role: Born a daughter by ritual error, made a man, then a woman again — and the mother of a dynasty either way
epithets: Sudyumna — her name as a man
domains: the founding of the Lunar dynasty
entities.abode: Pratishthana, and the forest where Shiva's decree held
entities.bio: Manu asked for a son and got a daughter, because a priest mispronounced one word.
entities.longBio: Manu performed a sacrifice for a son; the officiating priest made an error, and a daughter was born instead — Ila. She was turned into a man, Sudyumna, and while hunting rode into a grove where Shiva, wanting privacy with Parvati, had decreed that every male who entered became female. Ila returned. Budha found her there and married her, and their son was Pururavas, from whom the whole Lunar dynasty descends. In most tellings she alternates thereafter, a month as each, remembering nothing of the other life. The Puranas treat the change as a fact of the world rather than a scandal.
entities.variantTraditions: The Bhagavata, Vishnu and Devi Bhagavata Puranas differ over whether the alternation is monthly, yearly or permanent, and over whether Ila or Sudyumna is the original state.

entities.name: Pururavas
entities.role: The first king of the Lunar dynasty, who lost an apsara over a pair of stolen rams
domains: the founding of the Lunar dynasty
symbols: the two rams tethered by the bed
the aranis of the fire ritual
entities.abode: Pratishthana on the Ganges
entities.bio: Urvashi would stay on three conditions. Gandharvas broke one of them on purpose.
entities.longBio: Son of Budha and Ila, and the first king of the Lunar line. The apsara Urvashi agreed to live with him on conditions: he must care for her two rams, and she must never see him naked. The gandharvas, wanting her back in heaven, stole the rams at night; he sprang up to chase them and a flash of lightning showed him bare. She left that instant. He wandered the country half mad looking for her and found her at last with her companions in the form of swans on a lake at Kurukshetra. Their dialogue in Rig Veda X.95 is one of the oldest recorded conversations in any language.
entities.variantTraditions: The Rig Vedic hymn is bleak and gives them no reunion; the Puranas and Kalidasa's play soften it, and Kalidasa gives them a happy ending outright.

entities.name: Urvashi
entities.role: The apsara who left a king over a technicality, and cursed Arjuna for refusing her
entities.abode: Svarga, in Indra's court
entities.bio: She turned Arjuna down as a lover, so he spent a year as a eunuch for the insult.
entities.longBio: The chief of the apsaras, born — the name is read this way — from the thigh of the sage Narayana, produced to shame Indra's dancers with something better. She lived with Pururavas under conditions and left the moment one was broken. Her other great appearance is in the Mahabharata: sent to Arjuna in Indra's heaven, she is refused on the grounds that she is an ancestress of his line, and curses him to live as a eunuch — a curse Indra reduces to a single year, which Arjuna then spends usefully in hiding as the dance teacher Brihannala.
entities.variantTraditions: The Rig Veda already knows her and Pururavas; the Arjuna episode is Mahabharata material and much later.

entities.name: Ayu
entities.role: The generation between Pururavas and Nahusha, and almost nothing else
entities.abode: Pratishthana
entities.bio: A name in the list, and honestly not much more than that.
entities.longBio: Son of Pururavas and Urvashi, father of Nahusha, and a king of the Lunar dynasty in every genealogy that records the line. Beyond the succession he carries almost no narrative: no test, no curse, no quarrel worth preserving. He is included here because leaving him out would put a false gap between Pururavas and Nahusha, and the Puranic king lists are one of the few places where Indian tradition is scrupulous about generations. Some figures in a genealogy are load-bearing and some are simply the next name, and the honest thing is to say which is which.
entities.variantTraditions: The Puranas agree on his position in the line and disagree on the number and names of his brothers.

entities.name: Nahusha
entities.role: Promoted to king of heaven, and demoted to a python for asking Indra's wife to sleep with him
entities.abode: Svarga, then a forest in the Himalaya, as a snake
entities.bio: He got Indra's throne, Indra's honours, and then asked for Indra's wife. The sages were carrying his chair at the time.
entities.longBio: When Indra fled and hid after the killing of Vritra, heaven needed a king and Nahusha was raised to the throne. It went to his head within a reign. He demanded Shachi, Indra's queen; she stalled by insisting she be fetched in a palanquin carried by brahmin sages. He agreed to that too, and when the sage Agastya moved too slowly under the pole, Nahusha kicked him — and was cursed on the spot to crawl as a python. He lay in the forest for an age until Yudhishthira, wandering in exile, answered his questions on dharma correctly and released him.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahabharata tells the fall and the release; the Puranas add the detail of the word sarpa, which Nahusha used carelessly and which became the form of his punishment.

entities.name: Yayati
entities.role: Cursed with instant old age, he borrowed his son's youth for a thousand years and learned nothing until the end of it
symbols: the chariot of a thousand years
entities.abode: Pratishthana
entities.bio: Desire is not put out by indulgence. It took him a thousand extra years to work that out.
entities.longBio: Son of Nahusha. He married Devayani, daughter of Shukra, and took her servant Sharmishtha as well; when Shukra found out he cursed Yayati into immediate old age. Yayati asked each of his five sons to take the curse and give him their youth. Only the youngest, Puru, agreed. Yayati then spent a thousand years in every pleasure available to a king, and at the end of it concluded that desire is never extinguished by feeding it, but grows like fire fed with butter. He returned the years to Puru, gave him the kingdom over his elder brothers, and went to the forest.
entities.variantTraditions: His verse on desire — that it is never quieted by enjoyment — is quoted independently of the story throughout later Sanskrit literature.

entities.name: Puru
entities.role: The youngest son, the only one who agreed to grow old for his father, and the one who got the kingdom
symbols: the throne given out of turn
entities.abode: Pratishthana
entities.bio: Four brothers said no. He said yes, and inherited everything for it.
entities.longBio: Youngest son of Yayati and Sharmishtha. When his father, cursed to sudden old age, asked his sons to trade youth for decrepitude, the four elder refused and were disinherited on the spot. Puru accepted, aged a thousand years in his father's place, and had them all returned to him at the end with the throne on top. From him descend the Pauravas, and from the Pauravas the Kurus, and from the Kurus both sides of the war at Kurukshetra — so every figure in the Mahabharata sits downstream of one son's answer to an unreasonable question.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahabharata opens with this genealogy precisely to establish that the Pandavas and Kauravas share it.

entities.name: Dushyanta
entities.role: Married her in the forest, forgot her completely, and remembered when a fisherman found the ring
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.bio: The ring came off in the river. Everything went wrong from there.
entities.longBio: A king of the Paurava line who, hunting near Kanva's hermitage, met and married Shakuntala by gandharva rite — consent alone, no witnesses — and left her his signet ring before returning to the capital. In the Mahabharata he simply denies her when she arrives pregnant, and yields only when a voice from the sky confirms the child. Kalidasa, rewriting it, could not accept a hero behaving that way and added a curse: the ring slips off in a river, the memory goes with it, and a fisherman finds it inside a carp years later. Their son was Bharata.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahabharata version has no curse and no ring — Dushyanta's denial is deliberate. The exculpating curse is Kalidasa's invention.

entities.name: Shakuntala
entities.role: Abandoned as a baby to birds, abandoned again by a husband who claimed not to know her
symbols: the shakunta birds that sheltered her
entities.abode: The hermitage of Kanva, and afterwards Hastinapura
entities.bio: Her mother was an apsara sent to ruin her father's austerities. Both of them left her in the forest.
entities.longBio: Vishvamitra's penance alarmed the gods, who sent the apsara Menaka to break it. It worked; the child was left behind when both parents moved on, sheltered by shakunta birds until the sage Kanva took her in. She grew up in his hermitage, married Dushyanta there, and went to his court pregnant to be told he had never seen her before. In the Mahabharata she answers him with one of the fiercest speeches in the epic and wins on argument. Kalidasa's play, the most famous drama in Sanskrit, softens the confrontation into a curse and a lost ring.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahabharata Shakuntala argues and prevails; Kalidasa's is gentler and is rescued rather than victorious. They are two quite different characters.

entities.name: Bharata (the emperor)
entities.role: The boy who prised open lion cubs' mouths to count their teeth — and the man India is named after
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.bio: The Republic of India is named for a child who used to count lions' teeth for fun.
entities.longBio: Son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala, raised in the forest at Kanva's hermitage, where the standing image of him is a small boy forcing open the jaws of lion cubs to count their teeth — which is how the court recognises him. He became a chakravartin, a wheel-turning universal sovereign, and the land was named Bharatavarsha after him; the Republic of India still carries the name officially as Bharat. He is also remembered for passing over his own sons in favour of an adopted heir he judged more capable, which the Puranas record approvingly and without much elaboration.
entities.variantTraditions: Distinct from Bharata the brother of Rama, who is a Solar-dynasty figure in the Ramayana and appears separately in this pack.

entities.name: Kuru
entities.role: He ploughed a field for so long that the gods made it the place where dharma is decided
entities.abode: Hastinapura, and the field that carries his name
entities.bio: Kurukshetra is called that because he would not stop ploughing it.
entities.longBio: A descendant of Puru and the ancestor from whom the Kurus take their name — which makes him the common forefather of the Pandavas and the Kauravas both. His one story is agricultural and strange: he ploughed the plain of Kurukshetra with a golden plough for years on end as an act of austerity, refusing to stop, until Indra asked what he wanted and granted that whoever died there would go to heaven regardless of their deeds. The Bhagavad Gita opens by calling the place dharmakshetra, the field of dharma. This is why.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahabharata gives the ploughing story briefly; later Puranas expand the boon and disagree on its exact terms.

entities.name: Manu
entities.role: The one man the flood was allowed to keep, because he was decent to a fish
epithets: Vaivasvata Manu — son of the sun
symbols: the boat tied to the fish's horn
the seeds and the seven sages
entities.abode: Mount Himavat, where the boat came to rest
entities.bio: A fish in his cupped hands asked not to be thrown back, and kept asking for a bigger vessel.
entities.longBio: Washing at the river, Manu caught a small fish that begged not to be returned to the water where larger fish would eat it. He kept it in a jar; it outgrew the jar, then the tank, then the river, and by the time he released it into the sea it was Matsya, Vishnu's first avatar, who told him a flood was coming and to build a boat. Manu loaded it with the seven sages and the seeds of every plant, tied it to the fish's horn, and was towed to the northern mountain. Humanity descends from him, and his sons Ikshvaku and Ila begin the Solar and Lunar lines.
entities.variantTraditions: The Shatapatha Brahmana version is the oldest and has no Vishnu in it at all — the fish is simply a fish. The identification with Matsya is Puranic.

entities.name: Ikshvaku
entities.role: The eldest son of Manu, and the root of the dynasty that produced Rama
entities.abode: Ayodhya
entities.bio: Every Solar-dynasty king in the Ramayana is counted from him, including Rama.
entities.longBio: The eldest of Manu's sons and the first king of Ayodhya, from whom the Suryavamsha — the Solar dynasty — takes its formal name, Ikshvaku-kula. The line runs from him through Harishchandra, Sagara, Bhagiratha and Raghu down to Dasharatha and Rama, and the Ramayana recites the descent whenever it wants to establish that Rama's claim is older than any argument about it. Jain and Buddhist tradition both claim the same lineage: the Buddha is described as an Ikshvaku by clan, and several Jain tirthankaras are placed in the line as well.
entities.variantTraditions: The Puranic king lists for the Ikshvakus run to a hundred names and disagree with one another after the first dozen.

entities.name: Harishchandra
entities.role: Sold his kingdom, then his wife and son, then himself — rather than break one promise
epithets: the king who worked the burning ground
entities.abode: Ayodhya, and then the burning ghats of Kashi
entities.bio: He would not lie, so he ended up charging his own wife a fee to cremate their son.
entities.longBio: A Solar-dynasty king whose byword is truthfulness, tested by Vishvamitra past the point of cruelty. Having promised the sage his kingdom, he gave it, and was then told a promise of gold remained outstanding. He sold his wife Shaibya and his son Rohitashva into service, then sold himself to an outcaste keeper of the cremation ground. The story reaches its point when his wife arrives carrying their dead son and he cannot let the body burn without the fee, because that is his master's due. He holds; the gods stop it there and restore everything.
entities.variantTraditions: The Markandeya Purana and the Aitareya Brahmana tell substantially different versions; the harrowing cremation-ground scene is the Puranic one and is what later drama and film use.

entities.name: Sagara
entities.role: His sixty thousand sons dug up the whole earth looking for a horse and were burned to ash for it
entities.abode: Ayodhya
entities.bio: The ocean is called sagara after him, because his sons are the ones who dug the hole.
entities.longBio: Sagara set a horse loose for the ashvamedha and Indra, not wanting the sacrifice completed, hid it in the hermitage of the sage Kapila deep underground. Sagara's sixty thousand sons excavated the earth to find it — which is how the ocean basin was made, and why the sea is sagara — and on finding the horse beside the meditating Kapila accused him of theft. He opened his eyes and they were burnt to ash where they stood. The ash could not receive funeral rites without the waters of the Ganges, which were still in heaven, and so the problem passed down four generations.
entities.variantTraditions: The Ramayana and the Vishnu Purana agree on the outline; the number sixty thousand is constant, which is unusual for Puranic figures.

entities.name: Bhagiratha
entities.role: Stood on one leg for a thousand years to bring a river down out of the sky for ancestors he never met
entities.abode: Ayodhya, and the bank of the river he brought down
entities.bio: Bhagirath prayatna — a Bhagiratha effort — is still ordinary Hindi for a superhuman undertaking.
entities.longBio: Sagara's sixty thousand sons lay as ash that could not be released without the waters of the Ganges, and Ganga was in heaven. Two generations tried and failed. Bhagiratha gave up the throne and performed austerities until Brahma agreed to release her — and then had to petition again, because the fall would have split the earth, until Shiva consented to take the impact on his head and let her out slowly through his hair. Bhagiratha then walked ahead of the river the whole way to the sea so she would follow, and the ashes were finally watered. The Ganges is still called Bhagirathi in her upper course.
entities.variantTraditions: The Ramayana, Mahabharata and Bhagavata all carry the descent; they differ over how many ancestors attempted it before him.

entities.name: Raghu
entities.role: So generous he gave away his own treasury and then went to war with a god to refill it
domains: generosity past the point of sense
entities.abode: Ayodhya
entities.bio: Rama's patronymic is Raghava. This is the Raghu it points at.
entities.longBio: A Solar-dynasty king of Ayodhya, great-grandfather of Rama, and the one the dynasty is usually named after in poetry — Raghuvamsha, the line of Raghu, which is also the title of Kalidasa's great dynastic epic. He is remembered for a conquest of the four quarters and, more characteristically, for giving away everything he owned after a sacrifice, leaving nothing for a student who then came asking for his teacher's fee. Rather than refuse, Raghu prepared to attack Kubera's treasury; Kubera, hearing of it, rained gold on the city instead. Rama is called Raghava after him.
entities.variantTraditions: Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha is the fullest treatment and is a literary work of the fifth century, not a Purana.

entities.name: Marichi
entities.role: Brahma's mind-born son, and the grandfather of essentially everything alive
symbols: the ray of light his name means
entities.abode: Brahmaloka, and the Great Bear
entities.bio: Almost every deva, asura, naga and beast in this pack descends from his son.
entities.longBio: One of the mind-born sons of Brahma and among the first of the Prajapatis, the progenitors. His importance is almost entirely genealogical: his son is Kashyapa, and Kashyapa by his thirteen wives fathers the devas, the asuras, the nagas, the garudas and most of the animal world, so the traffic of the entire pantheon passes through Marichi's household in two generations. He is counted among the Saptarishi, the seven sages fixed in the stars of the Great Bear, and named in the standard invocation lists, but he does very little in his own right.
entities.variantTraditions: The lists of Brahma's mind-born sons vary between seven, nine and ten depending on the Purana; Marichi is in all of them.

entities.name: Angiras
entities.role: Born from Brahma's own fire, and the father of the teacher of the gods
entities.abode: Brahmaloka, and the Great Bear
entities.bio: Brihaspati, the guru of all the gods, had to get it from somewhere.
entities.longBio: One of Brahma's mind-born sons, so closely associated with fire that several texts have him born from a coal or from the flame of the first sacrifice, and the Rig Veda sometimes treats the Angirasas as a whole class of fire-priests rather than one man. He is the father of Brihaspati, preceptor of the devas, which places him at the head of the priestly line the way Marichi stands at the head of the creaturely one. Much of the Atharvaveda is attributed to him and his descendants, and the text is still sometimes called the Atharvangirasa for that reason.
entities.variantTraditions: The Rig Veda uses Angiras both for an individual sage and for a group of semi-divine fire-priests, and does not always distinguish them.

entities.name: Atri
entities.role: The moon was born out of his eyes after he held a posture for a hundred years
domains: the fifth mandala of the Rig Veda
symbols: the drop of light from the eye
entities.abode: Brahmaloka, the Great Bear, and a hermitage in the forest
entities.bio: Chandra the moon has a father, and this is him.
entities.longBio: One of the Saptarishi and a mind-born son of Brahma, to whom the fifth mandala of the Rig Veda is attributed. The Puranas say he stood in austerity so long that a light gathered in his eyes and fell as a drop, and the ten directions bore it, and the child was Soma — Chandra, the moon. His wife Anasuya is one of the standard exemplars of a faithful wife and is credited with reducing the Trimurti themselves to infants when they came to test her. Their sons in the fuller lists are Chandra, the irascible Durvasa and Dattatreya.
entities.variantTraditions: The Puranas disagree over which of the three sons belongs to which of the Trimurti in the Anasuya episode.

entities.name: Bharadvaja
entities.role: A Saptarishi whose son was born in a pot and grew up to teach both sides of the war
entities.abode: A hermitage at the confluence at Prayaga, and the Great Bear
entities.bio: Drona's name means vessel, because that is literally what he was carried in.
entities.longBio: One of the Saptarishi and the seer to whom the sixth mandala of the Rig Veda is attributed. He kept a hermitage at Prayaga, where the Ramayana has Rama stop on the way into exile. His importance to this pack is his son: seeing the apsara Ghritachi, he spilled his seed and caught it in a drona, a wooden trough, and the child born from it was Drona — the archery master who trains the Pandavas and the Kauravas together and then has to command against half of his own students. Bharadvaja is also named in the medical tradition as the one who brought Ayurveda from Indra.
entities.variantTraditions: The Rig Vedic Bharadvaja and the Mahabharata's father of Drona are treated as one figure by tradition and as probably distinct by philology.

entities.name: Gautama Maharishi
entities.role: Came home, saw what Indra had done, and turned his own wife to stone for it
symbols: the cock that crowed too early
entities.abode: A hermitage on the road to Mithila, and the Great Bear
entities.bio: Indra imitated his voice to get him out of the house. The punishment landed on everyone.
entities.longBio: One of the Saptarishi, husband of Ahalya. Indra, wanting Ahalya, crowed like a cock before dawn so that Gautama would leave for his morning ablutions, then took the sage's form and went in. Gautama returned too early and understood at once. He cursed Indra — in the older tellings with a thousand marks on his body, later softened to a thousand eyes — and cursed Ahalya to lie invisible, or in the popular version as a stone, until Rama should pass that way. The severity of what he does to a woman he knows was deceived is not defended by the texts; it is simply recorded.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Ahalya knew it was Indra differs by text — the Ramayana implies she did and Gautama's curse follows from that; most later retellings make her wholly deceived.

entities.name: Jamadagni
entities.role: Ordered his sons to behead their mother, and only the youngest picked up the axe
entities.abode: A hermitage in the forest
entities.bio: He asked four sons to kill their mother. Three refused and were burnt for it.
entities.longBio: A Saptarishi of the Bhrigu line, married to Renuka, and the owner of Kamadhenu the wish-granting cow — which is what gets him killed. When Renuka's absolute mental fidelity lapsed for a moment, he ordered each son in turn to behead her; the four eldest refused and he reduced them to ash, and the fifth, Parashurama, did it, and was granted a boon with which he asked for his mother's life and his brothers'. Later the sons of King Kartavirya Arjuna came for the cow and killed Jamadagni for it, and Parashurama's twenty-one campaigns against the kshatriyas follow directly from that.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahabharata and the Bhagavata both carry the beheading; neither offers any comment on it, which is itself notable.

entities.name: Ahalya
entities.role: Made by Brahma as the most beautiful woman alive, and left as a stone at the side of a road
entities.abode: Gautama's abandoned hermitage, on the road to Mithila
entities.bio: Rama's first act on the road to his wedding is stepping on her.
entities.longBio: Brahma made her the most beautiful woman in creation and gave her to the sage Gautama. Indra wanted her, imitated Gautama's voice to empty the house before dawn, took his form and went in. Gautama returned early, cursed Indra, and cursed Ahalya to lie unseen — or, in the version everyone now knows, as a stone — until Rama came past. He does, on the road to Mithila and his marriage to Sita; the dust of his foot restores her, and she walks out of the story without saying much. She is counted among the panchakanya, the five women recited daily to dispel sin.
entities.variantTraditions: The Ramayana suggests she recognised Indra and consented; every major later retelling removes that and makes her purely deceived. The change is the most-argued single edit in the epic's reception.

entities.name: Renuka
entities.role: Beheaded by her own son on her husband's orders, and restored by the same son an hour later
entities.abode: Jamadagni's hermitage; and a great many village shrines
entities.bio: Her chastity was so exact she could carry water in an unfired pot. One stray thought and the pot dissolved.
entities.longBio: Renuka's discipline was such that she could shape a pot from wet river clay each morning and carry water home in it unfired. One morning she saw a gandharva king reflected in the water, admired him for a moment, and the pot fell apart in her hands. Jamadagni knew immediately and ordered his sons to behead her; only Parashurama obeyed, and then used the boon he was offered to ask for her life back. She is worshipped across the Deccan in her own right as Yellamma or Renuka Devi, quite independently of the story, and her temples are among the busiest village shrines in Karnataka and Maharashtra.
entities.variantTraditions: The southern goddess Yellamma and the Puranic Renuka were probably distinct and were identified with each other later; the head-and-body transposition legends belong to the goddess tradition.

entities.name: Nirriti
entities.role: The goddess of everything going wrong, and the only direction-guardian nobody wants to face
epithets: the one asked only to leave
entities.mount: An ass, or a corpse
entities.abode: The southwest quarter, and the ground where things rot
entities.bio: Every hymn to her is a request that she go somewhere else.
entities.longBio: One of the eight Dikpala, the guardians of the directions, holding the southwest — and the only one of them who is a personification of things going badly. The Rig Veda addresses her a handful of times and never in praise: the hymns ask her to pass by, to take her bonds elsewhere, to accept an offering at a distance and leave. She is dissolution, decay, misfortune and the disintegration of things that were whole. Later texts sometimes make her male, a rakshasa rather than a goddess, and the Puranas tend to quietly replace her in the Dikpala list with Rakshasa or Nairrita.
entities.variantTraditions: Her sex changes between the Vedic and Puranic material; the Vedic Nirriti is unambiguously a goddess.

entities.name: Ishana
entities.role: Shiva's fifth face, the one that points straight up, guarding the corner where temples put their shrines
entities.mount: Nandi the bull
entities.abode: The northeast quarter, and the summit of Kailasa
entities.bio: Four faces look at the horizon. The fifth looks up, and that one is him.
entities.longBio: Ishana is the fifth and uppermost of the Panchabrahma, the five faces of Shiva — Sadyojata, Vamadeva, Aghora, Tatpurusha and Ishana — and the one that faces the sky rather than a compass point. As a Dikpala he holds the northeast, the quarter traditionally treated as the most auspicious in a building: the household shrine goes in the northeast corner, and so does the temple's own. He is a form of Shiva rather than a separate deity, which is why he is easy to miss in a list of eight guardians who are otherwise distinct gods.
entities.variantTraditions: Because he is an aspect of Shiva rather than an independent god, some Dikpala lists give the northeast to Shiva directly and drop the name.

entities.name: Yashodhara
entities.role: Woke up to find her husband had left in the night to solve the problem of suffering
domains: renunciation, from the side of the person left behind
entities.abode: Kapilavastu, and afterwards the order of nuns
entities.bio: He left without waking her. She cut her own hair, ate one meal a day, and waited.
entities.longBio: Wife of Siddhartha Gautama and mother of his son. On the night he left the palace he looked in at them both and did not wake her, and she woke to an empty room. The accounts say she took on his austerities from a distance — one meal a day, plain robes, no ornament — for the years he was gone. When he returned to Kapilavastu as the Buddha she sent their son to ask for his inheritance. She later joined the order of nuns and is recorded as attaining arhatship. She belongs to Buddhist tradition and is included here only because the Puranas make the Buddha an avatar of Vishnu without ever mentioning that he had a family.
entities.variantTraditions: Yashodhara is a Buddhist figure, drawn here from the Buddhacarita and the Pali tradition, not from the Puranas. The Puranic Buddha-as-avatar is a polemical construction with no household at all.

entities.name: Rahula
entities.role: His father named him Fetter, then left, then came back and ordained him at seven
entities.abode: Kapilavastu, and then the order
entities.bio: Told to ask his father for his inheritance, he was given a begging bowl.
entities.longBio: Born to Siddhartha and Yashodhara on or near the night his father left the palace, and named Rahula — fetter, an obstacle — which tells you plainly what his father thought a son was at that moment. Seven years later the Buddha returned to Kapilavastu and Yashodhara sent the boy out to ask for his inheritance. He was given ordination instead, becoming the first samanera, the first novice in the order, and the tradition records that his grandfather Suddhodana was upset enough about it that the rule requiring parental consent for a child's ordination was made on the spot.
entities.variantTraditions: Rahula is a Buddhist figure from the Pali tradition and the Buddhacarita, included here for the same reason as Yashodhara — the Puranic Buddha avatar has no family attached to it.

entities.name: Vidura
entities.role: The wisest man at Hastinapura, and the one nobody had to listen to because his mother was a maid
symbols: the letter of warning in code
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.bio: He was right about everything and outranked by everyone, because of who his mother was.
entities.longBio: Vyasa fathered three sons on the widowed queens and their maid: Dhritarashtra born blind, Pandu born pale, and Vidura born to the servant and therefore born out of the succession. He is Dharma himself incarnate, serves as counsellor at Hastinapura, and is right at every turn - he warns the Pandavas about the lacquer house in coded speech so the messenger cannot repeat it, argues against the dice game, and tells Dhritarashtra plainly that his son will destroy the family. Nobody with power ever acts on it. He is the epic's standing demonstration that being correct is not the same as being heard.
entities.variantTraditions: His identification with Dharma is a Puranic overlay; the Mahabharata itself is mostly content to make him simply the clever one.

entities.name: Ashvatthama
entities.role: Cut down the sleeping camp after the war was over, and was cursed to wander for three thousand years
symbols: the gem set in his forehead
the sword taken up at night
entities.abode: The battlefield, and afterwards nowhere
entities.bio: The war was decided. He went into the camp at night anyway and killed everyone asleep in it.
entities.longBio: Drona's son, born with a gem in his forehead that kept him safe from hunger and disease, and told at the war's end that his father was dead by a lie the Pandavas had arranged. On the last night, with the fighting finished, he entered the sleeping camp and killed Dhrishtadyumna, the five sons of Draupadi and everyone else he found, then loosed a brahmastra at Uttara's unborn child. Krishna's curse on him is the heaviest in the epic: the gem is torn from his head and he is left to wander for three thousand years, wounded and alone, unable to die.
entities.variantTraditions: He is one of the chiranjivi, the deathless, and there are places in India where he is still said to be seen.

entities.name: Kripa
entities.role: Found abandoned in a clump of reeds, and still alive at the end of everything
symbols: the reeds he was found in
entities.abode: Hastinapura
entities.bio: He taught both sets of princes before Drona did, and outlived nearly all of them.
entities.longBio: Kripa and his twin sister Kripi were abandoned as infants in a clump of grass and taken in by King Shantanu, who named them for the pity he felt - kripa. He became the first archery teacher of the Kuru princes, before Drona arrived and took over, and his sister married Drona, which makes Ashvatthama his nephew. He fought for the Kauravas out of obligation rather than conviction and survived the war, one of only three on that side to do so. He is counted among the chiranjivi, the immortals, and the epic leaves him teaching the next generation.
entities.variantTraditions: The Mahabharata keeps him consistently sympathetic despite his side, which is rare among the Kaurava commanders.

entities.name: Mandodari
entities.role: Ravana's queen, who told him to give Sita back and was right for ten years
entities.abode: Lanka
entities.bio: She spent the whole war telling her husband he was going to lose it.
entities.longBio: Daughter of the asura architect Maya and chief queen of Ravana, Mandodari is the voice of sense in Lanka and is ignored as completely as Vibhishana is.
