She tells Ravana repeatedly to return Sita, points out what Rama has already destroyed, and keeps telling him after there is nothing left to save. Her lament over his body at the end of the Yuddha Kanda is one of the most sustained speeches given to a woman in the epic. She is counted among the panchakanya, the five women named in the daily prayer said to dispel sin, alongside Ahalya, Draupadi, Tara and Kunti.
entities.variantTraditions: Some southern and Jain versions make her the true mother of Sita, which turns the whole war into a family matter.

entities.name: Maricha
entities.role: Turned himself into a golden deer because he was more frightened of Ravana than of Rama
symbols: the golden deer with silver spots
the voice that cried out in Rama's
entities.abode: A hermitage in the forest, and then the clearing at Panchavati
entities.bio: He had already been shot by Rama once. He knew exactly how it would end.
entities.longBio: Maricha had met Rama before - flung into the sea by one of his arrows years earlier - and had retired to the forest to live as an ascetic precisely to stay out of his way. When Ravana ordered him to become the golden deer that would draw Rama away from Sita, he refused, argued, explained that it would kill him, and was told he would die either way. So he did it: a deer of gold with silver spots that Sita wanted, and when Rama's arrow found him he cried out in Rama's own voice for Lakshmana, which emptied the hut. The whole abduction turns on him.
entities.variantTraditions: The Ramayana gives him an unusual amount of interiority for a demon, and lets him be right about everything.

entities.name: Angada
entities.role: Son of the monkey king Rama killed, sent as ambassador to the enemy
symbols: the planted foot no one could lift
entities.abode: Kishkindha, and the war camp before Lanka
entities.bio: He planted his foot in Ravana's hall and told the court to move it if they could.
entities.longBio: Angada is the son of Vali, the vanara king Rama shot from cover, and he serves Rama anyway - which the Ramayana notes and does not soften. He leads one of the search parties for Sita, and is sent into Lanka as ambassador, where he plants his foot on the floor of Ravana's hall and invites anyone present to shift it. Nobody can, including Ravana's son. It is a piece of theatre rather than diplomacy and it is meant to be: the point is to show the court what is coming. He fights through the war and is made heir at the end.
entities.variantTraditions: His acceptance of Sugriva and Rama after his father's death is handled briefly in the text and has been the subject of a great deal of later commentary.

entities.name: Chyavana
entities.role: Buried in an anthill for so long that a princess mistook his eyes for glow-worms and poked them
domains: the Ashvins' share of the sacrifice
entities.abode: A hermitage beside a lake
entities.bio: Sukanya put a thorn in each of his eyes on a dare, and had to marry him for it.
entities.longBio: Chyavana, son of Bhrigu, meditated in one place so long that an anthill grew over him with only his eyes showing. King Saryati's daughter Sukanya, out walking, took them for something glittering and pushed a thorn into each, blinding him; the sage's anger stopped the kingdom's bodily functions until her father gave her to him in marriage. She kept faith with a blind old husband, and the Ashvins - divine physicians barred from the soma sacrifice - offered a trade: they would restore his youth if he got them a share. He did, over Indra's furious objection, and the Ashvins have drunk soma ever since.
entities.variantTraditions: The story appears in the Shatapatha Brahmana long before the Mahabharata, which is unusual and makes it one of the older narratives in the corpus.

profile.cosmicNature: Cyclical and immense. The world is made, kept and dissolved over and over: one day of Brahma lasts a thousand cycles of the four ages, and the tenth avatar closes the Kali Yuga only so that a new Satya Yuga can begin. Time is a wheel, not a line, and no ending is final.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Non-dual and polymorphic. Brahman, the formless supreme reality, is described only by negation, and every named deity is understood as a face it wears. Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions each identify that reality with their own supreme god, so the crowded pantheon resolves into one ground of being seen from different angles.
profile.afterlife: Governed by karma and rebirth rather than a single verdict. Yama, the first mortal to die, judges what a life earned and assigns the next birth or realm; release from the round of rebirth, not a better seat within it, is the goal the philosophical texts point to.
profile.systemMechanism: Rooted in Brahman as unmanifest supreme consciousness. The ultimate power manifests as three cosmic functions - creation, preservation and dissolution - sustained by the feminine energy of Shakti, supported by devas who govern the elements and uphold dharma, and repaired at intervals by the descents of Vishnu when that order slips.
profile.canonTexts: The Vedas and Upanishads, the two epics (Ramayana and Mahabharata, the latter carrying the Bhagavad Gita), and the Puranas, which supply most of the narrative pantheon as it is known today.

hierarchy.title: Transcendent Source
hierarchy.blurb: The unmanifest supreme reality, and the supreme feminine power through which it acts. Neither has genealogy; every later figure is a face this level wears.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Manifests as the three cosmic functions

hierarchy.title: The Trimurti — Cosmic Functions
hierarchy.blurb: Creation, preservation and dissolution held as three offices rather than three rival kings. Each governs one movement of a universe that is made, kept and unmade in cycles.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Dynamic feminine energy (Shakti) sustains cosmic equilibrium

hierarchy.title: The Tridevi — Cosmic Feminine Energies
hierarchy.blurb: Knowledge, fortune and power as the active energies without which the three functions are inert. Each is named as the consort of a member of the Trimurti and worshipped in her own right.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Devas govern the elements and uphold dharma

hierarchy.title: Celestial Devas & Guardians
hierarchy.blurb: The gods of the elements and of moral order: storm and rain, fire, the cosmic waters, wind, the sun, and the judgment that waits at the end of a life.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Vishnu descends across the ages to restore dharma

hierarchy.title: The Dashavatara — Descents of Vishnu
hierarchy.blurb: Ten descents in which the Preserver enters the world to restore an order that has slipped, running from the fish of the flood to the rider still in the future.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Sages transmit it, heroes enact it, asuras oppose it

hierarchy.title: The Two Dynasties — Solar and Lunar
hierarchy.blurb: Every mortal king in this pack belongs to one of two lines, and both start with Manu. The Solar line runs through Ikshvaku to Rama; the Lunar line runs through Budha to the field at Kurukshetra. The Ramayana is the first line's story and the Mahabharata is the second's.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: And from the two dynasties, the two epics

hierarchy.title: Sages, Heroes & Adversaries
hierarchy.blurb: The human and near-human level where the epics happen: the seers who carry the texts, the champions who fight in them, and the asura kings whose opposition gives the stories their shape.
